      points to a StudyGroup object that describes characteristics of the population
      that the frequency data was generated from (e.g. 'East Asian', 'Female').
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - StudyResult
    range: StudyGroup
    required: false
    multivalued: false
  is_about:
    name: is_about
    description: An entity or concept in the world that the information entity describes/is
      about.
    comments:
    - e.g. In the context of a Statement object, this attribute may be used to indicate
      entities/concepts it is about, in lieu of providing a more precise description
      of what the Statement asserts to be true using subject, predicate, object, and
      qualifier properties. e.g. the Statement that "BRCA2 c.8023A>G is pathogenic
      for Breast Cancer" might be annotated to be about the variant 'BRCA2 c.8023A>G',
      and the disease 'Breast Cancer'.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Informative
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - InformationEntity
    range: string
    required: false
    multivalued: true
  contributions:
    name: contributions
    description: Specific actions taken by an Agent toward the creation, modification,
      validation, or deprecation of an Information Entity.
    comments:
    - This attribute holds one or more Contribution objects, which provide structured
      descriptions of a contribution made to the Information Entity by a particular
      agent.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - InformationEntity
    - RecordMetadata
    range: Contribution
    required: false
    multivalued: true
  date_authored:
    name: date_authored
    description: Indicates when the information content expressed in the Information
      Entity was generated.
    comments:
    - The term 'authored' as used in the model refers to the generation of 'information
      content' in the abstract  sense, as opposed to a concrete encoding of this information
      in a specific language or format. e.g. for a Statement, this attribute captures
      when the information content expressed in the Statement was first generated
      by an agent.  Information about when a particular concrete encoding of this
      information was created (e.g. as row in a table, or object in a json document)
      would live in a RecordMetadata object attached to the Information Entity).
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - InformationEntity
    range: string
    required: false
    multivalued: false
  specified_by:
    name: specified_by
    description: A specification that describes all or part of the process that led
      to creation of the Information Entity.
    comments:
    - Examples - an experimental protocol or data analysis specification that describe
      how data were generated, or an evidence interpretation guideline that describes
      steps taken to interpret data in making a variant pathogenicity classification.
    - Note that this attribute captures specific *instances* of specifications/methods
      (e.g. the specific electron microscopy method described in https://doi.org/10.1002/
      cpz1.1045) - as opposed to reporting a *type* of method applied (e.g. "Transmission
      Electron Microscopy").
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - InformationEntity
    - Activity
    range: string
    required: false
    multivalued: true
  supporting_methods:
    name: supporting_methods
    description: Specific methods that were executed to directly or indirectly support
      creation of the Information Entity.
    comments:
    - These may include methods that directly produced the Information Entity, or
      upstream/accessory methods that indirectly support creation of the Information
      Entity - e.g. methods used to produce data that was interpreted as evidence
      to generate a Statement of knowledge.
    - This field captures terms representing specific INSTANCES of methods applied,
      vs the 'supporting_method_types' attribute which captures TYPES of methods used.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Informative
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - InformationEntity
    range: string
    required: false
    multivalued: true
  supporting_method_types:
    name: supporting_method_types
    description: Types of methodological approaches that were executed to directly
      or indirectly support creation of the Information Entity.
    comments:
    - This field captures terms representing TYPES of methods applied, vs the 'specified_by'
      or'supporting_methods' attributes which capture specific INSTANCES of methods
      used. These may include types of methods that directly produced the Information
      Entity, or upstream/accessory methods that indirectly support creation of the
      Information Entity
    - Implementers should define a relevant source or set of method type codes/terms
      to use here, based on the needs of the domain or application.'
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Informative
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - InformationEntity
    range: Coding
    required: false
    multivalued: true
  derived_from:
    name: derived_from
    description: Another Information Entity from which this Information Entity is
      derived, in whole or in part.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - InformationEntity
    range: InformationEntity
    required: false
    multivalued: true
  reported_in:
    name: reported_in
    description: A document in which the Information Entity is reported.
    comments:
    - This attribute is used specifically to reference documents/publications where
      the Information Entity is expressed or reported.  For a Statement, this might
      be a publication where the authors express the statement in text. For a Data
      Item, this might be a publication with a table or figure that reports the value
      of the  data.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - InformationEntity
    range: string
    required: false
    multivalued: true
  sources:
    name: sources
    description: A document or other informtion resource in which the information
      entity, or evidence supporting it, is reported.
    comments:
    - This attribute is more general than InformationEntity.reported_in (which is
      used to references a Docuement that directly reports the infrormation), and
      Statement.has_evidence_from_sources (which is used to reference resources that
      provided evidence used to generate the knowledge expressed in a Statement).
      It can be used to cover both cases, in situations where a data provider does
      not know which is the case, or does not wish to make the distinction.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - InformationEntity
    range: string
    required: false
    multivalued: true
  information_quality:
    name: information_quality
    description: A qualitative term indicating the scientific rigor or reliability
      with which the information was generated/collected.
    comments:
    - This is typically based on the quality of design and execution of the study
      or curation activity that generated it (e.g. were relevant controls assessed
      to show instruments were working, were all samples taken care of and handled
      identically, are methods sound and well documented, etc.).
    - The quality of information is intrinsic to the information itself, and not to
      a particular application of the information (e.g. as evidence for making an
      Assertion)
    - The quality of information is one factor that goes into the confidence we have
      in the information''s veracity (i.e. that it is an accurate reflection of reality
      it intends to measure or describe). Other factors informing confidence may include
      who did it (we may just not trust some Agents), when (if data created 500 years
      ago, we may have less confidence in it), and for Assertions, the relevance and
      abundance of supporting evidence.
    - Implementers should define a relevant source of codes or terms to use here,
      based on the needs of the domain or application.'
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Informative
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - InformationEntity
    range: Coding
    required: false
    multivalued: false
  record_metadata:
    name: record_metadata
    description: Provenance metadata about a specific concrete record of information
      as encoded/serialized in a particular data set or object (as opposed to provenance
      about the abstract information content the encoding carries).
    comments:
    - This attribute holds a structured RecordMetadata objects, which can be used
      to capture when, how, and by whom a record serialization was generated or modified;
      what upstream resources it was derived or retrieved from; and record-level administrative
      information such as versioning and lifecycle status.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - InformationEntity
    range: RecordMetadata
    required: false
    multivalued: false
  id:
    name: id
    description: The 'logical' identifier of the entity in the system of record, e.g.
      a UUID.  This 'id' is unique within a given system, but may or may not be globally
      unique outside the system. It is used within a system to reference one object
      from another.
    comments:
    - Note that it is common for implementers to create their own internal logical
      ids - typically a serially or randomly generated value like a UUID that is assigned
      to the data object as it is created in a system. But an implementer may choose
      to reuse an existing, globally unique id from an external system or authority
      for this purpose (e.g. an HGNC id for a Gene object) - as long as it is unique
      within the implementing system, and can be used to reference the identified
      object in this context.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - Entity
    range: string
    required: true
    multivalued: false
  identifiers:
    name: identifiers
    description: A globally-unique 'business' identifier or accession number for the
      real-world entity represented by a data object. These are typically assigned
      by an external system or authority, and used to connect entities and share content
      across different systems.
    comments:
    - Preferred values for this attribute are CURIEs or URIs - so the system that
      provisioned the identifier is clear.
    - A given real world entity - e.g. a genetic variant - may have many business
      identifiers defined by different systems, which can be captured in the "identifiers"
      property to indicate that they represent the same thing.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Informative
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - Entity
    range: string
    required: false
    multivalued: true
  type:
    name: type
    description: The name of the class that is instantiated by a data object representing
      the Entity.
    comments:
    - MUST be the label of a concrete class from the data model.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - Entity
    range: string
    required: true
    multivalued: false
  label:
    name: label
    description: A primary name for the Entity.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - Entity
    - Coding
    range: string
    required: false
    multivalued: false
  alternative_labels:
    name: alternative_labels
    description: Alternative name(s) for the Entity.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - Entity
    range: string
    required: false
    multivalued: true
  description:
    name: description
    description: A free text description of the Entity.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - Entity
    range: string
    required: false
    multivalued: false
  extensions:
    name: extensions
    description: A list of extensions to the Entity, that allow for capture of information
      not directly supported by elements defined in the model.
    comments:
    - Extension objects have a key-value data structure that allows definition of
      custom fields in the data itself. Extensions are not expected to be natively
      understood, but may be used for pre-negotiated exchange of message attributes
      between systems.
    from_schema: https://w3id.org/sepio-model
    status: Draft
    rank: 1000
    owner: StudyResult
    domain_of:
    - Entity
    range: Extension
    required: false
    multivalued: true
</code></pre>

docs.title: Class: Utility
docs.text: An abstract organizational class that groups classes acting as complex datatypes in the model - providing reusable collections of fields that can be plugged into other objects to capture sets of related information.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• The Utility class itself is abstract and has no direct attributes. Implementers would always use one of its concrete subtypes with specifically defined fields (e.g. Coding, Expression, Extension).

URI: sepio_linkml:Utility

docs.title: Slot: confidence_interval
docs.text: A measure of the probability that a parameter of interest will fall within a defined range of values around a mean or other statistical calculation.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• Confidence intervals reflect the degree of uncertainty in a sampling method. They may be bounded on one or both sides, and are computed for a designated confidence level (most often 95% or 99%.. For example, a Hazard Ratio of 0.47 might have a 95% confidence interval between 0.42 and 0.55, with a p-value of = 0.001.
  • The DataItem used to represent a confidence interval will indicate what type of interval is reported (e.g. ''95% CI''), and will contain separate componentDataItems representing the upper and lower bounds of the interval (e.g. ''0.42'' and ''0.55'').'

docs.title: Slot: data_items
docs.text: One or more data items that are included in the StudyResult because it pertains to the 'focus' of the result. This can be data that directly describes this 'focus' (e.g. the population frequency of an allele focus), or be metadata about how data about the 'focus' were generated (e.g the quality measures for the sequencing run used to determine this allele frequency).

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• Any type of data item from a Study may be captured in a StudyResult - including raw experimental/observational data, derived calculations or quality measures, provenance information about how the data were generated in the study, or qualitative expert interpretations of the primary study data (e.g. the interpretation of a blood cholesterol value of 250 mg/dL as being 'high', or a Polyphen functional impact score of 0.115 as being 'deleterious').
  • The model specifies use of a key-value based 'DataItem' object to capture the meaning and value of each type of data item captured in a given StudyResult. But in practice, profiles for specific StudyResult types may choose to define one or more specializations of the generic 'data_items' property as named attributes. This makes the data more succinct and parsable, and allows specific constraints to be applied and validated for different data items. For example, a PopulaitonAlleleFrequencyStudyResult profile may define a named 'focusAlleleFrequency' attribute that is required, and a named 'focusAlleleCount' attribute that is optional - both of which conceptually specialize the core-im 'data_items' property. Under this approach, the core 'data_items' acts as a placeholder to seed such specializations, but is not used directly in StudyResult profiles.

docs.title: Slot: direction
docs.text: A term indicating whether the Statement supports, disputes, or remains neutral w.r.t. the validity of the Proposition it evaluates.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• Statements put forth a Proposition that expresses some possible fact about the world, and may provide an assessment of this proposition's validity (i.e. how likely it is to be true or false based on evaluated evidence). The semantics of the Proposition are captured in the 'subject', 'predicate', 'object', and optional 'qualifier' attributes. An assessment of the Proposition's validity can be captured using 'direction', 'strength', and 'score' attributes. The 'direction' attribute is used to indicate whether the Statement's Proposition is supported by the agent's assessment (when evidence favors its validity), is disputed by the agent's assessment (when evidence argues against its validity), or remains neutral (when conflicting or insufficient evidence exists to assert one direction or the other). (Enumerated values = 'supports', 'disputes', 'neutral').

docs.title: Slot: focus
docs.text: A specific subject or experimental unit in a Study, that data in the StudyResult object is about - e.g. a particular variant in a population allele frequency dataset like ExAC or gnomAD.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• The 'focus' of a StudyResult is the what anchors selection of all data items and provenance information that it contains. This focus may be a single participant or subject of a study (e.g. one patient in a clinical study, or one allele in a population frequency analysis). It may be a study group defined as an experimental unit in the study (e.g. a specific treatment arm of a clinical study). Or it may be a variable defined as a unit of analysis in the study (e.g. 'exposure to nicotine' in an analysis correlating this variable with clinical outcomes).

docs.title: Slot: has_evidence
docs.text: A piece of information that represents or contributes to an argument for or against the validity of the Proposition put forth in a Statement. This is a shortcut relation that links a Statement directly to a piece of evidence supporting it, bypassing the Evidence Line class when used data creators do not utilize an Evidence Line object.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• Evidence is any information that is interpreted in assessing the truth of the proposition a Statement puts forth as true or false. A piece of information only becomes evidence when it is interpreted in this way. Different types of information entities can be used and cited as evidence, including direct observation or measurement data, derived statistical calculations, data tables or figures in a publication, conclusions/findings from a particular study, or prior assertions of knowledge that themselves are based on their own set of evidence.
  • This is a shortcut relation that links a Statement directly to a piece of evidence supporting it, bypassing the Evidence Line class - to be used data creators cannot or do not wish to create an Evidence Line object.

docs.title: Slot: has_evidence_items
docs.text: An individual piece of information that was evaluated as evidence in building the argument represented by an Evidence Line.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• A given Evidence Line may be supported by one or many individual evidence items. What matters is that all evidence items in a given Evidence Line get collectively assessed and assigned direction and strength as a single argument for or against a target proposition.
  • Different types and scales of information entity can serve as evidence (experimental measurements or observations, data tables or figures, images, prior assertions, etc.) Only when assessed as evidence do we consider the information to be an 'Evidence Item'. For example, a piece of population frequency data about BRCA2 c.8023A>G becomes an Evidence Item when it is assessed for the support it may offer for a target proposition (e.g. the prospect of the variant’s pathogenicity).

docs.title: Slot: has_evidence_lines
docs.text: An evidence-based argument that supports or disputes the validity of the proposition that a Statement assesses or puts forth as true. The strength and direction of this argument (whether it supports or disputes the proposition, and how strongly) is based on an interpretation of one or more pieces of information as evidence (i.e. 'Evidence Items).

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• Evidence Lines result from the interpretation of one or more pieces of information to build an argument for or against a particular Proposition. These arguments have direction (supporting / disputing) and strength (e.g. strong, moderate, weak) relative to the Proposition they are evaluated against. For example, ExaC allele counts and frequency calculations for the BRCA2 c.8023A>G variant in different populations may be collectively assessed to provide an argument of 'moderate' strength in 'support of ' a proposition that the variant is pathogenicity for breast cancer.
  • Evidence Lines are useful in cases where a data provider wants to describe in detail how information was assessed as evidence to generate and score different arguments for or against a Statement''s proposition. Evidence Lines can be omitted if such information is not available or needed.

docs.title: Slot: id
docs.text: The 'logical' identifier of the entity in the system of record, e.g. a UUID. This 'id' is unique within a given system, but may or may not be globally unique outside the system. It is used within a system to reference one object from another.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• Note that it is common for implementers to create their own internal logical ids - typically a serially or randomly generated value like a UUID that is assigned to the data object as it is created in a system. But an implementer may choose to reuse an existing, globally unique id from an external system or authority for this purpose (e.g. an HGNC id for a Gene object) - as long as it is unique within the implementing system, and can be used to reference the identified object in this context.

docs.title: Slot: information_quality
docs.text: A qualitative term indicating the scientific rigor or reliability with which the information was generated/collected.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• This is typically based on the quality of design and execution of the study or curation activity that generated it (e.g. were relevant controls assessed to show instruments were working, were all samples taken care of and handled identically, are methods sound and well documented, etc.).
  • The quality of information is intrinsic to the information itself, and not to a particular application of the information (e.g. as evidence for making an Assertion)
  • The quality of information is one factor that goes into the confidence we have in the information''s veracity (i.e. that it is an accurate reflection of reality it intends to measure or describe). Other factors informing confidence may include who did it (we may just not trust some Agents), when (if data created 500 years ago, we may have less confidence in it), and for Assertions, the relevance and abundance of supporting evidence.
  • Implementers should define a relevant source of codes or terms to use here, based on the needs of the domain or application.'

docs.title: Slot: score
docs.text: A quantitative score that indicates the strength of a Proposition's validity assessment in the direction indicated (i.e. how strongly supported or disputed the Proposition is believed to be). Depending on its implementation, a score may reflect how confident that agent is that the Proposition is true or false, or the strength of evidence they believe supports or disputes it.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• Statements put forth a Proposition that expresses some possible fact about the world, and may provide an assessment of this proposition's validity (i.e. how likely it is to be true or false based on evaluated evidence). The semantics of the Proposition are captured in the 'subject', 'predicate', 'object', and optional 'qualifier' attributes. The assessment of the Proposition's validity are captured in 'direction', 'strength', and 'score' attributes. The 'score' attribute serves the same purpose as 'strength', but allows for a quantitative assessment based on a numerical score.

docs.title: Slot: strength
docs.text: A term used to report the strength of a Proposition's assessment in the direction indicated (i.e. how strongly supported or disputed the Proposition is believed to be). Implementers may choose to frame a strength assessment in terms of how confident an agent is that the Proposition is true or false, or in terms of the strength of all evidence they believe supports or disputes it.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• Statements put forth a Proposition that expresses some possible fact about the world, and may provide an assessment of this proposition's validity (i.e. how likely it is to be true or false based on evaluated evidence). The semantics of the Proposition are captured in the 'subject,' 'predicate', 'object', and optional 'qualifier' attributes. An assessment of the Proposition's validity can be captured using 'direction', 'strength', and 'score' attributes. The 'strength' attribute is used to report the strength of this assessment in the direction indicated. Strength can be framed as a level of confidence that the Proposition is true or false, or as a level of evidence that supports or disputes it. Data creators can define the permissible values for the 'strength' attribute to indicate which of these facets is being assessed (e.g. 'high confidence' vs 'low confidence', or 'strong evidence' vs 'weak evidence') - or they can choose values that don't commit to one or the other if they don't want to make the distinction (e.g. 'high' vs 'medium' vs 'low').

docs.text: A single term or phrase summarizing the outcome of direction and strength assessments of a Statement's proposition, in terms of a classification of its subject.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• Permissible values for this attribute are typically selected to be succinct and familiar in the target community of practice - and can be provided to report of a statement's conclusion in user-friendly terms. For example, in a Statement assessing the proposition that "BRCA2 c.8023A>G is pathogenic for Breast Cancer", and reporting a direction of 'supports' and strength of 'likely', the term 'likely pathogenic' from the ACMG Variant Interpretation Guidelines would be used as a subject classification.

docs.title: Slot: target_proposition
docs.text: The possible fact against which evidence items contained in an Evidence Line were collectively evaluated, in determining the overall strength and direction of support they provide. For example, in an ACMG Guideline-based assessment of variant pathogenicity, the support provided by distinct lines of evidence are assessed against a target proposition that some variant is pathogenic for a specific disease.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• An example based on the ACMG Guidelines for germline variant pathogenicity interpretation: Consider a curator assessing the evidence provided by population frequency data for a specific variant based on the ACMG criteria. In order to assign a strength (e.g. moderate vs strong) and direction (supports vs disputes) to this data as evidence, there must be some 'target proposition' toward which the evidence is assessed - which in this cases is the proposition that the variant is pathogenic for the disease of interest. If the PM2 criteria is deemed 'met', this indicates that the population frequency evidence provides 'moderate' (strength) 'support' (direction) for this target proposition.

docs.title: START HERE — SEPIO Requirements Collection
docs.text:
This folder contains the resources you need to ask an AI agent to complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms for your biomedical knowledge project.

The goal is to capture what your project currently represents and what it should support, with a clean separation between:

  • current-state requirements, grounded strictly in a defined canonical source/dataset/distribution; and
  • desired-state requirements, which may draw on a broader evidence base to capture a maximal, evidence-supported requirements set for later human review.

At this stage, the agent should describe the project in its own terms rather than trying to choose SEPIO classes or properties.

After you review and confirm the completed forms, a separate SEPIO requirements-to-model step can determine which SEPIO model elements are relevant, where current SEPIO provides only partial coverage, and where follow-up or model extensions may be needed.

docs.title: How Requirements Collection Fits into the SEPIO Modeling Process
docs.text:
Requirements collection is the first phase of a broader, four-phase process for developing and validating SEPIO-based models that meet the representational needs of participating projects.

  1. Project Requirements Collection: Identify what the project currently represents and what capabilities it needs in a future SEPIO-based representation. Review relevant project resources, complete the Requirements Collection Forms, and confirm the requirements with a project representative.

  2. Requirements-to-SEPIO Mapping: Map the confirmed requirements to classes, properties, and modeling patterns in the SEPIO Core Model. Identify requirements that are directly supported, only partially supported, or may require model extensions.

  3. Covering Model Derivation and Review: Use the confirmed requirements and their SEPIO mappings to systematically generate an initial candidate Covering Model. SEPIO modelers and project representatives review and refine this model. Covering Models identify shared representational capabilities and are distinct from project-specific implementation profiles.

  4. Project Data Mapping and Validation: Map representative project records into the proposed SEPIO-based representation and evaluate whether the required information and semantics are preserved. Use the findings to refine the model and mappings as needed.

AI-assisted execution is recommended but optional. The starter-kit guidance and prompts are designed to help AI agents support these phases, including resource discovery, requirements elicitation, proposed SEPIO mappings, and initial Covering Model generation. Agents may prepare drafts for human review or collaborate directly with project representatives in an interactive interview-style process.

This Quick Start focuses on Phase 1. Once your requirements are reviewed and confirmed, they become the input for Phases 2–4. You do not need to understand or select SEPIO model elements while completing the requirements forms.

For the detailed four-phase workflow, see Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md.

docs.title: What is in this folder
docs.text:
• Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx — the authoritative blank requirements workbook your agent should complete.
  • Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx — a separate workbook for the agent’s post-completion feedback on the forms and process.
  • Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_Agents.md — detailed semantic and field-by-field instructions intended primarily for the AI agent.
  • REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md — the ready-to-copy prompt for asking an AI agent to complete the forms.
  • RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md — an optional prompt that asks an AI agent to discover, classify, and organize project resources and propose candidate scope statements.
  • RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md — practical guidance for assembling and reviewing a Resource Inventory.
  • Requirements_Collection_Overview.md — the comprehensive human-facing overview of the requirements-collection workflow.
  • examples/example_scope_statement.md — examples of project scope statements.
  • examples/example_completed_requirements_review.md — an example Requirements Review Memo.
  • CONTENTS.md — a list of files included in this package.

docs.title: Process at a glance
docs.text:
1. Discover resources and establish scope. Identify relevant project materials, designate authoritative current-state sources and broader desired-state support, and confirm the selected scope.
  2. Finalize the Resource Inventory. Document the selected resources, source roles, versions, representative examples, and any conflicts or uncertainties; review and approve the inventory before form completion.
  3. Give the agent everything it needs; have it complete the Requirements Forms, Review Memo, and Feedback Log.
  4. Inspect the workbook and review memo; triage Feedback Log suggestions separately. Resolve uncertainties and correct anything that does not reflect the project.
  5. Move to SEPIO mapping. Once confirmed, use the requirements record as input to the separate requirements-to-model workflow.

docs.title: Step 1 — Define the Scope Statement
docs.text:
Before the requirements agent starts, define a project scope statement.

The scope statement is important because biomedical projects often have several different representations around them: internal curation data, canonical public distributions, intermediate pipeline artifacts, alternate releases, APIs, downstream knowledge graphs, and user-interface representations.

The scope statement tells the agent which of these resources control current-state answers and which additional resources may inform desired-state answers.

docs.title: Minimal vs maximal scope
docs.text:
A minimal scope describes only the canonical source/dataset/distribution selected for the review.

Example:

Current-state canonical source: MeDIC matrix_indication_list.xlsx, version 1.3.0. Current-state and desired-state requirements should both be limited to information represented in this canonical distribution.

This produces a conservative requirements record describing that specific distribution.

A maximal scope still defines a strict canonical source set for current state, but allows a broader evidence base for desired-state requirements.

Example:

Current-state canonical source: MeDIC matrix_indication_list.xlsx, version 1.3.0. Current-state answers must be based only on this distribution. Desired-state evidence: additional MeDIC-maintained intermediate curation artifacts, alternate distributions, the MeDIC paper and project documentation, and explicit project requirements may be used to identify a broader, evidence-supported desired-state requirements set. Where desired state differs from current state, the supporting source must be named in Explanation / Considerations.

This keeps the current-state answers reproducible while allowing the first-pass desired-state requirements to be intentionally broad. A human reviewer can later narrow that maximal set.

docs.title: How to create the scope statement
docs.text:
If the appropriate scope is already obvious, write it yourself.

If not, use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md. The resource-discovery agent will propose:

  • a minimal / canonical-distribution-only scope;
  • a maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state scope;
  • additional alternatives when justified;
  • a recommended scope.

Review or refine one of those candidate statements, then paste the finished scope statement into the SELECTED PROJECT SCOPE section of REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md.

If the project has genuinely different canonical products with different evidence/provenance behavior, consider completing separate requirements reviews.

docs.title: Step 2 — Create a Resource Inventory
docs.text:
A Resource Inventory is a structured list of the project materials that can support the requirements review.

It is useful because it tells the requirements agent:

  • which resources are canonical for current state;
  • which additional resources may inform desired state;
  • which examples to inspect;
  • which sources are historical, upstream, downstream, or context only;
  • which versions should be used;
  • what conflicts or uncertainties exist;
  • what the agent should retrieve itself versus what a human may need to provide.

You can assemble the inventory yourself, or use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md to have an AI agent take a first pass.

If you use the agent-generated inventory, review its source roles, versions, proposed scopes, and exclusions before proceeding.

For detailed instructions, source categories, examples, and inventory structure, see:

RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md

docs.title: Step 3 — Give the Agent Everything It Needs and Have It Populate the Requirements Forms
docs.text:
Give the requirements agent:

  1. REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md (edited to include a PROJECT NAME and SCOPE STATEMENT)
  2. Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx (may be referenced in PROMPT or uploaded with PROMPT)
  3. Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md (may be referenced in PROMPT or uploaded with PROMPT)
  4. A [PROJECT]_Resource_Inventory.mdfile (upload with prompt)
  5. (optional) any additional private/local project files or datasets that the inventory identified as necessary (upload with PROMPT)

Once these materials are provided, ask the agent to complete the forms using REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md.

The agent should follow these principles:

  • Current-state answers must come only from the canonical source set named in the selected scope.
  • Desired-state answers may use the broader evidence set allowed by the selected scope.
  • Desired state should be maximal but evidence-supported, not speculative.
  • When desired state differs from current state, the agent should say what source supports the broader requirement in Explanation / Considerations.
  • The agent should distinguish:
  • canonical project data from upstream or downstream representations;
  • current representation from desired capability;
  • evidence items from evidence interpretation;
  • evidence strength from confidence in extraction/alignment;
  • stored provenance from process documentation.
  • If the available information does not support a confident answer, the agent should use M / Maybe / Needs discussion or otherwise flag uncertainty rather than guessing.
  • The agent should not use SEPIO mappings to decide what the project requirements are. Requirements come first; mapping comes later.

docs.title: Step 4 — Inspect the Deliverables
docs.text: The requirements agent should return three deliverables. The Feedback Log is a separate process-improvement artifact, not part of the project requirements.

docs.title: 1. Completed Requirements Workbook
docs.text:
The completed workbook should preserve the original template formatting and contain the project's current-state and desired-state responses.

The filename should include project name, version, date, and time, for example:

MeDIC_Requirements_v0.2_20261013_1643.xlsx

docs.title: 2. Requirements Review Memo
docs.text:
The memo should summarize:

  • the selected project scope;
  • the exact sources used for current-state answers;
  • the broader sources used for desired-state answers;
  • source versions/releases/commits where relevant;
  • high-confidence conclusions;
  • answers that need human review;
  • conflicts, assumptions, and missing information;
  • inaccessible resources, if any;
  • observations about the forms/guidance;
  • a small set of representative data examples.

The memo should include:

  • a few examples directly from the canonical current-state source; and
  • a few broader/maximal examples from desired-state sources when they reveal additional requirements.

Examples should be represented as close to the source structure as practical—for example, table rows for tabular data, JSON/YAML for structured documents, or triples/edges for graph data.

docs.title: 3. Project Feedback Log
docs.text: Return a project-specific copy of Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx, named [PROJECT]_Requirements_Feedback_Log_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].xlsx. Follow the template’s Agent Instructions and Controlled Vocabularies. Record concrete problems or improvements in form wording, field structure, instructions, validation, or workflow, including the affected sheet/field where possible. Do not duplicate ordinary project-specific uncertainties that belong in the Review Memo. Feedback is for human triage; it does not authorize changing the master forms or guidance.

docs.title: What to review
docs.text:
Focus especially on places where the agent had to interpret ambiguous evidence or infer desired-state intent.

Ask:

  • Did it assess the right canonical current-state source?
  • Did it use only that source set for current-state answers?
  • Did it use the broader desired-state sources only where the selected scope allowed them?
  • When current and desired state differ, did it identify the supporting desired-state source?
  • Did it capture the major claim types?
  • Did it correctly identify what the project treats as evidence?
  • Did it distinguish evidence items from evidence interpretation?
  • Did it capture provenance at the correct level?
  • Did it avoid importing rich information that exists only in upstream sources unless the selected scope explicitly allows it as desired-state evidence?
  • Did it avoid treating downstream API/display enrichments as canonical current-state requirements?
  • Did it flag unsupported answers instead of guessing?
  • Do the worksheets and memo tell a coherent story?

Correct anything that does not accurately reflect the project. Review the Feedback Log separately for proposed improvements to the collection process; accept or reject these through the maintained improvement process, not by silently editing the template.

Once you are comfortable with the workbook, treat it as the confirmed project requirements input.

docs.title: Step 5 — What Can Happen Next
docs.text:
The confirmed forms can then be passed into the separate SEPIO requirements-to-model workflow:

Confirmed Requirements Forms
        +
Requirement→SEPIO Mapping Registry
        +
SEPIO source schema
        ↓
Requirements-to-Model Output Package

That downstream package can include:

  1. Candidate SEPIO Covering Model
  2. Requirements Summary
  3. Requirements-to-Model Traceability
  4. Requirements Follow-Up & Modeling Decisions
  5. Gap & Extension Analysis
  6. Implementation Guidance
  7. Requirements Collection & Form Feedback (downstream mapping artifact; distinct from the agent’s Starter Kit Feedback Log)
  8. Generation Manifest

During the current pilot phase, an AI agent can generate these outputs with transparent provenance. Later, deterministic code can take over schema extraction, dependency closure, validation, traceability, and manifest generation.

The project representative does not need to perform these mappings manually.

docs.title: Key principle
docs.text:
Requirements first, SEPIO mapping second.

The requirements-collection workflow should first answer:

What does the selected canonical source currently represent, and what broader capabilities does the project evidence support as desired requirements?

Only after those requirements are reviewed should the mapping workflow ask:

How well does SEPIO represent those needs?

docs.title: More detailed guidance
docs.text:
A more comprehensive overview of the workflow and tasks can be found in Requirements_Collection_Overview.md.

Detailed guidance for building and reviewing the project evidence set can be found in RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md.

docs.title: Requirements Form Prompt — Complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms
docs.text:
Use this AI-specific prompt when choosing AI-assisted requirements collection. The underlying requirements-collection process may also be performed by humans. Before proceeding, establish a project scope and review relevant source materials, ideally with a Resource Inventory prepared using RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md.

The requirements workflow deliberately distinguishes current-state representation from desired-state requirements:

  • Current state is controlled by the canonical source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or explicitly designated companion artifacts named in the selected project scope statement.
  • Desired state may be informed by a broader set of project-specific supporting resources identified in the selected scope statement and Resource Inventory.

This separation is intentional. The current-state columns should remain conservative and reproducible, while the desired-state columns may capture a broader maximal but project-supported requirements set for later project-representative review and refinement.

Publicly accessible resources may be supplied as attachments, GitHub links, direct-download URLs, DOI/archive links, or version-pinned URLs. The agent should retrieve public resources itself whenever possible; human upload is a fallback.

docs.title: Copyable prompt
docs.text:
Copy the prompt below into your AI agent's interface and replace the bracketed text. Select INDEPENDENT_DRAFT for a source-based first pass followed by human review, or COLLABORATIVE_ELICITATION for an interview-style session in which the agent and project representative develop answers together. Both approaches produce the same requirements artifacts; AI-assisted execution is recommended but optional in the overall SEPIO process.

You are acting as a requirements analyst supporting [PROJECT NAME]. You are not the authoritative project representative; your draft findings and responses require confirmation by an authorized project representative.

Your task is to help populate the SEPIO Requirements Forms workbook based on the selected project scope and the project materials and workflow resources I provide. Use the execution mode specified below. Preserve the project's terminology and separate requirements elicitation from downstream SEPIO mapping.

PROJECT

[PROJECT NAME]

EXECUTION MODE (select one)

[INDEPENDENT_DRAFT / COLLABORATIVE_ELICITATION]

- INDEPENDENT_DRAFT (default): Inspect the allowed sources, prepare a first-pass workbook and Review Memo, and explicitly flag answers requiring the representative's confirmation. Do not present unreviewed answers as project-approved.
- COLLABORATIVE_ELICITATION: Work with the project representative in a structured interview. For each row or a manageable group of related rows, summarize the question in project terms, offer a proposed response and its source basis when available, show a concrete record/example, and ask for clarification or confirmation. Record the agreed answer, rationale, source references, and unresolved points. Do not claim that an answer has been confirmed unless the representative actually confirms it. When the representative delegates particular answers for you to draft, mark them as **agent-proposed / unconfirmed** until reviewed. Allow later decisions to revise earlier answers and keep a brief, traceable decision log (in the Review Memo or another agreed project record) when the discussion requires it.

Both modes apply the same source rules, field definitions, requirements-first boundary, and completion checks. A project may switch modes or use a hybrid approach when needed. In collaborative mode, the forms may be populated incrementally as the interview proceeds; generate final deliverables from the recorded responses when the session is completed. If the user has not selected a mode, use INDEPENDENT_DRAFT.

SELECTED PROJECT SCOPE

[Paste the selected scope statement here. Prefer a scope statement produced by RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md and reviewed/selected/refined by the project representative.]

The selected scope statement must identify, explicitly or by reference to the Resource Inventory:

1. CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET
   The exact source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or explicitly designated companion artifacts that control answers in the "Used in Current Data?" / current-state columns.

2. DESIRED-STATE SUPPORTING-SOURCE SET
   The broader set of project resources that may be used to identify desired/future requirements.

If the selected scope statement does not make these two source sets clear enough to apply reproducibly, stop and ask the project representative to clarify the scope before completing the forms.

REQUIREMENTS-COLLECTION MATERIALS

You will be provided access to the materials needed for this task. They may be supplied as:

- files attached directly to this prompt;
- public GitHub repository links;
- direct-download URLs;
- version-pinned GitHub URLs identifying a specific commit, tag, or release;
- DOI/archive links;
- other public project URLs or repository paths;
- a reviewed Resource Inventory produced using `RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md` — which may contain pointers/links to the types of resources above.

The core requirements-collection materials are:

1. `Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx`
2. `Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_Agents.md`
3. `Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx` (for process feedback)

A reviewed project Resource Inventory should also be supplied when available; a scope selected without one must still clearly designate its allowed sources.

REQUIREMENTS MATERIAL LOCATIONS

Requirements forms:
[ATTACHMENT OR URL TO Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx]

Instructions and guidance:
[ATTACHMENT OR URL TO Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_Agents.md]

Resource Inventory, if available:
[ATTACHMENT OR URL TO PROJECT_Resource_Inventory.md]

Feedback Log template:
[ATTACHMENT OR URL TO Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx]

Additional project materials, if any:
[ATTACHMENTS, URLS, DOI LINKS, OR REPOSITORY PATHS]

MATERIAL ACCESS RULES

1. If a public GitHub, DOI/archive, or other repository URL is provided, retrieve and use the referenced material directly.

2. For Markdown, YAML, JSON, CSV, text, schema, or similar files:
   - read the repository file directly when possible;
   - prefer the exact referenced version when the URL is version-pinned.

3. For `Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx` or any other binary spreadsheet:
   - retrieve/download the actual XLSX file;
   - do not rely on a rendered GitHub preview as a substitute for the workbook;
   - use the downloaded workbook itself as the template to populate.

4. If both a repository page URL and a direct/raw download URL are available for an XLSX file, prefer the direct downloadable file for workbook processing.

5. Do not require the project representative to manually download and re-upload a publicly accessible file unless you are unable to retrieve it yourself.

6. If a required file cannot be accessed:
   - identify the exact file/resource you could not retrieve;
   - provide the URL/path you attempted to use;
   - explain why the file is needed;
   - state whether the requirements review can proceed provisionally without it;
   - ask the project representative to upload that specific file only when necessary.

7. If a repository, DOI landing page, release page, or archive contains multiple plausible files, versions, or artifacts and the canonical one cannot be identified confidently, do not guess. Flag the ambiguity and ask for confirmation.

VERSION AND REPRODUCIBILITY RULES

8. Prefer version-pinned URLs when they are provided.

A version-pinned source may identify:
- a Git commit;
- a release tag;
- a versioned release;
- a DOI/archive version;
- another immutable version identifier.

9. If a version-pinned URL is provided, treat that exact version as authoritative for this requirements run unless explicitly instructed otherwise.

10. If only a moving branch such as `main` or `master` is provided:
   - use the current version available at the time of the review;
   - record the repository path and, when possible, the commit SHA, release identifier, or retrieval date used;
   - do not silently substitute an older cached or historical version.

11. If both a version-pinned source and a newer unpinned source are supplied:
   - do not silently merge them;
   - follow the source-role rules in the selected scope statement;
   - record materially relevant differences.

12. Record enough source-version information in the Requirements Review Memo that another agent could reproduce the review later.

RESOURCE INVENTORY / EVIDENCE PACKAGE

13. When a reviewed Resource Inventory is supplied:
   - use the selected scope statement as the controlling rule for current-state and desired-state evidence;
   - use sources classified as CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL only for current-state answers unless the scope statement explicitly designates additional canonical companion artifacts;
   - use DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT sources only for desired-state reasoning, unless they are also designated CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL;
   - use REPRESENTATIVE EXAMPLES to verify actual data usage;
   - do not treat sources marked CONTEXT_ONLY / DO NOT TREAT AS CANONICAL as evidence of requirements;
   - preserve unresolved issues for human review rather than guessing.

14. If the Resource Inventory identifies public files that should be inspected during requirements elicitation, attempt to retrieve those files yourself before asking the project representative to upload them.

15. If the Resource Inventory and a directly inspected canonical source disagree:
   - the selected canonical current-state source controls the current-state answer;
   - flag the discrepancy;
   - do not silently alter the current-state answer based on a noncanonical source.

16. If the Resource Inventory identifies material that a human may need to provide, first determine whether you can retrieve it yourself. Human upload is a fallback, not the default.

Use `Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_Agents.md` to understand each form, question, controlled value, and response convention.

CURRENT-STATE VS DESIRED-STATE RULES

17. Treat the two requirements columns as answering different questions.

CURRENT STATE / [F1]:
"What is represented in the canonical current-state source set selected for this review?"

DESIRED STATE / [F2]:
"What should the SEPIO-based representation support, based on the maximal project-supported project requirements allowed by the selected scope?"

18. Populate CURRENT STATE strictly from the selected CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET.

Do not mark a requirement as currently represented merely because it appears in:
- an intermediate curation artifact;
- an earlier or alternate release;
- a different distribution;
- a paper or documentation page;
- a roadmap;
- an upstream source;
- a downstream application;
unless that resource is explicitly included in the selected current-state canonical source set.

19. Populate DESIRED STATE from the broader DESIRED-STATE SUPPORTING-SOURCE SET permitted by the selected scope statement.

This may include, when relevant and not explicitly out of scope:
- explicit future requirements or roadmaps;
- current project documentation and papers;
- intermediate curation/analysis artifacts;
- information captured elsewhere in the project's own pipeline but dropped from the canonical export;
- alternate or earlier project distributions;
- other project-maintained representations;
- project examples, competency questions, or implementation guidance.

20. For the initial requirements pass, prefer a MAXIMAL BUT PROJECT-SUPPORTED desired-state requirements set when the selected scope authorizes it.

"Maximal" does NOT mean speculative. Every [F2] `Y` or `M` must have an identifiable project-specific basis; `M` must additionally specify a genuine uncertainty rather than a speculative possibility.

An authorized project representative must review and confirm the resulting requirements, and may refine, narrow, or remove proposed desired-state capabilities.

21. For every desired-state `Y` or `M`, document the project-specific basis in [F4] Basis for F2 Response, including maturity and unresolved questions where relevant. Summarize the basis in the independently readable [F5] Explanation / Considerations. When [F2] differs from [F1], make that distinction explicit.

When useful, classify the desired-state support using one of these labels:

- EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
  A roadmap, issue, requirements document, competency question, or explicit statement says the project wants/needs the capability.

- EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
  The project already captures or uses the information in an intermediate artifact, alternate distribution, curation workflow, analysis product, or other project-maintained representation, but it is absent from the selected canonical current-state distribution.

- DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
  A paper, model/design document, curation guide, or other authoritative project documentation describes the capability as part of the intended project model or data product, even if it is absent from the selected canonical current-state source.

Recommended explanation format when [F1] and [F2] differ:

"Current state: [brief canonical-source observation].
Desired-state support: [SUPPORT TYPE] — [Source ID/title/version]: [brief evidence and rationale]."

22. If several desired-state sources support the same requirement, cite the strongest and most direct source(s) rather than listing everything.

23. A source that explicitly says a capability is out of scope, rejected, deprecated, or intentionally excluded should not be used to justify a desired-state requirement unless another authoritative source explicitly reverses that decision.

IMPORTANT REQUIREMENTS-ELICITATION RULES

24. Answer the forms based on what this project actually represents or explicitly requires. Do not choose answers because they map conveniently to SEPIO.

25. Respect the selected project scope statement. Distinguish the scoped project/data product from:
   - upstream source systems;
   - internal systems outside scope;
   - downstream APIs;
   - user-interface/display enrichments;
   - derived products outside scope, unless explicitly admitted as desired-state evidence.

26. Distinguish:
   - information represented by the selected canonical current-state source;
   - information supported only as a desired-state requirement;
   - information available only in upstream sources;
   - information created or enriched only downstream;
   - process metadata that documents how data were generated but is not itself represented in the canonical source.

27. Use representative data/examples to confirm how the model is actually used, but do not infer a project-wide requirement from a single unusual record unless other evidence supports it.

28. Ground answers in supplied or discovered evidence. Distinguish what a source explicitly establishes from what you infer.

29. Do not invent missing requirements. If available project materials do not provide enough information to answer confidently:
   - use the form's uncertainty/review mechanism where available;
   - preserve the uncertainty;
   - flag the issue clearly for human review.

30. Preserve project-specific terminology and examples in explanatory fields where useful.

31. For each non-obvious answer, keep track of the source material that supports it so that the answer can be reviewed and traced back to its source.

32. Assess the project comprehensively across:
   - claim/assertion types;
   - claim representation structure;
   - semantic structure of reified claims;
   - evidence item types and representations;
   - evidence interpretation, grouping, direction, strength, and stacking;
   - provenance about information artifacts, agents, methods, processes, semantic alignment, encoding, and retrieval;
   - relationships between claim types and evidence types.

33. Do not use the Requirement→SEPIO mapping registry to decide what the project's requirements should be. Requirements elicitation must remain independent of current SEPIO coverage.

34. Do not proceed to Requirement→SEPIO mapping or generate a SEPIO covering model unless explicitly asked.

WORKBOOK HANDLING RULES

35. Populate the provided `Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx` workbook itself rather than recreating the forms from scratch.

36. Preserve the workbook's existing visual formatting and structure, including:
   - sheet names;
   - row and column positions;
   - fills/shading;
   - fonts;
   - borders;
   - alignment;
   - word wrapping;
   - row heights;
   - column widths;
   - data validation;
   - other template formatting.

37. Change only the cells needed to enter project responses, explanations, examples, or explicitly requested review notes.

38. Do not redesign, restyle, normalize, or rebuild the workbook.

39. If technical limitations prevent safe editing of the workbook without altering its formatting, stop and report the limitation rather than silently rebuilding the workbook in a different style.

40. The returned XLSX should open normally in Excel without triggering a repair/recovery warning. Do not "fix" workbook internals by reconstructing the workbook if doing so changes the visible template formatting. If an Excel-integrity problem cannot be corrected without risking formatting changes, report it for human review.

COMPLETENESS AND CONSISTENCY REVIEW

41. Before finalizing the workbook, perform a completeness and consistency pass:
   - check every applicable field;
   - compare answers across forms;
   - identify contradictions;
   - identify unanswered or weakly supported questions;
   - identify places where free text implies a requirement not captured by a structured response;
   - verify that each [F1] assessment is traceable to the selected current-state canonical source set, with a clear distinction between demonstrated absence and insufficient inspection;
   - verify that each [F2] `Y` or `M` has project-specific support from an allowed desired-state source, documented in [F4], and that each `M` specifies what remains unresolved;
   - verify that [F1] and [F2] were not conflated, and that current features intentionally excluded from the future design are not automatically marked desired;
   - make sure upstream evidence/provenance capabilities were not incorrectly attributed to the canonical project source;
   - make sure process provenance described in documentation is not automatically treated as provenance stored in canonical records;
   - make sure downstream transformations are not treated as native current-state representation unless the selected scope says otherwise;
   - verify that [F5] Explanation / Considerations gives a self-contained rationale for both assessments and, when [F2] differs materially from [F1], identifies the supporting source and explains the distinction.

42. Preserve unresolved issues rather than forcing a Y/N answer when the project materials support uncertainty. When collaborative elicitation changes an earlier answer, record the reason for the revision and update the workbook consistently.

DELIVERABLES

A. Completed requirements workbook

Return a completed copy of the supplied workbook.

FILE NAMING:
Use:

[PROJECT]_Requirements_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].xlsx

Example:
MeDIC_Requirements_v0.2_20261013_1643.xlsx

Use 24-hour/military time. Use `HHMM` without a colon for cross-platform filename compatibility.

If a prior requirements version is supplied, increment or retain the version according to the project representative's instruction. If no version is specified, use `v0.1`.

Preserve the original workbook formatting and structure, including existing row heights and any validation rules. Do not rebuild the template, change its field numbering, or add validation rules not present in the supplied workbook. In EIT, [F7] Example(s) from Your Data and [F12] Specific Kinds of this Item Type are optional; Evidence Item Group is an informational column, not a requirement row. In PROV, levels are identified by the Provenance Level column, not informational rows. Use the supplied workbook's current headings, including [F3] Basis for F1 Response and [F4] Basis for F2 Response.

B. Requirements Review Memo

Return a Markdown memo named:

[PROJECT]_Requirements_Review_Memo_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].md

The memo must contain:

1. Project scope used
   - reproduce or precisely summarize the selected scope statement;
   - explicitly identify the CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET;
   - explicitly identify the DESIRED-STATE SUPPORTING-SOURCE SET.

2. Requirements-workflow materials used

3. Sources used for CURRENT-STATE requirements
   - list the exact datasets/distributions/schema artifacts that controlled [F1]/current-state responses;
   - record exact versions/releases/commits/DOI/archive versions/retrieval dates as applicable;
   - explain any explicitly designated canonical companion artifacts.

4. Sources used for DESIRED-STATE requirements
   - list the broader sources actually used to populate [F2]/desired-state responses;
   - group or annotate them where useful as:
     EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT,
     EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT,
     DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT;
   - identify sources considered but excluded from desired-state reasoning and why.

5. Project data landscape and current-state requirements findings
   - begin with a concise executive overview of the project's EPC representation and principal findings;
   - describe the principal datasets or products, their approximate scale when grounded, and their relationships;
   - summarize what [F1] establishes across CT, CRS, RCS (where applicable), EIT, EINT, and PROV, and how the forms relate;
   - explain important source-native semantics, especially where records combine several provenance or evidence meanings.

6. High-confidence conclusions

7. Answers requiring human review

8. Apparent conflicts or missing information

9. Files/resources the agent was unable to access, if any

10. Form/guidance questions that were difficult to interpret

11. Important assumptions made

12. Project observations that suggest improvements to the requirements forms or guidance

13. Diverse representative data examples

Include a small but diverse set of concrete examples that make the requirements tangible; use stable IDs `EX01`, `EX02`, etc., with descriptions, compact source-native field/value snippets, and a verifiable record pointer where available.

Provide:
- a few CURRENT-STATE examples directly from the selected canonical source set; and
- a few broader/maximal DESIRED-STATE examples drawn from allowed desired-state sources when these reveal additional requirements.

For each example, record:
- Example ID
- Current-state or desired-state example
- Source ID/title/version
- What requirement pattern it demonstrates

Represent the example as close to its source representation as practical:

- tabular/database source:
  show the example as a row/table with the original field/column names where possible.
  If a complete logical record is distributed across multiple tables, it is acceptable to denormalize the relevant fields into a single illustrative row, but label it as DENORMALIZED and identify the contributing source tables.

- JSON/YAML document:
  show a compact JSON/YAML object preserving source field names and nesting.

- RDF/graph data:
  show triples/quads/edge properties as appropriate.

- free text/document source:
  show only the minimal relevant excerpt/fields necessary to demonstrate the requirement; do not reproduce unnecessary copyrighted text.

- composite/maximal example assembled from several project sources:
  label it COMPOSITE/ILLUSTRATIVE, identify every contributing source, and do not present the assembled record as if it existed verbatim in one source.

Do not fabricate values to make examples look complete.

C. Source-access status (section of the Review Memo, not a separate required file)

Include a concise statement confirming:

- which linked resources were successfully retrieved;
- which attached files were used;
- whether any fallback human uploads were required;
- whether the review used version-pinned or moving-source URLs;
- any public resources that could not be retrieved.

D. Requirements-collection Feedback Log (separate process-improvement artifact)

Return a completed project-specific copy of `Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx`, named `[PROJECT]_Requirements_Feedback_Log_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].xlsx`. Follow the template’s `Agent Instructions` and `Controlled Vocabularies`. Record concrete suggestions to improve forms, fields, controlled responses, instructions, or the process, with sheet/field references and rationale where possible. Do not use this log to replace the Review Memo’s project-specific unresolved questions. Do not change the master requirements template or guidance on the basis of feedback. If no issues are identified, report that explicitly in the log or handoff. Do not put starter-kit feedback in place of project requirements or unresolved project-specific questions.

Do not proceed to Requirement→SEPIO mapping or generate a SEPIO covering model unless I explicitly ask you to do so.

docs.title: What to provide to the agent
docs.text:
Provide access to:

  • Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx
  • Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx
  • Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_Agents.md
  • the selected project scope statement
  • the reviewed [PROJECT]_Resource_Inventory.md, when available
  • any private or local project materials identified as necessary

The selected scope statement should clearly identify:

  1. the canonical current-state source set controlling current-state answers; and
  2. the broader supporting-source set allowed to inform desired-state answers.

If the Resource Inventory provides multiple provisional scope alternatives, the project representative should normally select one before requirements completion.

docs.title: Recommended GitHub-link pattern
docs.text:
During active development, links to main are acceptable:

Requirements forms:
https://github.com/sepio-framework/sepio-linkml/blob/main/docs/requirements-collection/Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx

Instructions and guidance:
https://github.com/sepio-framework/sepio-linkml/blob/main/docs/requirements-collection/Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_Agents.md

For a reproducible requirements run, prefer links pinned to an exact commit or release.

A direct/raw URL for the XLSX may also be supplied when convenient.

docs.title: Recommended project-specific invocation
docs.text:
Complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms for the following project using REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md.

PROJECT:
[PROJECT NAME]

SELECTED PROJECT SCOPE:
[PASTE THE SELECTED SCOPE STATEMENT]

EXECUTION MODE:
[INDEPENDENT_DRAFT or COLLABORATIVE_ELICITATION]

REQUIREMENTS FORM PROMPT:
[URL TO REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md]

REQUIREMENTS FORMS:
[URL TO Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx]

REQUIREMENTS GUIDANCE:
[URL TO Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_Agents.md]

FEEDBACK LOG TEMPLATE:
[URL OR ATTACHMENT TO Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx]

RESOURCE INVENTORY:
[URL OR ATTACHMENT FOR PROJECT_Resource_Inventory.md]

Use the selected current-state canonical source set strictly for [F1]/current-state answers.
Use the broader desired-state source set allowed by the selected scope to build a maximal but project-supported [F2]/desired-state requirements set.
If [F2] differs from F1, name the desired-state supporting source and support type in Explanation / Considerations.

docs.title: Relationship to resource discovery
docs.text:
For projects where the evidence base or appropriate review scope is not already obvious, run RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md first.

The resulting Resource Inventory should provide: - candidate canonical current-state sources; - broader desired-state evidence sources; - multiple provisional scope statements; - a recommended scope; - representative examples; - access/retrieval guidance; - unresolved questions.

docs.title: What not to provide for this stage
docs.text:
The Requirement→SEPIO mapping registry is intentionally not part of the requirements-elicitation task.

Requirements elicitation should determine what the project currently represents and what it should support independently of current SEPIO coverage. Mapping to SEPIO occurs only after the requirements record has been reviewed and stabilized.

docs.title: Resource Inventory — Guidance for SEPIO Requirements Collection
docs.text:
A Resource Inventory is a structured catalog of project materials used to establish the scope and supporting basis for a SEPIO requirements review. It is more than a list of files: it records which resources are authoritative, how they may be used, which versions and examples should be inspected, and what uncertainty remains.

The inventory may be assembled by a project representative, another human facilitator, an AI agent, or a human–AI team. The guidance applies to all these approaches. AI assistance is recommended but optional; RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md can help generate a first draft for human review.

A useful inventory makes clear:

  • which exact source(s) control current-state responses ([F1]);
  • which additional sources may support desired-state responses ([F2]);
  • which sources are context only and must not determine requirement responses;
  • which versions, releases, and commits are in scope;
  • which real example records best demonstrate the project's claim, evidence, provenance, and confidence semantics;
  • what conflicts, missing information, or access limitations remain.

The selected project scope statement governs source use. The Resource Inventory documents and supports that choice, but an inventory entry does not by itself authorize use of a resource for [F1] or [F2]. An authorized project representative should review and confirm the selected scope before the requirements are treated as authoritative.

docs.title: 1. Start with the canonical current-state source
docs.text:
Identify the exact source, dataset, distribution, schema, or release that should control answers to the forms' [F1] current-state questions (such as Used in Current Data? or Represented in Current Data?).

Examples:

  • a specific version of indications.xlsx;
  • a current LinkML schema release plus designated canonical records;
  • a particular knowledge-graph build/export;
  • a database schema plus one named production distribution.

Prefer version-pinned resources where possible. If several artifacts must be interpreted together—for example, a data table and its authoritative data dictionary—identify the additional resources explicitly as canonical companion artifacts.

Do not automatically include intermediate files, alternate releases, upstream databases, downstream APIs or user interfaces, or papers in the current-state source set. These may supply context or desired-state support, but they control [F1] only if the selected scope explicitly includes them as canonical sources or canonical companions.

Be precise about what the designated artifact actually represents. Documentation that a process exists does not establish that provenance about that process is stored in canonical data; information available in an upstream system does not establish that the scoped project retains it.

docs.title: 2. Identify sources that may inform desired state
docs.text:
[F2] desired-state requirements may draw on a broader set of project-specific materials when the selected scope allows it. The goal is to capture a maximal but source-supported account of the capabilities the project wants in a future SEPIO-based representation—not an inventory of potentially useful features proposed by the facilitator or agent.

Useful sources may include:

  • explicit future requirements, approved roadmaps, or decisions;
  • current project papers, model descriptions, and documentation;
  • curation, evidence interpretation, review, or scoring guidance;
  • intermediate curation or analysis artifacts;
  • fields captured by a project pipeline but omitted from the canonical export;
  • alternate or earlier project distributions;
  • competency questions;
  • implementation and design documents;
  • project-representative statements obtained during collaborative elicitation, with their status and rationale recorded.

Where useful, classify desired-state support by the following types:

docs.title: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
docs.text:
An authoritative project source expressly says that a capability is wanted or needed.

Examples: an approved roadmap item, a GitHub issue expressing an accepted requirement, a requirements document, or an approved competency question.

docs.title: EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
docs.text:
The project already captures or uses information somewhere in its own ecosystem, but that information is absent from the selected canonical current-state distribution.

Examples: semantic-alignment intermediates retained in curation files but dropped from a compact export; provenance in an internal curation record that is not emitted publicly.

docs.title: DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
docs.text:
Authoritative project materials describe a capability as part of the intended model or product even though the selected canonical distribution does not yet represent it.

Examples: a current project paper describing intended qualifiers not present in the selected release; a modeling guide describing proposed evidence structures.

Do not treat every proposed idea, undocumented possibility, or feature available in SEPIO as a project requirement. A resource explicitly describing a capability as out of scope, rejected, intentionally excluded, or deprecated does not support a positive desired-state requirement unless a later authoritative decision reverses that position.

For every [F2] Y or M, there must be identifiable project-specific support. A response of M must indicate both an affirmative basis for considering the capability and what remains unresolved; it should not merely mean “this might be useful.” Record source IDs and relevant decisions so that the basis can later be summarized in [F4] Basis for F2 Response and [F5] Explanation / Considerations.

docs.title: 3. Gather representative examples
docs.text:
Real examples are essential because schemas and prose documentation may not reveal how fields are actually populated or what implicit conventions mean. Select a small but diverse set of concrete records that illustrates important semantic and workflow patterns, for example:

  • a typical empirical claim or concept-definition statement;
  • a statement with qualifiers or contextual information;
  • a statement linked to a source or Evidence Item;
  • a record with richer provenance, review, or confidence information;
  • a record illustrating interpretation of evidence relative to a target statement;
  • a record showing normalization, semantic alignment, encoding, or retrieval;
  • a case where an intermediate artifact contains information omitted from the canonical export;
  • an alternate distribution exposing a capability absent from the canonical one;
  • an unusual but important edge case.
