Concept-definition statements—including synonyms, classifications, mappings, and naming or definition assertions—are within scope when the project has relevant evidence, provenance, interpretation, or confidence requirements. Do not exclude them categorically.

Assign stable example IDs such as E01, E02, and E03. For each example, record:

  • source ID, release/version, and exact record locator or link;
  • claim/record type and relevant original field names;
  • what requirement pattern or semantic distinction it demonstrates;
  • why it was selected;
  • whether it comes from the canonical current-state set or a broader desired-state source.

Prefer accessible record-specific URLs, dataset-and-record identifiers, API queries, or stable file/line pointers. A project homepage is not a substitute for a record locator. Identify whether a link resolves to an actual record, documentation, or a general resource page.

If examples combine data from multiple tables, label them DENORMALIZED and identify the contributing records. If examples combine different sources or illustrate a proposed future shape, label them COMPOSITE/ILLUSTRATIVE or SCHEMATIC, respectively. Such examples are useful for discussion but do not establish what is represented in the canonical [F1] source set.

Where source semantics are implicit—for instance, several distinct meanings encoded in one free-text or provenance slot—it may be necessary to inspect actual values, develop a codebook, and discuss their meanings with a project representative before completing the forms. Document those decisions or uncertainties alongside the inventory.

docs.title: 4. Useful source categories
docs.text: Depending on the project, useful resources may include:

docs.title: Schemas and formal models
docs.text:
• LinkML, JSON Schema, SQL schemas, SHACL, or UML/class models;
  • data dictionaries, field descriptions, controlled vocabularies;
  • export or serialization specifications.

docs.title: Canonical distributions
docs.text:
• release spreadsheets;
  • JSON/YAML datasets;
  • KGX/RDF exports;
  • database dumps;
  • versioned API payload specifications when explicitly designated as canonical.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• model overviews and README files;
  • architecture/design documents;
  • semantic conventions or source field codebooks;
  • project papers.

docs.title: Curation and evidence materials
docs.text:
• curation SOPs;
  • evidence classification or interpretation rules;
  • scoring, confidence, and quality guidance;
  • review, approval, or decision workflows.

docs.title: Pipeline and provenance materials
docs.text:
• ingestion/transformation documentation;
  • normalization and grounding procedures;
  • intermediate curation artifacts;
  • source-attribution and encoding rules;
  • logs or outputs showing relevant information generated or intentionally retained by the project.

docs.title: Requirements and future intent
docs.text:
• roadmaps and issue trackers;
  • requirements documents and user stories;
  • competency questions;
  • approved design proposals;
  • documented decisions from project-representative interviews.

A project does not need every source category. The goal is sufficient relevant, traceable support for accurate requirements assessment, not a comprehensive archive of everything related to the project.

docs.title: 5. Distinguish neighboring resources from project requirements
docs.text:
Resources closely associated with the project may not be part of its selected current-state source set. Examples include:

  • upstream source databases or curated knowledge resources;
  • regulatory or scientific documents from which the project extracts information;
  • external ontologies used for terminology normalization;
  • downstream knowledge graphs;
  • APIs and user interfaces that add derived or display-only information;
  • historical or superseded releases.

These may help explain what the project does, but should not automatically determine [F1] answers. They may inform [F2] only if allowed by the selected scope and if they establish a project-specific requirement rather than just a capability of an adjacent system.

Maintain distinctions among:

  • scientific evidence: information evaluated as supporting or disputing a claim or concept-definition statement;
  • provenance: information about origins, activities, decisions, agents, and transformations;
  • requirements support: sources and rationale justifying why a form response is Y, N, or M.

A copied external assertion may establish where a record came from without independently corroborating its truth. The same external source can play different roles in different workflows; explain its actual role rather than treating the resource name alone as sufficient.

docs.title: 6. Record versions and conflicts
docs.text:
For every important resource, record the most specific reproducible identifier available:

  • version or release number;
  • release tag;
  • commit SHA;
  • DOI/archive version;
  • retrieval date if the source is mutable or lacks an immutable version identifier.

If two resources disagree:

  1. describe the conflict and the relevant source IDs;
  2. identify which scoped source controls [F1];
  3. explain whether the other source is permitted to support [F2];
  4. record unresolved interpretation or authority questions for human review;
  5. do not silently merge or reconcile the accounts.

Example: Release v1.3 lacks qualifier fields, but a current project paper explicitly describes intended contextual hyperrelations. Release v1.3 controls current state; the paper may support desired state under a scope that permits it.

If a later curator discussion or project decision changes an earlier interpretation, retain a traceable decision note rather than silently replacing the old rationale. The inventory need not become a full decision-management system, but it should point to a separate decision log or review memo when that is where the rationale is maintained.

docs.title: 7. Recommended Resource Inventory fields
docs.text:
A useful inventory table includes:

Field What to record Source ID Stable identifier for citing this resource in forms and review materials Name Descriptive resource title Type Dataset, schema, data dictionary, documentation, guideline, issue, record collection, etc. URL / repository path Direct, usable locator, preferably version-pinned Version / release / commit Reproducible version information and retrieval date as appropriate Authority level Whether the resource is canonical, authoritative for future intent, supporting, or contextual Requirements role Permitted use for current-state, desired-state, or context only Desired-state support type Nature of any affirmative future-requirement support Requirement dimensions supported Claim types/semantics, Evidence Items, interpretation, confidence, provenance, etc. Important directly observed facts Concise findings, distinguished from interpretation or inference Example record link(s) Actual representative record IDs/URLs and what they illustrate Access status Accessible, restricted, missing, broken link, unverified, etc. Retrieval / human-assistance guidance What may be fetched directly and what needs provision or confirmation Notes / cautions Conflicts, scope restrictions, limitations, unresolved interpretations

Suggested requirements-role values:

  • CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL
  • CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION
  • DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT
  • CURRENT_AND_DESIRED
  • CONTEXT_ONLY

Suggested desired-state support values:

  • EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
  • EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
  • DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
  • N/A

If using CURRENT_AND_DESIRED, be explicit about the source's canonical authority for [F1]; a general dual-role label must not silently broaden the current-state source set. The selected scope remains the controlling authority.

A single markdown table, spreadsheet, or other structured inventory is acceptable if it preserves these distinctions. For complex projects, companion sections for example records, scope alternatives, access problems, and unresolved decisions may be easier to review than extremely long table cells.

docs.title: 8. Access and retrieval guidance
docs.text:
When AI assistance is used, the agent should normally attempt to retrieve publicly accessible materials directly, including specified source files and versioned examples, rather than requiring a representative to upload everything in advance.

Human assistance may be needed when:

  • public retrieval fails;
  • authentication or private access is required;
  • a resource exists only locally;
  • several plausible versions or files exist and the canonical one is unclear;
  • a project representative must decide the authoritative scope or interpretation.

For each blocker, record:

  • the exact file/resource and attempted locator;
  • why it matters and what question it would resolve;
  • the access problem or required decision;
  • whether the review can proceed provisionally without it.

Human-led inventory creation can use the same access-status and provenance conventions; no AI agent or automated retrieval capability is required. Never assume that a link has been inspected merely because it appears in the inventory.

docs.title: 9. Candidate scope statements
docs.text: A Resource Inventory should support selection of a project scope statement before definitive requirements completion. If the appropriate scope is already known, it may simply document that selected scope; if not, prepare and compare reasonable alternatives.

docs.title: Minimal / canonical-distribution-only
docs.text:
Use the designated canonical source set for [F1] and limit [F2] to requirements supported by that same set.

Best when the goal is a conservative description of one concrete release or distribution. Do not infer broad future requirements merely from what the release makes technically possible.

docs.title: Maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state
docs.text:
Use only the named canonical source(s) and explicitly designated companions for [F1], while allowing a broader, approved set of project-specific sources for [F2].

Best when the goal is to identify the broadest supported requirements set for subsequent project-representative review and refinement.

Additional scope alternatives may be appropriate for projects with multiple canonical products, domain subsets, or significantly different publication/curation pathways. Separate reviews may be preferable when the products have materially different EPC requirements.

The project representative should review, select, and, if necessary, refine the scope. Do not silently combine alternative scopes. Record the final selected statement and which sources have authority under it.

docs.title: 10. Final handoff
docs.text:
Before the inventory is used to complete the requirements forms, confirm that it answers:

  • What exact resources control [F1] current-state responses?
  • What additional resources may support [F2] desired-state responses?
  • Which scope has been selected, and who confirmed it?
  • Which sources are context only?
  • Which representative records should be inspected, and where can they be accessed?
  • What versions or immutable identifiers should be used?
  • Which resources are accessible, and which are not yet inspected?
  • What materials must a human provide or what decisions require representative input?
  • What conflicts, implicit data conventions, or unanswered questions remain?

If these questions are adequately addressed, the inventory is ready for use with REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md and Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_Agents.md.

The forms may then be populated through human-led work, independent AI drafting followed by review, or collaborative interview-style elicitation. In the collaborative approach, a facilitator or AI agent can present each requirement, examine real examples with the representative, propose responses, and record decisions or open questions. This is particularly useful where a source's semantics are implicit in curation conventions or expert practice.

The completed requirements remain provisional until an authorized project representative confirms them. Mapping those requirements to SEPIO and deriving a candidate Covering Model are separate downstream activities; neither should determine the project's requirement responses during elicitation.

docs.title: Resource Inventory Prompt
docs.text:
Use this prompt as the preliminary evidence-discovery and scope-definition step before completing the SEPIO Requirements Forms when the authoritative project evidence base or appropriate requirements-review scope is not already obvious.

The purpose of this task is to:

  1. identify, evaluate, and organize the project resources that can inform requirements elicitation;
  2. distinguish resources that should control current-state requirements from broader resources that may inform desired-state requirements; and
  3. only after the resource inventory has been assembled and source IDs assigned, propose one or more provisional project scope statements for human selection before the requirements forms are completed.

The discovery agent should not complete the requirements forms and should not map requirements to SEPIO.

docs.title: Copyable prompt
docs.text:
<pre><code>You are acting as a resource-discovery, scope-definition, and evidence-preparation agent for the SEPIO requirements-collection workflow.

Your task is to identify, evaluate, and organize the best available resources for understanding the following project/data/model and then recommend one or more reasonable scopes for a subsequent requirements review.

PROJECT
[PROJECT NAME]

INITIAL PROJECT CONTEXT / SCOPE NOTES
[Optional. Insert any initial project description, known canonical distribution, exclusions, questions, or tentative scope notes from the project representative. If nothing is supplied, discover and propose the scope from the available project resources.]

GOAL

Assemble a proposed Resource Inventory / Evidence Package that another AI agent can later use to complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms accurately and reproducibly.

Do not complete the requirements forms yet.
Do not map project concepts to SEPIO yet.
Do not infer project requirements from what SEPIO supports.

A central output of this task is one or more PROVISIONAL SCOPE STATEMENTS that the project representative can review and select before requirements elicitation.

IMPORTANT ORDER-OF-OPERATIONS RULE

Do NOT author the final provisional scope statements before you have:

1. discovered the relevant project resources;
2. assigned each source a stable Source ID such as S01, S02, S03;
3. classified each source's authority and requirements role;
4. identified representative examples;
5. documented important source conflicts, ambiguities, version issues, and scope exclusions; and
6. identified the recommended current-state canonical source set and broader desired-state evidence set.

The scope statements should be written AFTER the Resource Inventory and source classification are established so that they can refer to concrete resources by **Source ID + name/version**.

Think of the workflow this way:

RESOURCE DISCOVERY
    ↓
RESOURCE INVENTORY WITH SOURCE IDs
    ↓
SOURCE ROLE / AUTHORITY CLASSIFICATION
    ↓
RECOMMENDED CURRENT-STATE AND DESIRED-STATE SOURCE SETS
    ↓
PROVISIONAL SCOPE STATEMENTS
    ↓
HUMAN SCOPE SELECTION
    ↓
REQUIREMENTS FORM COMPLETION

The Resource Inventory should make explicit:

- which exact source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or companion artifacts should control CURRENT-STATE requirements answers;
- which broader project resources may be used to identify DESIRED-STATE requirements;
- what resources are context only and must not be used as requirements evidence;
- which materials are publicly accessible and should normally be retrieved directly by the later requirements agent;
- which materials, if any, require a human project representative to download, upload, or clarify.

SCOPE-DESIGN PRINCIPLES

1. Separate current-state scope from desired-state scope.

The subsequent requirements forms contain two distinct concepts:

CURRENT STATE:
What is represented in the selected canonical project source(s) for this review?

DESIRED STATE:
What should the SEPIO-based representation support, based on the broader, evidence-supported project requirements allowed by the selected scope?

Do not assume the same source set must control both.

2. Every provisional scope statement must contain TWO EXPLICIT SUBSECTIONS.

Each proposed scope must be structured with at least:

### Current-state canonical scope

This subsection must state:

- what project/data product is being assessed for current state;
- the exact Source IDs + source names/versions that control current-state / F1 / "Used in Current Data?" answers;
- any explicitly designated canonical companion artifacts;
- what kinds of related resources are excluded from current-state reasoning.

Use language such as:

"Current-state/F1 answers must be based only on S05 — [source name/version] and S06 — [source name/version]. No other resource may change an F1 answer unless the scope is revised."

The later requirements agent must strictly stick to this set for current-state answers.

3. Every provisional scope statement must also contain:

### Desired-state scope

This subsection must state:

- what broader project capabilities are in scope for desired-state/F2 requirements;
- the exact Source IDs + source names/versions that may inform desired state;
- whether each broader source is being used as:
  - EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
  - EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
  - DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
- important exclusions from desired-state reasoning;
- the rule that any F2 answer that differs from F1 must identify its supporting source in `Explanation / Considerations`.

Use language such as:

"Desired-state/F2 answers may additionally draw on S01 — [paper], S08 — [intermediate artifact], and S09 — [alignment/QC artifact] to identify a maximal, evidence-supported requirements set. When F2 differs from F1, the requirements agent must identify the supporting source and support type in `Explanation / Considerations`."

4. The CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET must be precise and reproducible.

This is the exact set of source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or explicitly designated companion artifacts that the later requirements agent must use to populate current-state / "Used in Current Data?" columns.

Examples:
- one versioned `indications.xlsx` distribution;
- one current LinkML schema release plus explicitly designated canonical example data;
- one KG release artifact;
- one database export and its required schema/data dictionary.

Do not broaden current state simply because richer information exists elsewhere in the project.

5. The DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET may be broader.

When relevant and not explicitly out of scope, desired-state evidence may include:
- explicit future requirements or roadmaps;
- current project/model documentation and papers;
- intermediate curation/analysis artifacts;
- data captured elsewhere in the project pipeline but dropped from the canonical export;
- alternate or earlier project distributions;
- other project-maintained representations;
- competency questions;
- curation guidance;
- implementation/design documents.

The purpose is to support an initial MAXIMAL EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED requirements set that a human reviewer can later narrow.

"Maximal" does not mean speculative. Every desired-state capability must be supported by project-specific evidence.

6. Classify desired-state support where useful.

Use these labels when characterizing why a noncanonical resource is informative for desired state:

- EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
  A roadmap, issue, requirements document, competency question, or explicit statement says the project wants/needs the capability.

- EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
  The project already captures or uses the information in an intermediate artifact, alternate distribution, curation workflow, analysis product, or other project-maintained representation, but it is absent from the proposed canonical current-state distribution.

- DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
  A paper, model/design document, curation guide, or other authoritative project document describes the capability as part of the intended project model/data product, even if absent from the proposed canonical current-state source.

7. Do not use a source as desired-state evidence when it explicitly says the capability is out of scope, rejected, deprecated, or intentionally excluded, unless another authoritative project source explicitly reverses that decision.

SOURCE-DISCOVERY RULES

8. Respect supplied project context and discover scope boundaries.

Distinguish the scoped project/data product from:
- upstream source databases;
- internal systems that are outside scope;
- downstream APIs;
- user-interface/display enrichments;
- unrelated derived exports;
- historical/superseded project versions.

For every source, consider whether it describes:
- the canonical project/data model itself;
- a candidate canonical current-state distribution;
- an alternate or historical project representation;
- an intermediate curation/analysis artifact;
- an upstream source;
- a downstream representation;
- an implementation detail;
- future/project intent.

9. Prefer current, authoritative sources, but do not discard older/alternate/intermediate project artifacts that may legitimately inform desired state.

For CURRENT-STATE canonical-source recommendations, prioritize:
a. current authoritative schema/data model;
b. current canonical distribution/release;
c. current authoritative data dictionary;
d. current representative data/examples;
e. explicitly designated canonical companion artifacts.

For DESIRED-STATE evidence, also consider:
f. current model/design documentation and papers;
g. current curation/evidence/provenance guidance;
h. current ingest/transformation/pipeline artifacts;
i. explicit requirements, competency questions, roadmap documents, or issues;
j. intermediate curation/analysis artifacts;
k. alternate or earlier project distributions that expose project capabilities or intent.

When sources conflict:
- identify the conflict;
- state which source should control current state;
- explain whether the conflicting resource remains useful for desired-state evidence;
- do not silently reconcile the difference.

10. Look for sources that can answer questions about:

- the kinds of claims/associations/statements represented;
- how claims are structurally packaged;
- whether claims are represented as reified objects, direct graph edges, slot/value pairs, tabular records, or other forms;
- how subject, relationship/predicate, object, and qualifiers are represented;
- what kinds of evidence items are retained or referenced;
- whether evidence items are represented locally, externally, or both;
- whether evidence direction, strength, grouping, or higher-order synthesis is represented;
- confidence or scoring information;
- provenance about agents, methods, resources, dates, review, extraction, grounding, normalization, encoding, retrieval, or ingest;
- what information is retained from upstream sources versus discarded or transformed;
- what richer information is captured in intermediate project artifacts but lost in the canonical distribution;
- current capabilities versus documented future/intended requirements.

11. Include representative data/examples.

When possible, identify a small but diverse set of examples that covers the major claim and EPC patterns.

Include examples from:
- candidate canonical current-state sources; and
- broader desired-state sources when they reveal additional project requirements.

Prefer examples that collectively test different situations, such as:
- a claim with publication or regulatory support;
- a claim with structured evidence metadata;
- a claim with qualifiers/context;
- a claim with source/provenance but little explicit evidence;
- a case where richer project-internal EPC is dropped from the canonical export;
- a case involving normalization/transformation;
- an alternate distribution exposing a capability absent from the canonical one;
- any unusual but important pattern.

Do not collect large datasets when a small representative sample will establish the relevant structure and semantics.

Assign each representative example a stable ID such as E01, E02, E03.

12. Record precise source locations and source roles BEFORE writing the scope statements.

Assign each source a stable ID such as S01, S02, S03.

For each source, record:
- Source ID
- Source title/name
- Source type
- URL or repository path
- Repository/release/tag/commit/version when available
- Authority level
- Requirements role
- Desired-state support type, when applicable
- Scope relevance
- Requirement dimensions supported
- Important directly observed facts
- Access status
- Whether the later requirements agent should retrieve it directly or human assistance may be required
- Notes/cautions

Use these authority labels where appropriate:
- PRIMARY_AUTHORITATIVE
- SUPPORTING_CURRENT
- REPRESENTATIVE_EXAMPLE
- HISTORICAL_BACKGROUND
- OUT_OF_SCOPE_CONTEXT

Use these REQUIREMENTS ROLE labels:
- CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL
- CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION
- DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT
- CURRENT_AND_DESIRED
- CONTEXT_ONLY

A source should receive CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL or CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION only if you recommend that the later requirements agent be allowed to use it for current-state answers under at least one proposed scope.

13. Capture directly observed facts from key sources.

For each major authoritative source, record concise facts explicitly supported by the source.

Examples:
- "The canonical table contains subject ID, object ID, and a source-text field."
- "The canonical record does not contain evidence-direction or evidence-strength fields."
- "Intermediate curation records retain Name Resolver candidates and LLM QC outcomes, but the final export drops them."
- "The project paper describes hyperrelations absent from the selected release."

Distinguish these directly observed facts from interpretation.

Use labels where helpful:
- DIRECT
- INFERRED
- UNRESOLVED

14. Retrieve publicly accessible materials before asking the human to provide them.

When a potentially important source is publicly accessible:
- first attempt to access/download it yourself;
- follow GitHub, DOI/archive, release, and direct-download links;
- inspect actual files/artifacts when record-level or schema-level details matter.

Human assistance is a fallback, not the default.

15. Identify inaccessible, ambiguous, or human-supplied materials precisely.

Human intervention may be needed when:
- the agent cannot access/download the resource;
- authentication, institutional permission, or a private repository is required;
- the source exists only locally/internally;
- multiple plausible files/versions exist and the canonical one cannot be identified confidently;
- the public copy is stale/incomplete and the representative may have a better copy;
- a human decision is required to choose the canonical source/version or scope.

If human assistance is needed:
- identify the exact file/resource;
- provide the URL/path when known;
- explain why it matters;
- state what question it is needed to answer;
- state whether discovery/requirements elicitation can proceed provisionally without it;
- tell the project representative exactly what to download, upload, or clarify.

16. Distinguish process documentation from stored project content.

A project may document curation, extraction, review, normalization, mapping, evidence assessment, encoding, or transformation.

For each such source, determine whether it shows:
- information actually stored in the proposed canonical current-state source;
- information captured elsewhere by the project but omitted from the canonical export;
- only an implementation process with no evidence that its outputs are retained.

This distinction is especially important for desired-state scope design.

17. Do not begin filling the SEPIO Requirements Forms until the Resource Inventory has been reviewed and one project scope statement has been selected, or the project representative explicitly authorizes the requirements agent to use the recommended scope.

PROVISIONAL SCOPE STATEMENTS

18. Author provisional scope statements ONLY AFTER the Resource Inventory and recommended source sets have been completed.

The scope statements should function as selections over the Resource Inventory.

Do not write vague statements such as:
"Use the current dataset and relevant documentation."

Instead write:
"Use S05 — `matrix_indication_list.xlsx`, v1.3.0 and S06 — `matrix_contraindication_list.xlsx`, v1.3.0 for current state. Desired state may additionally use S01 — MeDIC primary publication and S09 — FDA semantic-alignment/QC intermediates..."

Every named resource should be identifiable from the Resource Inventory by Source ID and name/version.

19. At minimum, provide:

SCOPE A — MINIMAL / CANONICAL-DISTRIBUTION-ONLY

This scope should:
- identify the narrowest defensible CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET;
- restrict current-state answers to those canonical source(s);
- normally restrict desired-state answers to the same canonical source(s), unless a small number of explicitly inseparable canonical companion artifacts are required;
- produce a conservative requirements record describing the canonical distribution itself.

Structure it as:

### Current-state canonical scope
- Scope statement
- Sources: Sxx — [name/version], Syy — [name/version]
- Explicit exclusions

### Desired-state scope
- Scope statement
- Sources: usually the same source set for the minimal option
- Explicit exclusions

### Strengths / tradeoffs

20. Also provide:

SCOPE B — MAXIMAL / CANONICAL CURRENT STATE + BROAD DESIRED STATE

This scope should:
- identify the exact CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET;
- require the later agent to use only that set for current-state/F1 answers;
- identify a broader DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET;
- allow desired-state/F2 answers to draw on project-specific evidence such as:
  - intermediate curation/analysis artifacts;
  - alternate/earlier project distributions;
  - other maintained project outputs;
  - authoritative papers/documentation;
  - curation/modeling guidance;
  - roadmaps/issues/explicit requirements;
- aim for a maximal evidence-supported desired-state requirements set that the human reviewer can later whittle down;
- require the requirements agent to name the desired-state supporting source in `Explanation / Considerations` whenever F2 differs from F1.

Structure it as:

### Current-state canonical scope
- Scope statement
- Exact Source IDs + names/versions
- Canonical companions, if any
- Explicit exclusions
- Rule that no noncanonical source may change F1 unless the scope is revised

### Desired-state scope
- Scope statement
- Exact Source IDs + names/versions
- Desired-state support type for each broader source
- Explicit exclusions
- Rule that F2 differences must cite supporting source + support type in `Explanation / Considerations`

### Strengths / tradeoffs

21. If other reasonable project scopes emerge, provide additional alternatives such as:
- CURRENT RELEASE + CURRENT PIPELINE ARTIFACTS;
- CORE PRODUCT + DESIGNATED COMPANION DATASETS;
- DOMAIN-SPECIFIC SUBSET;
- STRICT HISTORICAL RELEASE;
- CURRENT PRODUCT FAMILY / MULTI-DISTRIBUTION SCOPE.

Every additional scope must use the same explicit two-part structure:

### Current-state canonical scope
### Desired-state scope

22. Recommend one scope.

After presenting alternatives:
- identify the scope you recommend for the initial requirements exercise;
- explain why;
- state the tradeoff between reproducibility/conservatism and broader requirements discovery.

Unless project context argues otherwise, prefer recommending the MAXIMAL scope for the initial requirements pass because it preserves a strict canonical basis for current state while surfacing a broader evidence-supported desired-state requirements set for human review.

DELIVERABLE

Return a Markdown document named:

[PROJECT_NAME]_Resource_Inventory.md

IMPORTANT: Use the following section order. The Resource Inventory and source classification must appear BEFORE the provisional scope statements so that the scope can reference established Source IDs.

A. Project context used

Restate the supplied project context/scope notes and any important assumptions used during discovery.

B. Resource inventory

Provide a table with these columns:

- Source ID
- Name
- Type
- URL / repository path
- Version / release / commit
- Authority level
- Requirements role
- Desired-state support type
- Requirement dimensions supported
- Important directly observed facts
- Access status
- Retrieval / human-assistance guidance
- Notes / cautions

For Desired-state support type, use when applicable:
- EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
- EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
- DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
- N/A

For Access status, use concise values where possible:
- PUBLIC_ACCESSIBLE
- PUBLIC_DOWNLOADABLE
- ACCESS_NOT_VERIFIED
- ACCESS_FAILED
- AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED
- PRIVATE_OR_LOCAL
- CANONICAL_FILE_AMBIGUOUS

For Retrieval / human-assistance guidance, use:
- AGENT_RETRIEVE
- HUMAN_PROVIDE_IF_AGENT_ACCESS_FAILS
- HUMAN_PROVIDE_REQUIRED
- HUMAN_CONFIRM_CANONICAL_VERSION
- HUMAN_CONFIRM_SCOPE
- CONTEXT_ONLY_NO_DOWNLOAD_NEEDED

C. Representative data/examples

List selected examples using stable IDs.

For each:
- Example ID
- Current-state or desired-state example
- Source ID + source name
- Claim/record type
- EPC/model pattern demonstrated
- Why selected
- Whether directly inspected or still needs retrieval

Prefer examples from both:
- canonical current-state sources;
- broader desired-state sources that reveal additional requirements.

D. Upstream/downstream/context resources that should NOT be treated as canonical requirements evidence

List neighboring systems/resources that could cause scope confusion.

Explain whether each is:
- context only;
- allowed only as desired-state evidence under a specific scope;
- fully out of scope.

E. Known source conflicts, ambiguities, or version concerns

Document:
- conflicting sources;
- stale documentation;
- unclear implementation behavior;
- unresolved version questions;
- differences between canonical distribution and richer intermediate/alternate representations;
- uncertainty about which release/file is canonical.

For each conflict:
- state what controls current state;
- state whether another source may still inform desired state.

F. Recommended source sets

Complete this section BEFORE authoring provisional scope statements.

### F1. Recommended current-state canonical source set

Identify the exact sources that should control F1/current-state answers under the scope you expect to recommend.

For each source:
- provide Source ID + source name/version;
- explain why it is canonical;
- identify any canonical companion artifact that must be interpreted together with it;
- state what it is allowed to establish for current state.

### F2. Recommended desired-state evidence set

Identify broader sources that may inform F2/desired-state requirements under a maximal scope.

For each:
- provide Source ID + source name/version;
- state why it is relevant;
- assign one of:
  - EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
  - EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
  - DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
- note limitations or caveats.

### F3. Sources excluded from requirements evidence

List Source IDs that should remain context only or fully out of scope, with a brief reason.

G. Provisional scope statements

Now author the provisional scopes using the Resource Inventory IDs established above.

### Scope A — Minimal / canonical-distribution-only

#### Current-state canonical scope

Provide:
- paste-ready scope text;
- exact Source IDs + names/versions controlling F1;
- canonical companions, if any;
- explicit exclusions.

#### Desired-state scope

Provide:
- paste-ready scope text;
- exact Source IDs + names/versions controlling F2;
- explicit exclusions.

#### Strengths / tradeoffs

### Scope B — Maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state

#### Current-state canonical scope

Provide:
- paste-ready scope text;
- exact Source IDs + names/versions controlling F1;
- canonical companions, if any;
- explicit exclusions;
- explicit statement that noncanonical resources may not change F1 answers.

#### Desired-state scope

Provide:
- paste-ready scope text;
- exact Source IDs + names/versions allowed for F2;
- desired-state support type for each broader source;
- explicit exclusions;
- explicit statement that whenever F2 differs from F1, the requirements agent must identify the supporting source + support type in `Explanation / Considerations`.

#### Strengths / tradeoffs

### Additional reasonable scope alternatives

Include only when justified. Use the same explicit two-part structure:
- Current-state canonical scope
- Desired-state scope

### Recommended scope

State which scope you recommend and why.

H. Materials the requirements agent should retrieve vs. materials a human may need to provide

Start with this rule:

The requirements-completion agent should first attempt to retrieve all publicly accessible materials itself. The project representative should not need to manually download and upload public resources merely because they are listed in the Resource Inventory.

Then provide:

### H1. Materials the requirements agent should retrieve directly

For each:
- Source ID
- exact resource/file
- URL/path
- why needed
- what should be inspected

### H2. Materials a human may need to provide only if agent retrieval fails

For each:
- Source ID
- exact resource
- why it matters
- what the human should upload if requested

Do not ask the human to provide these preemptively.

### H3. Materials that genuinely require human provision or clarification

List only resources that:
- are private/local;
- require authentication;
- cannot be publicly accessed;
- require a human canonical-version decision;
- require a human scope-selection decision.

If none:
"None identified at this stage."

I. Evidence gaps / unresolved questions

For each unresolved question, indicate whether it:
- can likely be resolved by retrieving a public source;
- requires human-provided material;
- requires a human semantic/project decision;
- requires scope selection;
- can remain unresolved during preliminary requirements elicitation.

J. Recommended handoff for requirements elicitation

End with a compact machine-readable block.

Use this structure:

RECOMMENDED SCOPE:
- Scope B — Maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state

CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCES:
- S01: [name/version]
- S02: [name/version]

CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL COMPANIONS:
- S03: [name/version]

DESIRED-STATE SUPPORT SOURCES:
- S04: EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT — [name/version]
- S05: DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT — [name/version]
- S06: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT — [name/version]

REPRESENTATIVE EXAMPLES:
- E01
- E02
- E03

CONTEXT ONLY / DO NOT USE AS REQUIREMENTS EVIDENCE:
- S08
- S09

AGENT SHOULD RETRIEVE DURING REQUIREMENTS REVIEW:
- S02: [specific file/artifact]
- S04: [specific file/artifact]

HUMAN PROVIDE ONLY IF AGENT RETRIEVAL FAILS:
- S07: [specific file/artifact]

HUMAN-PROVIDED MATERIAL REQUIRED:
- NONE
or
- [specific resource and why]

HUMAN CONFIRMATION REQUIRED:
- Select/approve one provisional scope before final requirements completion
- [other issue]

UNRESOLVED:
- [brief issue]

HANDOFF INSTRUCTION:
Use only CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCES and explicitly designated CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL COMPANIONS to populate F1/current-state requirements.

Use the DESIRED-STATE SUPPORT SOURCES allowed by the selected scope to populate an evidence-supported maximal F2/desired-state requirements set.

When F2 differs from F1, identify the supporting Source ID + source name and desired-state support type in the form's `Explanation / Considerations` field.

Do not use CONTEXT ONLY sources as requirements evidence.

Attempt to retrieve public resources before asking the project representative to upload them.

Flag unresolved issues for human review rather than guessing.

K. Short resource-discovery summary

Conclude with 5–10 bullets summarizing:
- the canonical model/data product identified;
- the recommended current-state canonical source set;
- the broader desired-state evidence set;
- the recommended scope;
- the main EPC patterns observed;
- important scope exclusions;
- critical source/version conflicts;
- additional public materials the requirements agent should retrieve;
- whether any material currently requires human provision;
- whether the package is ready for scope selection and requirements elicitation.
</code></pre>

docs.title: Human handoff principle
docs.text:
The Resource Inventory should make the division of responsibility explicit:

  1. Public and accessible: the requirements agent retrieves it.
  2. Public but retrieval may fail: the human provides it only if the agent asks.
  3. Private/local/authenticated: the human provides access or uploads it.
  4. Canonical version ambiguous: the human decides which version is authoritative.
  5. Scope alternatives remain: the human selects/approves the scope before final requirements completion.

docs.title: Scope-selection principle
docs.text:
The discovery agent proposes the scope; the project representative owns the scope decision.

The important architectural rule is:

The Resource Inventory defines the evidence catalog; the scope statement selects which catalog entries control current state and which may inform desired state.

For most initial requirements exercises, the recommended default is:

strict canonical current state + maximal evidence-supported desired state

This gives the modeling workflow a conservative, reproducible account of what the selected canonical distribution represents today while exposing a broader set of project-supported capabilities for human review before SEPIO modeling.

docs.title: Relationship to the requirements-form workflow
docs.text:
The completed [PROJECT_NAME]_Resource_Inventory.md is intended to be provided to the requirements-completion agent alongside:

  • Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx
  • Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md
  • the selected project scope statement
  • any materials explicitly identified as genuinely requiring human provision

The selected scope statement should be copied from or derived directly from the Resource Inventory and should preserve its Source IDs.

The later requirements agent should attempt to retrieve all other publicly accessible resources itself.

The Requirement→SEPIO mapping registry is intentionally not used during resource discovery or requirements elicitation.

docs.title: SEPIO Requirements Collection — Project Representative Overview
docs.text:
Audience: Project representatives, human facilitators, and others participating in SEPIO requirements collection, whether working independently or with AI agents.

How to use this overview: Requirements collection is a general project-led process. The starter kit supports human-led collection, AI-generated drafts reviewed by humans, and collaborative interviews in which an agent and project representative develop responses together. AI assistance is recommended but optional; an authorized project representative confirms the requirements before they are used for SEPIO mapping.

docs.title: 1. What this process is for
docs.text:
The SEPIO Requirements Forms describe what a biomedical knowledge project currently represents and what it should support about claims and concept-definition statements, evidence, evidence interpretation, provenance, and confidence.

The goal is not to redesign your project or force it into SEPIO while the forms are being completed.

Instead, the process asks two related questions:

Current state: What does the selected canonical source, dataset, distribution, or model actually represent now?

Desired state: What broader capabilities does project-specific sources support as requirements for a future SEPIO-based representation?

This distinction is important. Current-state answers should be conservative and reproducible: they are grounded only in the canonical source set explicitly selected for the review. Desired-state answers may use a broader set of project-specific sources to identify a maximal, source-supported requirements set for representative review. This can include requirements for concept-definition statements, such as synonym, mapping, and subclass assertions, when the project needs to represent their evidence, provenance, or confidence.

docs.title: How requirements collection fits into the larger SEPIO process
docs.text:
Requirements collection is Phase 1 of a broader four-phase workflow:

  1. Project Requirements Collection: Establish the project's current and desired representational needs, grounded in source materials and confirmed by its representative.
  2. Requirements-to-SEPIO Mapping: Map confirmed requirements to the SEPIO Core Model using the maintained Requirement → SEPIO Mapping Registry and identify direct coverage, partial coverage, modeling alternatives, and gaps.
  3. Covering Model Derivation and Review: Systematically derive a candidate SEPIO Covering Model from the approved requirement mappings, then have SEPIO modelers and participating projects review and refine it. The Covering Model identifies shared representational capabilities; it is not a project-specific implementation profile with dataset-level constraints or cardinalities.
  4. Project Data Mapping and Validation: Transform representative records into the candidate SEPIO-based representation, assess whether required semantics are preserved, and feed findings back into the model and mappings.

AI assistance may be used in any phase, but is not required. The detailed four-phase explanation is in Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_Agents.md.

This Overview and its five practical steps focus on Phase 1. The completed forms describe your project's requirements, not a selection of SEPIO features. Requirements mapping and model derivation come after project confirmation.

docs.title: 2. What is in this starter package
docs.text:
This folder contains:

  • QUICK_START.md — a short orientation and five-step entry point.
  • Requirements_Collection_Overview.md — this comprehensive overview of the requirements-collection workflow.
  • Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx — the authoritative requirements workbook to complete and confirm.
  • Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx — a separate template for documenting feedback on the forms and collection process, particularly useful in AI-assisted workflows.
  • Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_Agents.md — detailed semantic and field-by-field guidance for human and AI participants, written with sufficient specificity for AI-assisted execution.
  • REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md — a ready-to-copy AI prompt for preparing a requirements draft; collaborative interviewing is also a valid approach.
  • RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md — an optional agent prompt for discovering, classifying, and organizing project resources and proposing candidate scope statements.
  • RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md — practical guidance for assembling and reviewing a Resource Inventory.
  • examples/example_scope_statement.md — example project scope statements.
  • examples/example_completed_requirements_review.md — an example Requirements Review Memo.
  • CONTENTS.md — a list of files included in the package.

These files are designed to stay together in one directory in the repository.

docs.title: 3. The five-step workflow
docs.text:
At a high level:

  1. Discover resources and establish scope. Identify relevant project sources and representative examples, select the authoritative canonical current-state set, and define broader sources that may support desired-state requirements. A Resource Inventory can be assembled before or alongside scope selection.
  2. Finalize a Resource Inventory. Record source roles, versions, example records, conflicts, access needs, and the approved scope; review any agent-generated inventory.
  3. Complete the forms and Review Memo. Use human-led work, an AI-generated draft, or a facilitated interview in which an agent and project representative discuss questions and agree on responses. Record substantive bases and examples; use the Feedback Log separately for process-improvement observations when helpful.
  4. Review and confirm the results. An authorized project representative validates the workbook and Review Memo, resolves uncertainties, and reviews process feedback separately.
  5. Move to SEPIO mapping. Use the confirmed requirements as input to the separate requirements-to-model workflow.

The remainder of this document explains each part in more detail.

docs.title: 4. Step 1 — Define the project scope
docs.text:
Before completing the forms, define a project scope statement. A human participant or an AI agent may help discover resources and propose the scope, but the project representative should confirm it.

Biomedical projects often have several related representations:

  • an internal curation model;
  • a canonical public distribution;
  • intermediate curation or analysis artifacts;
  • one or more source databases;
  • an ingest/transformation pipeline;
  • alternate or historical releases;
  • an API representation;
  • a knowledge-graph export;
  • a user-interface representation.

Without an explicit scope, anyone preparing the forms can inadvertently mix these together and produce answers that are neither reproducible nor clearly interpretable.

A useful scope statement identifies two source sets for requirements assessment.

docs.title: 4.1 Current-state canonical source set
docs.text:
This is the exact source, dataset, distribution, release, schema, or explicitly designated companion artifact that controls the workbook's current-state / “Used in Current Data?” answers.

Whoever prepares the forms should strictly use only this source set when populating current-state [F1] columns.

Examples include:

  • one versioned indications.xlsx distribution;
  • one current LinkML schema release plus designated canonical example records;
  • one KG release/export;
  • one production database schema plus its canonical data dictionary.

The fact that richer information exists elsewhere in the project does not make it part of current state unless the scope explicitly includes that resource in the canonical source set.

docs.title: 4.2 Desired-state supporting-source set
docs.text:
This is the broader set of project-specific resources permitted for use when deciding what the future SEPIO-based representation should support.

Depending on the selected scope, this can include:

  • explicit future requirements or roadmap items;
  • current papers and project documentation;
  • model/design documentation;
  • intermediate curation or analysis artifacts;
  • information captured elsewhere in the project pipeline but dropped from the canonical export;
  • alternate or earlier project distributions;
  • competency questions;
  • curation guidance;
  • implementation/design documents.

The desired-state source set supports a maximal but source-supported first-pass requirements record. “Maximal” does not mean speculative: every desired-state [F2] Y or M response should still have identifiable project-specific support.

docs.title: 4.3 Minimal versus maximal scope
docs.text: When alternatives are useful, the Resource Inventory workflow can identify at least two reasonable scope choices.

docs.title: Minimal / canonical-distribution-only
docs.text:
A minimal scope limits the review to one canonical source set.

Example:

Current-state canonical source: MeDIC matrix_indication_list.xlsx, version 1.3.0. Current-state and desired-state requirements should both be limited to information represented in this canonical distribution.

This produces a conservative description of one concrete release.

docs.title: Maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state
docs.text:
A maximal scope preserves a strict current-state source while allowing broader project evidence to inform desired state.

Example:

Current-state canonical source: MeDIC matrix_indication_list.xlsx, version 1.3.0. Current-state answers must be based only on this distribution. Desired-state evidence: additional MeDIC-maintained intermediate curation artifacts, alternate distributions, the MeDIC paper and project documentation, and explicit project requirements may be used to identify a broader, source-supported desired-state requirements set. Where desired state differs from current state, the supporting source must be named in Explanation / Considerations.

This is often the preferred starting point because it gives a reproducible account of current representation while surfacing a broader set of requirements for human review.

docs.title: 4.4 Other reasonable scopes
docs.text:
Some projects may justify additional alternatives, for example:

  • current release + current pipeline artifacts;
  • core product + designated companion datasets;
  • domain-specific subset;
  • strict historical release;
  • current product family / multi-distribution scope.

If substantially different products have different evidence/provenance behavior, separate requirements reviews may be clearer.

docs.title: 4.5 How to obtain a scope statement
docs.text:
If the scope is already obvious, write it directly.

If not, the scope can be developed through discussion and source review, optionally using RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md. When used, the resource-discovery agent should propose:

  • a minimal scope;
  • a maximal scope;
  • additional reasonable alternatives when appropriate; and
  • a recommended scope with tradeoffs.

The project representative should review and confirm the selected scope. For AI-assisted completion, place it into the SELECTED PROJECT SCOPE section of REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md.

docs.title: 5. Step 2 — Create a Resource Inventory
docs.text:
A Resource Inventory is a structured catalog of source materials supporting the requirements review. It documents the basis for requirements assessments; this is distinct from the scientific evidence that a project may represent about its claims.

It is more than a list of files. It should tell anyone preparing the forms:

  • which resources are canonical for current state;
  • which resources may inform desired state;
  • which examples should be inspected;
  • which sources are historical, upstream, downstream, or context only;
  • which versions/releases should be used;
  • what source conflicts or uncertainties exist;
  • which public resources the agent should retrieve itself;
  • which materials may require human provision or clarification.

Use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md for detailed guidance.

docs.title: 5.1 Two ways to create the inventory
docs.text:
Option A — Assemble it yourself. If you already know the key schema, canonical distribution, documentation, examples, curation guidance, and provenance materials, create a simple inventory or manifest with precise pointers to them.

Option B — Ask an AI agent to take a first pass. Use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md when project evidence is distributed across repositories, documentation sites, papers, DOI archives, generated artifacts, or multiple versions.

Whether drafted by a human or generated by an agent, the Resource Inventory and its source-role assignments should be reviewed before requirements completion.

docs.title: 5.2 Resource roles
docs.text:
The inventory should distinguish source roles such as:

  • CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL
  • CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION
  • DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT
  • CURRENT_AND_DESIRED
  • CONTEXT_ONLY

Only sources designated as current-state canonical or canonical companions should control current-state answers under the selected scope.

docs.title: 5.3 Desired-state support types
docs.text: When a broader source supports desired state, it is useful to distinguish why:

docs.title: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
docs.text: A roadmap, issue, requirements document, competency question, or explicit project statement says the capability is wanted or needed.

docs.title: EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
docs.text: The project already captures or uses the information in an intermediate artifact, alternate distribution, curation workflow, analysis product, or other project-maintained representation, but the selected canonical distribution does not expose it.

docs.title: DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
docs.text:
A paper, model/design document, curation guide, or other authoritative project document describes the capability as part of the intended project model or data product, even though it is absent from the selected canonical source.

A source that explicitly says a capability is out of scope, rejected, deprecated, or intentionally excluded should not normally be used to justify desired state unless another authoritative project source explicitly reverses that decision.

docs.title: 5.4 Useful resources
docs.text:
Typical resources include:

Resource type Why it helps Canonical dataset/distribution Establishes what is actually represented in current state. Authoritative schema or data model Shows entities, relationships, fields, structure, and constraints. Data dictionary / field documentation Explains field meaning, allowed values, cardinality, and intended use. Model/design documentation Explains why structures exist and what the project intends to represent. Representative example records Shows how the model is actually used in practice. Intermediate curation/analysis artifacts May reveal existing project capabilities omitted from the canonical export. Source/ingest documentation Shows which upstream information is retained, transformed, or discarded. Curation guidelines / SOPs Helps interpret claims, evidence evaluation, confidence, review, and provenance. Pipeline / normalization documentation Helps identify semantic-alignment and process provenance. Project papers / overview documents Provides project goals, intended semantics, and model intent. Requirements / competency questions / roadmap Captures desired capabilities not yet fully implemented.

You do not need every resource type. The goal is to assemble enough evidence to answer each form question responsibly.

docs.title: 5.5 Representative examples
docs.text:
The inventory should identify a small, diverse set of examples rather than hundreds of repetitive records.

Useful examples may include:

  • a typical claim;
  • a claim with qualifiers/context;
  • a claim with source or evidence support;
  • a claim with richer provenance;
  • a normalization or transformation example;
  • a case where intermediate information is dropped from the canonical export;
  • an alternate distribution that exposes a capability absent from the canonical one.

Assign stable IDs such as E01, E02, and E03.

docs.title: 5.6 Public resources and human uploads
docs.text:
For AI-assisted work, the agent should ordinarily attempt to retrieve publicly accessible materials itself, rather than requiring the project representative to upload them in advance. In human-led work, project participants may instead gather or link directly to the relevant materials.

Human assistance is appropriate when:

  • public retrieval fails;
  • authentication/private access is required;
  • a source exists only locally;
  • multiple plausible versions/files exist and the canonical one cannot be identified confidently;
  • a human scope or canonical-version decision is required.

If an AI agent needs human help, it should identify the precise resource, why it matters, and whether the review can proceed provisionally without it. In any execution mode, record unavailable sources and their consequences for the assessments.

docs.title: 6. Step 3 — Complete the requirements forms
docs.text: The forms may be completed directly by a project representative, by a human facilitator, by an AI agent preparing a draft for subsequent review, or collaboratively in a structured interview. AI assistance is recommended but optional; the same source rules, documentation expectations, and confirmation requirement apply in every mode.

docs.title: 6.1 AI-assisted preparation (when used)
docs.text:
For an independent agent draft or a collaborative AI-assisted interview, provide:

  1. REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md
  2. the selected project scope statement
  3. Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx
  4. Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_Agents.md
  5. the reviewed [PROJECT]_Resource_Inventory.md
  6. any private/local materials identified as necessary

For the forms and guidance, you may either upload the files or provide links/pointers to the exact versions you want used.

For project source materials, you may:

  • upload local files;
  • provide public repository/documentation/DOI links;
  • provide a manifest or Resource Inventory with precise pointers;
  • point to specific files/directories rather than entire repositories.

For large datasets, representative records plus structural documentation may be enough unless a specific assessment requires the full dataset.

Two valid AI-assisted modes:

  • Agent-generated draft: The agent inspects the permitted sources, fills the forms and Review Memo, and flags unresolved questions for human validation.
  • Collaborative elicitation/interview: The agent presents each form question to a project representative, proposes a source-grounded answer or asks for a concrete record, and collaborates with the representative to clarify and document the answer. This is especially useful where important requirements live in source-data conventions or expert knowledge rather than written documentation, as in the MONDO pilot. Record decisions and provisional assumptions so later answers can be revised consistently.

In either case, the project representative must confirm the final responses. Human-led collection can use the same forms, dictionaries, and review practices without using the AI prompt.

docs.title: 6.2 Current-state rule
docs.text:
For every current-state [F1] answer, ask:

Is this capability represented in the selected current-state canonical source set?

Do not mark something current merely because it appears in:

  • an intermediate artifact;
  • a historical or alternate distribution;
  • a paper;
  • a roadmap;
  • an upstream source;
  • a downstream API/UI;
  • process documentation;

unless the selected scope explicitly includes that resource in the current-state canonical source set.

docs.title: 6.3 Desired-state rule
docs.text:
For every desired-state [F2] answer, ask:

Is this capability supported as a project requirement by one or more resources allowed in the selected desired-state source set?

The initial desired-state pass should generally be maximal but source-supported.

When desired state differs from current state, cite the supporting source in [F4] Basis for F2 Response and summarize the rationale in [F5] Explanation / Considerations.

A useful pattern is:

Current state: [brief observation from canonical source]. Desired-state support: [SUPPORT TYPE] — [Source ID/title/version]: [brief source basis and rationale].

docs.title: 6.4 Assessing support for answers
docs.text:
The preparer should consider:

Selected project scope
        +
Current-state canonical source set
        +
Broader desired-state source set
        +
Representative records/examples
        +
Curation / pipeline / provenance documentation
        +
Known requirements / use cases

For each substantive answer, the preparer should be able to answer:

What project source supports this assessment, and is it permitted to support current state, desired state, or both?

If that cannot be answered, the response should be marked uncertain rather than guessed.

docs.title: Current representation vs desired requirement
docs.text: A capability may be absent from the canonical current-state distribution but still be a valid desired-state requirement.

docs.title: Upstream source capability vs project capability
docs.text: If an upstream source contains rich EPC information that the project neither stores nor explicitly requires, it should not automatically become a project requirement.

docs.title: Canonical distribution vs intermediate project capability
docs.text: An intermediate project artifact may contain information omitted from the canonical export. Under a maximal scope, this can support desired state as EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT without changing the current-state answer.

docs.title: Canonical model vs downstream API/UI enrichment
docs.text: Downstream computation or display enrichment should not be treated as current canonical representation unless explicitly included in scope.

docs.title: Claim semantics vs evidence/provenance
docs.text: A project may support many biomedical claim types while using one relatively simple evidence/provenance envelope. Assess these dimensions separately.

docs.title: Evidence item vs evidence interpretation
docs.text: A publication, source passage, dataset, or experimental result is not the same thing as an interpreted argument about whether evidence supports or disputes a proposition.

docs.title: Scientific evidence strength vs extraction/alignment confidence
docs.text: A score indicating confidence in entity normalization or extraction should not be treated as scientific evidence strength unless project semantics explicitly say so.

docs.title: Process documentation vs stored provenance
docs.text: Documentation that an LLM, normalization service, curator, or pipeline step was used does not prove that provenance about that process is stored in the canonical data.

docs.title: Missing information vs negative requirement
docs.text: Silence is not automatically “N.” Use M / Maybe / Needs discussion or another review flag when evidence is insufficient.

docs.title: 6.6 Requirements-first rule
docs.text:
The Requirement→SEPIO mapping registry should not be used to decide what the project's requirements are.

Determine project requirements independently of current SEPIO coverage, whether the forms are completed by a person or an AI agent.

docs.title: 7. Step 4 — Review and confirm the deliverables
docs.text: Requirements collection should produce two primary artifacts: a completed Requirements Workbook and a Requirements Review Memo. For AI-assisted collection, a project-specific Feedback Log is also recommended as a separate process-improvement artifact; human-led efforts may use the same template. Feedback should be reviewed separately and does not automatically change authoritative forms or guidance.

docs.title: A. Completed Requirements Workbook
docs.text:
Complete the provided Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx template while preserving its existing structure and formatting.

The output filename should include project name, version, date, and 24-hour time, for example:

MeDIC_Requirements_v0.2_20261013_1643.xlsx

The HHMM form avoids filename problems caused by colons on some operating systems.

docs.title: B. Requirements Review Memo
docs.text:
The memo filename should follow the same version/date/time convention, for example:

MeDIC_Requirements_Review_Memo_v0.2_20261013_1643.md

The memo should include:

  • the selected project scope;
  • the exact current-state canonical source set;
  • the broader desired-state source set;
  • exact versions/releases/commits/DOI archive versions/retrieval dates where relevant;
  • high-confidence conclusions;
  • answers requiring human review;
  • source conflicts or missing information;
  • inaccessible resources;
  • important assumptions;
  • difficult form/guidance questions;
  • observations that may improve the workflow;
  • representative data examples.

docs.title: 7.1 Representative examples in the memo
docs.text:
The memo should include a small, diverse set of concrete examples:

  • a few current-state examples directly from the selected canonical source; and
  • a few broader desired-state/maximal examples when noncanonical project evidence reveals additional requirements.

Represent examples as close to their source representation as practical:

  • tabular/database source: show rows/tables using source column names where possible;
  • JSON/YAML: show compact objects preserving source field names and nesting;
  • RDF/graph: show triples/quads/edge properties;
  • free text: show only the minimal excerpt needed;
  • multi-source example: label it COMPOSITE/ILLUSTRATIVE;
  • record assembled across tables: label it DENORMALIZED and identify contributing tables.

Do not fabricate values to create a complete-looking example.

docs.title: 7.2 Feedback on the tools and process
docs.text: When AI assistance is used, complete a project-specific copy of Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx following its Agent Instructions and Controlled Vocabularies tabs. Human-led collections may also use this template. Keep feedback about ambiguous form rows, instructions, process difficulties, and suggested improvements separate from substantive project requirements and unresolved project-specific questions in the Review Memo. Review and approve changes before modifying the starter-kit templates.

docs.title: 7.3 Project review and confirmation checklist
docs.text:
Focus review on:

Review question What to check Scope Did the preparer use the selected project/data product and correct canonical source set? Current state Is every [F1] current-state Y/M answer supported by the allowed canonical source set? Desired state Is every broader [F2] desired-state Y/M answer supported by an allowed project source? Source traceability When [F2] differs from [F1], do [F4] Basis for F2 Response and [F5] Explanation / Considerations identify the supporting desired-state source and rationale? Claims Are the major kinds of assertions represented by the project captured? Evidence Are important evidence item categories and relationships represented? Interpretation Did the preparer distinguish evidence from interpreted evidence, direction/strength, grouping, and higher-level synthesis? Provenance Are source, authorship, method, process, semantic alignment, encoding, retrieval, and other provenance requirements captured at the right level? Upstream EPC Did the preparer avoid treating richer upstream content as current project representation? Intermediate artifacts If used for desired state, were they kept separate from current-state claims? Downstream enrichment Did the preparer avoid treating API/UI enrichment as canonical current-state representation? Uncertainty Were unsupported or ambiguous answers flagged rather than guessing? Consistency Do responses across worksheets and the memo tell a coherent story? Examples Are current-state and desired-state examples accurate, sourced, and useful?

Correct anything that does not accurately reflect the project.

An authorized project representative should review, correct, and confirm the workbook and Review Memo before they are treated as the authoritative project requirements input for SEPIO mapping and Covering Model derivation.

docs.title: 8. Step 5 — What happens after the forms are confirmed
docs.text:
The confirmed workbook becomes the project requirements input for the later SEPIO requirements-to-model workflow.

That later workflow uses:

Confirmed Requirements Forms
        +
Requirement→SEPIO Mapping Registry
        +
SEPIO source schema
        ↓
Requirements-to-Model Output Package

That package can include:

  1. Candidate SEPIO Covering Model
  2. Requirements Summary
  3. Requirements-to-Model Traceability
  4. Requirements Follow-Up & Modeling Decisions
  5. Gap & Extension Analysis
  6. Implementation Guidance
  7. Requirements Collection & Form Feedback (downstream mapping artifact, not the Starter Kit agent Feedback Log)
  8. Generation Manifest

The mapping and candidate-model generation stages may be assisted by AI agents, deterministic tools, or human modeling work. The maintained Requirement → SEPIO Mapping Registry and authoritative SEPIO Core Model provide the basis for systematic candidate derivation; SEPIO modelers and participating projects review and refine the results. A candidate Covering Model is distinct from a project-specific implementation profile, which may subsequently add dataset-level constraints or cardinalities.

Project representatives need not perform the detailed mappings themselves; their central role is confirming requirements and reviewing the proposed representations for fidelity to their needs.

docs.title: 9. Evidence hierarchy and conflict handling
docs.text: A single global evidence hierarchy is no longer sufficient because current state and desired state intentionally use different source sets.

docs.title: For current-state answers
docs.text:
The selected scope controls the answer.

Within the allowed current-state source set, prefer:

  1. explicitly designated canonical release/distribution;
  2. canonical schema/data model;
  3. canonical companion data dictionary/specification;
  4. representative records from the same release;
  5. other explicitly designated canonical companion artifacts.

A noncanonical paper, intermediate artifact, or alternate distribution should not override current state.

docs.title: For desired-state answers
docs.text:
Use the broader source set allowed by the selected scope.

Prefer the strongest project-specific sources or documented bases, such as:

  1. explicit future requirements / approved roadmap / competency questions;
  2. current authoritative project/model documentation;
  3. existing project-maintained intermediate or alternate artifacts that demonstrate a capability;
  4. current curation/modeling guidance;
  5. current implementation/design documentation;
  6. older or historical project sources when they remain relevant and are not contradicted by authoritative current sources.

When sources disagree:

  • identify the conflict;
  • state which source controls current state;
  • state whether the conflicting resource may still inform desired state;
  • do not silently reconcile them.

docs.title: 10. What project representatives are not expected to do
docs.text:
Project representatives do not need to:

  • learn the complete SEPIO model before filling out the forms;
  • manually map project fields to SEPIO classes and slots;
  • decide whether a SEPIO gap exists;
  • design SEPIO extensions;
  • understand dependency closure; or
  • create the Candidate Covering Model themselves.

Their responsibility is to help establish:

  1. a defensible scope;
  2. an accurate evidence base; and
  3. accurate, confirmed project requirements.

docs.title: 11. Minimum evidence standard
docs.text:
Before considering a requirements workbook ready for confirmation, the workflow should ideally have:

  • a selected project scope statement;
  • a clearly named current-state canonical source set;
  • at least one authoritative structural source;
  • representative examples from the canonical source;
  • enough information to distinguish current project content from upstream/downstream information;
  • one or more project sources supporting desired-state requirements when [F2] goes beyond [F1];
  • source/version information sufficient to reproduce the review;
  • explicit review flags for questions the available evidence cannot answer.

Projects lacking one or more of these can still participate, but the resulting workbook should contain more uncertainty/review flags.

docs.title: 12. Key principle
docs.text:
The requirements process is requirements-first, not SEPIO-first.

The requirements-collection participants should first answer:

What does the selected canonical source currently represent, and what broader capabilities does project evidence support as desired requirements?

Only after those requirements are reviewed should the SEPIO mapping workflow ask:

How well does SEPIO represent those needs?

docs.title: Evidence, Provenance, Confidence (EPC) Requirements Collection
docs.text:
Detailed Instructions & Guidance for Agents Completing the SEPIO Requirements Forms

This document provides detailed semantic and field-level guidance for anyone responsible for completing Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx on behalf of a project, whether a human respondent, an AI agent, or a human–AI team. The instructions are written with AI-assisted requirements collection in mind, providing sufficient detail, examples, and explicit decision rules to support reliable agent execution, while remaining equally applicable to human-led collection. It is intended to be used with the selected project scope statement, the reviewed project Resource Inventory, and the project-specific source materials identified there. For AI-assisted work, REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md provides an accompanying execution prompt. Regardless of how requirements are collected, the responses should be reviewed and confirmed by an authorized project representative before serving as authoritative inputs to SEPIO mapping and model derivation.

For more focused human-facing orientation to the overall process, see QUICK_START.md and Requirements_Collection_Overview.md. For guidance on assembling and classifying the evidence base before requirements completion, see RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md and RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md.

docs.title: I. Why Start with Requirements Collection
docs.text:
Before defining a shared SEPIO Covering Model or a set of reusable profiles, the consortium should first establish what each participating project actually needs to represent. A structured requirements-collection exercise provides the evidence base for deciding which SEPIO concepts and patterns are needed, which requirements recur across projects, and where project-specific differences must be preserved.

The requirements process should be artifact-centered and use-case-centered rather than asking project representatives to reason directly in SEPIO terms. Project representatives are usually best positioned to describe the claims they represent, the information they treat as evidence, how that evidence is assessed, and what provenance must be retained. The SEPIO/modeling group can then perform the second-stage semantic analysis: determining whether those requirements map to concepts such as DataItem, StudyResult, Statement, EvidenceLine, Contribution, or other SEPIO structures.

This separation also supports later implementation with LinkML and LinkML-Map. If the requirements effort captures the semantics of source fields, important distinctions in the source model, and what must survive transformation, those results can directly inform the design of SEPIO-based profiles and declarative mappings between project models.

docs.title: Recommended Overall Process
docs.text:
The SEPIO modeling effort follows a four-phase workflow that progresses from project-specific requirements collection through semantic mapping, model derivation, and validation. The process is designed to be requirements-driven and grounded in real project data, with project representatives and SEPIO modelers providing review and oversight at appropriate stages.
