Where a confidence score exists, distinguish authored/stated values from computed values. Project-specific policy/decision-history needs can be described in [F5] and flagged for later model mapping if the existing rows do not capture them.
  • Encoding Provenance: Describe how an information artifact is expressed or serialized in a particular model, language or format when this is important to the project's representational requirements. Identify the encoding method or rules and their provenance especially when an encoding decision changes the meaning, specificity or interpretation of a statement (for example a cross-reference being emitted as an exact match). Different file formats alone do not automatically establish a requirement to preserve detailed encoding provenance.
  • Retrieval Provenance: Describe movement of an already encoded record between systems: the immediate system it was retrieved from, the destination/consuming system, each system's role, the retrieval event/time, and transformations along the way. Distinguish the original creator/source of the knowledge from the immediate provider of a retrieved representation. A system may be an upstream source in one activity and a downstream target in another, so specify the particular retrieval event and direction. Describe any transformation or export rule that changes the meaning of the retrieved record, rather than treating transfer as a purely technical step.

Cross-level example (schematic, not an observed record): An AI agent extracts a quotation from a paper (Evidence Item creation and semantic-alignment provenance), resolves a disease term (alignment method/confidence), assesses whether the quote supports a subclass claim (Evidence Interpretation), and a curator accepts the assertion under a documented policy (Assertion Provenance). This illustrates why recording extraction confidence alone is not the same as recording confidence in the asserted subclass relationship.

docs.title: 8. Claim–Evidence Matrix Form (CEM)
docs.text:
Purpose. Produce two project-specific matrices on the existing CEM worksheet: one for [F1]/current state, one for [F2]/desired state. The matrices relate Claim Types (C###) to Evidence Item Types (EI.*) and complement—not replace—the detailed forms.

How to complete. Use the completed CT and EIT forms and project-specific source support. Determine relevant claim-type rows and evidence-type columns for each state before writing. Preserve all applicable identifiers, preferably in a comparable ordering across [F1] and [F2]. Populate Y for an established supported relationship, M where source-supported applicability requires discussion, and leave blank if no relevant relationship is identified. Do not use X, N, or an unrelated illustrative matrix. For negative or disputing evidence, explain the polarity in the associated forms or memo rather than inventing a new cell-value convention.

Layout and validation. The worksheet has designated [F1] and [F2] titles/areas, but no prepopulated example matrix. If more [F1] rows are needed than the allocated space (initially 24 Claim Type data rows), insert rows above the [F2] title to move the entire [F2] section safely; then size [F2] and the evidence-type columns as necessary. Preserve headings, cell content, styles, validations and any formulas. Confirm no rows/columns were truncated, no [F1] content overwrote [F2], and that every marked relationship has traceable project support. Do not mechanically copy [F1] cells to [F2]; assess the two separately.

docs.title: IV. Completeness and Consistency Check Before Submission
docs.text:
Before treating a requirements workbook as complete and ready for project-representative review or confirmation, the person or agent preparing it should perform the following checks:

  • check every required respondent-facing field;
  • verify that controlled values use the labels defined in the workbook/guidance;
  • verify that every [F1]/current-state conclusion is supported only by the current-state canonical sources/companions allowed by the selected scope;
  • verify that every broader [F2]/desired-state conclusion is supported by an allowed desired-state source and not speculation;
  • for each [F2] Y or M, verify [F4] Basis for F2 Response cites a project-specific source and explains the rationale; for each M, verify uncertainty is explicit;
  • compare answers across forms for internal consistency;
  • identify contradictions between project sources or between current-state and desired-state answers;
  • identify required questions that remain unsupported or unresolved;
  • make sure free-text explanations do not imply uncaptured requirements;
  • verify that richer upstream-source information has not been incorrectly attributed to the project itself;
  • verify that intermediate project artifacts have not been treated as current canonical data unless the selected scope explicitly includes them;
  • verify that downstream/API/UI enrichments have not been treated as canonical project requirements unless the selected scope says otherwise;
  • retain traceability to the Resource Inventory sources supporting non-obvious conclusions; and
  • prepare the Requirements Review Memo described in the Core Principles and Rules above, including its current-state project/dataset overview and form-by-form synthesis.

A partially completed workbook with clearly marked unknowns is preferable to a fully populated workbook containing inferred or invented requirements.

docs.title: V. What Happens After the Requirements Are Confirmed?
docs.text:
After a project representative reviews and confirms the completed requirements workbook, the requirements-to-model workflow applies the maintained Requirement → SEPIO Mapping Registry against the controlled responses and stable Requirement IDs. That later stage can generate a candidate SEPIO covering model and associated summary, traceability, follow-up, gap/extension, implementation-guidance, form-feedback, and generation-manifest artifacts.

During the current pilot phase, an AI agent may perform this later analysis and generation step. The confirmed workbook remains the formal project-requirements input; the selected scope and Resource Inventory provide traceable support for how those requirements were derived. The completed requirements forms should nevertheless remain requirements-first: do not use the SEPIO Mapping Summary columns to decide what the project needs.

Detailed downstream mapping, routing, and output-generation behavior is documented separately in the Requirement → SEPIO Mapping Registry/README and the Requirements-to-Model Report Specification.

docs.title: Feedback on Requirements Collection Tools and Process
docs.text:
After completing the requirements workbook and Review Memo, those involved in the collection effort are encouraged to document actionable feedback about the forms, field wording, controlled responses, guidance, or workflow. For AI-assisted collection, a project-specific copy of Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx should be completed using its Agent Instructions and Controlled Vocabularies tabs. Human-led efforts may use the same template to record suggested improvements.

This feedback is separate from the project’s requirements and from unresolved project-specific questions captured in the Review Memo. Proposed improvements to the starter kit should be reviewed and approved before being incorporated into the authoritative forms or guidance.

docs.title: START HERE — SEPIO Requirements Collection
docs.text:
This folder contains the resources you need to ask an AI agent to complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms for your biomedical knowledge project.

The goal is to capture what your project currently represents and what it should support, with a clean separation between:

  • current-state requirements, grounded strictly in a defined canonical source/dataset/distribution; and
  • desired-state requirements, which may draw on a broader evidence base to capture a maximal, evidence-supported requirements set for later human review.

At this stage, the agent should describe the project in its own terms rather than trying to choose SEPIO classes or properties.

After you review and confirm the completed forms, a separate SEPIO requirements-to-model step can determine which SEPIO model elements are relevant, where current SEPIO provides only partial coverage, and where follow-up or model extensions may be needed.

docs.title: What is in this folder
docs.text:
• Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx — the authoritative blank requirements workbook your agent should complete.
  • Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx — a separate workbook for the agent’s post-completion feedback on the forms and process.
  • Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md — detailed semantic and field-by-field instructions intended primarily for the AI agent.
  • REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md — the ready-to-copy prompt for asking an AI agent to complete the forms.
  • RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md — an optional prompt that asks an AI agent to discover, classify, and organize project resources and propose candidate scope statements.
  • RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md — practical guidance for assembling and reviewing a Resource Inventory.
  • RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md — guidance for gathering and reviewing project schemas, documentation, examples, and other evidence.
  • Requirements_Collection_Overview.md — the comprehensive human-facing overview of the requirements-collection workflow.
  • examples/example_scope_statement.md — examples of project scope statements.
  • examples/example_completed_requirements_review.md — an example Requirements Review Memo.
  • CONTENTS.md — a list of files included in this package.

docs.title: Process at a glance
docs.text:
1. Define the scope. Decide exactly which canonical source(s) control current-state answers and which broader sources may inform desired-state requirements.
  2. Create a Resource Inventory. Identify the best evidence, examples, versions, conflicts, and candidate scope statements.
  3. Give the agent everything it needs; have it complete the Requirements Forms, Review Memo, and Feedback Log.
  4. Inspect the workbook and review memo; triage Feedback Log suggestions separately. Resolve uncertainties and correct anything that does not reflect the project.
  5. Move to SEPIO mapping. Once confirmed, use the requirements record as input to the separate requirements-to-model workflow.

docs.title: Step 1 — Define the Scope Statement
docs.text:
Before the requirements agent starts, define a project scope statement.

The scope statement is important because biomedical projects often have several different representations around them: internal curation data, canonical public distributions, intermediate pipeline artifacts, alternate releases, APIs, downstream knowledge graphs, and user-interface representations.

The scope statement tells the agent which of these resources control current-state answers and which additional resources may inform desired-state answers.

docs.title: Minimal vs maximal scope
docs.text:
A minimal scope describes only the canonical source/dataset/distribution selected for the review.

Example:

Current-state canonical source: MeDIC matrix_indication_list.xlsx, version 1.3.0. Current-state and desired-state requirements should both be limited to information represented in this canonical distribution.

This produces a conservative requirements record describing that specific distribution.

A maximal scope still defines a strict canonical source set for current state, but allows a broader evidence base for desired-state requirements.

Example:

Current-state canonical source: MeDIC matrix_indication_list.xlsx, version 1.3.0. Current-state answers must be based only on this distribution. Desired-state evidence: additional MeDIC-maintained intermediate curation artifacts, alternate distributions, the MeDIC paper and project documentation, and explicit project requirements may be used to identify a broader, evidence-supported desired-state requirements set. Where desired state differs from current state, the supporting source must be named in Explanation / Considerations.

This keeps the current-state answers reproducible while allowing the first-pass desired-state requirements to be intentionally broad. A human reviewer can later narrow that maximal set.

docs.title: How to create the scope statement
docs.text:
If the appropriate scope is already obvious, write it yourself.

If not, use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md. The resource-discovery agent will propose:

  • a minimal / canonical-distribution-only scope;
  • a maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state scope;
  • additional alternatives when justified;
  • a recommended scope.

Review or refine one of those candidate statements, then paste the finished scope statement into the SELECTED PROJECT SCOPE section of REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md.

If the project has genuinely different canonical products with different evidence/provenance behavior, consider completing separate requirements reviews.

docs.title: Step 2 — Create a Resource Inventory
docs.text:
A Resource Inventory is a structured list of the project materials that can support the requirements review.

It is useful because it tells the requirements agent:

  • which resources are canonical for current state;
  • which additional resources may inform desired state;
  • which examples to inspect;
  • which sources are historical, upstream, downstream, or context only;
  • which versions should be used;
  • what conflicts or uncertainties exist;
  • what the agent should retrieve itself versus what a human may need to provide.

You can assemble the inventory yourself, or use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md to have an AI agent take a first pass.

If you use the agent-generated inventory, review its source roles, versions, proposed scopes, and exclusions before proceeding.

For detailed instructions, source categories, examples, and inventory structure, see:

RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md

docs.title: Step 3 — Give the Agent Everything It Needs and Have It Populate the Requirements Forms
docs.text:
Give the requirements agent:

  1. REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md (edited to include a PROJECT NAME and SCOPE STATEMENT)
  2. Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx (may be referenced in PROMPT or uploaded with PROMPT)
  3. Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md (may be referenced in PROMPT or uploaded with PROMPT)
  4. A [PROJECT]_Resource_Inventory.mdfile (upload with prompt)
  5. (optional) any additional private/local project files or datasets that the inventory identified as necessary (upload with PROMPT)

Once these materials are provided, ask the agent to complete the forms using REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md.

The agent should follow these principles:

  • Current-state answers must come only from the canonical source set named in the selected scope.
  • Desired-state answers may use the broader evidence set allowed by the selected scope.
  • Desired state should be maximal but evidence-supported, not speculative.
  • When desired state differs from current state, the agent should say what source supports the broader requirement in Explanation / Considerations.
  • The agent should distinguish:
  • canonical project data from upstream or downstream representations;
  • current representation from desired capability;
  • evidence items from evidence interpretation;
  • evidence strength from confidence in extraction/alignment;
  • stored provenance from process documentation.
  • If the available information does not support a confident answer, the agent should use M / Maybe / Needs discussion or otherwise flag uncertainty rather than guessing.
  • The agent should not use SEPIO mappings to decide what the project requirements are. Requirements come first; mapping comes later.

docs.title: Step 4 — Inspect the Deliverables
docs.text: The requirements agent should return three deliverables. The Feedback Log is a separate process-improvement artifact, not part of the project requirements.

docs.title: 1. Completed Requirements Workbook
docs.text:
The completed workbook should preserve the original template formatting and contain the project's current-state and desired-state responses.

The filename should include project name, version, date, and time, for example:

MeDIC_Requirements_v0.2_20261013_1643.xlsx

docs.title: 2. Requirements Review Memo
docs.text:
The memo should summarize:

  • the selected project scope;
  • the exact sources used for current-state answers;
  • the broader sources used for desired-state answers;
  • source versions/releases/commits where relevant;
  • high-confidence conclusions;
  • answers that need human review;
  • conflicts, assumptions, and missing information;
  • inaccessible resources, if any;
  • observations about the forms/guidance;
  • a small set of representative data examples.

The memo should include:

  • a few examples directly from the canonical current-state source; and
  • a few broader/maximal examples from desired-state sources when they reveal additional requirements.

Examples should be represented as close to the source structure as practical—for example, table rows for tabular data, JSON/YAML for structured documents, or triples/edges for graph data.

docs.title: 3. Project Feedback Log
docs.text: Return a project-specific copy of Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx, named [PROJECT]_Requirements_Feedback_Log_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].xlsx. Follow the template’s Agent Instructions and Controlled Vocabularies. Record concrete problems or improvements in form wording, field structure, instructions, validation, or workflow, including the affected sheet/field where possible. Do not duplicate ordinary project-specific uncertainties that belong in the Review Memo. Feedback is for human triage; it does not authorize changing the master forms or guidance.

docs.title: What to review
docs.text:
Focus especially on places where the agent had to interpret ambiguous evidence or infer desired-state intent.

Ask:

  • Did it assess the right canonical current-state source?
  • Did it use only that source set for current-state answers?
  • Did it use the broader desired-state sources only where the selected scope allowed them?
  • When current and desired state differ, did it identify the supporting desired-state source?
  • Did it capture the major claim types?
  • Did it correctly identify what the project treats as evidence?
  • Did it distinguish evidence items from evidence interpretation?
  • Did it capture provenance at the correct level?
  • Did it avoid importing rich information that exists only in upstream sources unless the selected scope explicitly allows it as desired-state evidence?
  • Did it avoid treating downstream API/display enrichments as canonical current-state requirements?
  • Did it flag unsupported answers instead of guessing?
  • Do the worksheets and memo tell a coherent story?

Correct anything that does not accurately reflect the project. Review the Feedback Log separately for proposed improvements to the collection process; accept or reject these through the maintained improvement process, not by silently editing the template.

Once you are comfortable with the workbook, treat it as the confirmed project requirements input.

docs.title: Step 5 — What Can Happen Next
docs.text:
The confirmed forms can then be passed into the separate SEPIO requirements-to-model workflow:

Confirmed Requirements Forms
        +
Requirement→SEPIO Mapping Registry
        +
SEPIO source schema
        ↓
Requirements-to-Model Output Package

That downstream package can include:

  1. Candidate SEPIO Covering Model
  2. Requirements Summary
  3. Requirements-to-Model Traceability
  4. Requirements Follow-Up & Modeling Decisions
  5. Gap & Extension Analysis
  6. Implementation Guidance
  7. Requirements Collection & Form Feedback (downstream mapping artifact; distinct from the agent’s Starter Kit Feedback Log)
  8. Generation Manifest

During the current pilot phase, an AI agent can generate these outputs with transparent provenance. Later, deterministic code can take over schema extraction, dependency closure, validation, traceability, and manifest generation.

The project representative does not need to perform these mappings manually.

docs.title: Key principle
docs.text:
Requirements first, SEPIO mapping second.

The requirements-collection workflow should first answer:

What does the selected canonical source currently represent, and what broader capabilities does the project evidence support as desired requirements?

Only after those requirements are reviewed should the mapping workflow ask:

How well does SEPIO represent those needs?

docs.title: More detailed guidance
docs.text:
A more comprehensive overview of the workflow and tasks can be found in Requirements_Collection_Overview.md.

Detailed guidance for building and reviewing the project evidence set can be found in RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md.

docs.title: Requirements Form Prompt — Complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms
docs.text:
Use this prompt after the project evidence base has been reviewed and, ideally, after a Resource Inventory / Evidence Package has been prepared using RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md.

The requirements workflow deliberately distinguishes current-state requirements from desired-state requirements:

  • Current state is controlled by the canonical source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or explicitly designated companion artifacts named in the selected project scope statement.
  • Desired state may be informed by a broader, evidence-supported set of project resources identified in the selected scope statement and Resource Inventory.

This separation is intentional. The current-state columns should remain conservative and reproducible, while the desired-state columns may capture a broader maximal evidence-supported requirements set for later human review and refinement.

Publicly accessible resources may be supplied as attachments, GitHub links, direct-download URLs, DOI/archive links, or version-pinned URLs. The agent should retrieve public resources itself whenever possible; human upload is a fallback.

docs.title: Copyable prompt
docs.text:
Copy the prompt below into your AI agent's interface and replace the bracketed text.

You are acting as a requirements analyst and as a knowledgeable representative of [PROJECT NAME].

Your task is to populate the SEPIO Requirements Forms workbook based on the selected project scope and the project materials and workflow resources I provide.

PROJECT

[PROJECT NAME]

SELECTED PROJECT SCOPE

[Paste the selected scope statement here. Prefer a scope statement produced by RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md and reviewed/selected/refined by the project representative.]

The selected scope statement must identify, explicitly or by reference to the Resource Inventory:

1. CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET
   The exact source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or explicitly designated companion artifacts that control answers in the "Used in Current Data?" / current-state columns.

2. DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET
   The broader set of project resources that may be used to identify desired/future requirements.

If the selected scope statement does not make these two source sets clear enough to apply reproducibly, stop and ask the project representative to clarify the scope before completing the forms.

REQUIREMENTS-COLLECTION MATERIALS

You will be provided access to the materials needed for this task. They may be supplied as:

- files attached directly to this prompt;
- public GitHub repository links;
- direct-download URLs;
- version-pinned GitHub URLs identifying a specific commit, tag, or release;
- DOI/archive links;
- other public project URLs or repository paths;
- a reviewed Resource Inventory / Evidence Package produced using `RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md`-  which may contain pointers/links to the types of resources above.

The core requirements-collection materials are:

1. `Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx`
2. `Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md`

A project Resource Inventory / Evidence Package should also be supplied when available.

REQUIREMENTS MATERIAL LOCATIONS

Requirements forms:
[ATTACHMENT OR URL TO Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx]

Instructions and guidance:
[ATTACHMENT OR URL TO Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md]

Resource inventory / evidence package, if available:
[ATTACHMENT OR URL TO PROJECT_Resource_Inventory.md]

Additional project materials, if any:
[ATTACHMENTS, URLS, DOI LINKS, OR REPOSITORY PATHS]

MATERIAL ACCESS RULES

1. If a public GitHub, DOI/archive, or other repository URL is provided, retrieve and use the referenced material directly.

2. For Markdown, YAML, JSON, CSV, text, schema, or similar files:
   - read the repository file directly when possible;
   - prefer the exact referenced version when the URL is version-pinned.

3. For `Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx` or any other binary spreadsheet:
   - retrieve/download the actual XLSX file;
   - do not rely on a rendered GitHub preview as a substitute for the workbook;
   - use the downloaded workbook itself as the template to populate.

4. If both a repository page URL and a direct/raw download URL are available for an XLSX file, prefer the direct downloadable file for workbook processing.

5. Do not require the project representative to manually download and re-upload a publicly accessible file unless you are unable to retrieve it yourself.

6. If a required file cannot be accessed:
   - identify the exact file/resource you could not retrieve;
   - provide the URL/path you attempted to use;
   - explain why the file is needed;
   - state whether the requirements review can proceed provisionally without it;
   - ask the project representative to upload that specific file only when necessary.

7. If a repository, DOI landing page, release page, or archive contains multiple plausible files, versions, or artifacts and the canonical one cannot be identified confidently, do not guess. Flag the ambiguity and ask for confirmation.

VERSION AND REPRODUCIBILITY RULES

8. Prefer version-pinned URLs when they are provided.

A version-pinned source may identify:
- a Git commit;
- a release tag;
- a versioned release;
- a DOI/archive version;
- another immutable version identifier.

9. If a version-pinned URL is provided, treat that exact version as authoritative for this requirements run unless explicitly instructed otherwise.

10. If only a moving branch such as `main` or `master` is provided:
   - use the current version available at the time of the review;
   - record the repository path and, when possible, the commit SHA, release identifier, or retrieval date used;
   - do not silently substitute an older cached or historical version.

11. If both a version-pinned source and a newer unpinned source are supplied:
   - do not silently merge them;
   - follow the source-role rules in the selected scope statement;
   - record materially relevant differences.

12. Record enough source-version information in the Requirements Review Memo that another agent could reproduce the review later.

RESOURCE INVENTORY / EVIDENCE PACKAGE

13. When a reviewed Resource Inventory / Evidence Package is supplied:
   - use the selected scope statement as the controlling rule for current-state and desired-state evidence;
   - use sources classified as CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL only for current-state answers unless the scope statement explicitly designates additional canonical companion artifacts;
   - use DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT sources only for desired-state reasoning, unless they are also designated CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL;
   - use REPRESENTATIVE EXAMPLES to verify actual data usage;
   - do not treat sources marked CONTEXT_ONLY / DO NOT TREAT AS CANONICAL as evidence of requirements;
   - preserve unresolved issues for human review rather than guessing.

14. If the Resource Inventory identifies public files that should be inspected during requirements elicitation, attempt to retrieve those files yourself before asking the project representative to upload them.

15. If the Resource Inventory and a directly inspected canonical source disagree:
   - the selected canonical current-state source controls the current-state answer;
   - flag the discrepancy;
   - do not silently alter the current-state answer based on a noncanonical source.

16. If the Resource Inventory identifies material that a human may need to provide, first determine whether you can retrieve it yourself. Human upload is a fallback, not the default.

Use `Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md` to understand each form, question, controlled value, and response convention.

CURRENT-STATE VS DESIRED-STATE RULES

17. Treat the two requirements columns as answering different questions.

CURRENT STATE / F1:
"What is represented in the canonical current-state source set selected for this review?"

DESIRED STATE / F2:
"What should the SEPIO-based representation support, based on the maximal evidence-supported project requirements allowed by the selected scope?"

18. Populate CURRENT STATE strictly from the selected CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET.

Do not mark a requirement as currently represented merely because it appears in:
- an intermediate curation artifact;
- an earlier or alternate release;
- a different distribution;
- a paper or documentation page;
- a roadmap;
- an upstream source;
- a downstream application;
unless that resource is explicitly included in the selected current-state canonical source set.

19. Populate DESIRED STATE from the broader DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET permitted by the selected scope statement.

This may include, when relevant and not explicitly out of scope:
- explicit future requirements or roadmaps;
- current project documentation and papers;
- intermediate curation/analysis artifacts;
- information captured elsewhere in the project's own pipeline but dropped from the canonical export;
- alternate or earlier project distributions;
- other project-maintained representations;
- project examples, competency questions, or implementation guidance.

20. For the initial requirements pass, prefer a MAXIMAL EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED desired-state requirements set when the selected scope authorizes it.

"Maximal" does NOT mean speculative. Every desired-state Y/M answer must be supported by project-specific evidence.

The human reviewer may later narrow or remove desired-state requirements.

21. When a desired-state answer differs from the current-state answer, explicitly document the supporting source in the form's `Explanation / Considerations` field.

When useful, classify the desired-state support using one of these labels:

- EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
  A roadmap, issue, requirements document, competency question, or explicit statement says the project wants/needs the capability.

- EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
  The project already captures or uses the information in an intermediate artifact, alternate distribution, curation workflow, analysis product, or other project-maintained representation, but it is absent from the selected canonical current-state distribution.

- DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
  A paper, model/design document, curation guide, or other authoritative project documentation describes the capability as part of the intended project model or data product, even if it is absent from the selected canonical current-state source.

Recommended explanation format when F1 and F2 differ:

"Current state: [brief canonical-source observation].
Desired-state support: [SUPPORT TYPE] — [Source ID/title/version]: [brief evidence and rationale]."

22. If several desired-state sources support the same requirement, cite the strongest and most direct source(s) rather than listing everything.

23. A source that explicitly says a capability is out of scope, rejected, deprecated, or intentionally excluded should not be used to justify a desired-state requirement unless another authoritative source explicitly reverses that decision.

IMPORTANT REQUIREMENTS-ELICITATION RULES

24. Answer the forms based on what this project actually represents or explicitly requires. Do not choose answers because they map conveniently to SEPIO.

25. Respect the selected project scope statement. Distinguish the scoped project/data product from:
   - upstream source systems;
   - internal systems outside scope;
   - downstream APIs;
   - user-interface/display enrichments;
   - derived products outside scope, unless explicitly admitted as desired-state evidence.

26. Distinguish:
   - information represented by the selected canonical current-state source;
   - information supported only as a desired-state requirement;
   - information available only in upstream sources;
   - information created or enriched only downstream;
   - process metadata that documents how data were generated but is not itself represented in the canonical source.

27. Use representative data/examples to confirm how the model is actually used, but do not infer a project-wide requirement from a single unusual record unless other evidence supports it.

28. Ground answers in supplied or discovered evidence. Distinguish what a source explicitly establishes from what you infer.

29. Do not invent missing requirements. If available project materials do not provide enough information to answer confidently:
   - use the form's uncertainty/review mechanism where available;
   - preserve the uncertainty;
   - flag the issue clearly for human review.

30. Preserve project-specific terminology and examples in explanatory fields where useful.

31. For each non-obvious answer, keep track of the source evidence that supports it so that the answer can be reviewed and traced back to its source.

32. Assess the project comprehensively across:
   - claim/assertion types;
   - claim representation structure;
   - semantic structure of reified claims;
   - evidence item types and representations;
   - evidence interpretation, grouping, direction, strength, and stacking;
   - provenance about information artifacts, agents, methods, processes, semantic alignment, encoding, and retrieval;
   - relationships between claim types and evidence types.

33. Do not use the Requirement→SEPIO mapping registry to decide what the project's requirements should be unless explicitly instructed to do so. Requirements elicitation must remain independent of current SEPIO coverage.

34. Do not proceed to Requirement→SEPIO mapping or generate a SEPIO covering model unless explicitly asked.

WORKBOOK HANDLING RULES

35. Populate the provided `Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx` workbook itself rather than recreating the forms from scratch.

36. Preserve the workbook's existing visual formatting and structure, including:
   - sheet names;
   - row and column positions;
   - fills/shading;
   - fonts;
   - borders;
   - alignment;
   - word wrapping;
   - row heights;
   - column widths;
   - data validation;
   - other template formatting.

37. Change only the cells needed to enter project responses, explanations, examples, or explicitly requested review notes.

38. Do not redesign, restyle, normalize, or rebuild the workbook.

39. If technical limitations prevent safe editing of the workbook without altering its formatting, stop and report the limitation rather than silently rebuilding the workbook in a different style.

40. The returned XLSX should open normally in Excel without triggering a repair/recovery warning. Do not "fix" workbook internals by reconstructing the workbook if doing so changes the visible template formatting. If an Excel-integrity problem cannot be corrected without risking formatting changes, report it for human review.

COMPLETENESS AND CONSISTENCY REVIEW

41. Before finalizing the workbook, perform a completeness and consistency pass:
   - check every applicable field;
   - compare answers across forms;
   - identify contradictions;
   - identify unanswered or weakly supported questions;
   - identify places where free text implies a requirement not captured by a structured response;
   - verify that every F1/current-state Y/M answer is supported by the selected current-state canonical source set;
   - verify that every broader F2/desired-state Y/M answer is supported by an allowed desired-state source;
   - verify that F1 and F2 were not conflated;
   - make sure upstream evidence/provenance capabilities were not incorrectly attributed to the canonical project source;
   - make sure process provenance described in documentation is not automatically treated as provenance stored in canonical records;
   - make sure downstream transformations are not treated as native current-state representation unless the selected scope says otherwise;
   - verify that the Explanation / Considerations field names the desired-state supporting source whenever F2 differs materially from F1.

42. Preserve unresolved issues rather than forcing a Y/N answer when the evidence supports uncertainty.

DELIVERABLES

A. Completed requirements workbook

Return a completed copy of the supplied workbook.

FILE NAMING:
Use:

[PROJECT]_Requirements_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].xlsx

Example:
MeDIC_Requirements_v0.2_20261013_1643.xlsx

Use 24-hour/military time. Use `HHMM` without a colon for cross-platform filename compatibility.

If a prior requirements version is supplied, increment or retain the version according to the project representative's instruction. If no version is specified, use `v0.1`.

Preserve the original workbook formatting and structure, including existing row heights and any validation rules. Do not rebuild the template, change its field numbering, or add validation rules not present in the supplied workbook. In EIT, F7 (Specific Kinds of this Item Type) is optional; Evidence Item Group is a column, not a category row. In PROV, levels are identified by the Provenance Level column, not informational rows.

B. Requirements Review Memo

Return a Markdown memo named:

[PROJECT]_Requirements_Review_Memo_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].md

The memo must contain:

1. Project scope used
   - reproduce or precisely summarize the selected scope statement;
   - explicitly identify the CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET;
   - explicitly identify the DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET.

2. Requirements-workflow materials used

3. Sources used for CURRENT-STATE requirements
   - list the exact datasets/distributions/schema artifacts that controlled F1/current-state responses;
   - record exact versions/releases/commits/DOI/archive versions/retrieval dates as applicable;
   - explain any explicitly designated canonical companion artifacts.

4. Sources used for DESIRED-STATE requirements
   - list the broader sources actually used to populate F2/desired-state responses;
   - group or annotate them where useful as:
     EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT,
     EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT,
     DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT;
   - identify sources considered but excluded from desired-state reasoning and why.

5. High-confidence conclusions

6. Answers requiring human review

7. Apparent conflicts or missing information

8. Files/resources the agent was unable to access, if any

9. Form/guidance questions that were difficult to interpret

10. Important assumptions made

11. Project observations that suggest improvements to the requirements forms or guidance

12. Diverse representative data examples

Include a small but diverse set of concrete examples that make the requirements tangible.

Provide:
- a few CURRENT-STATE examples directly from the selected canonical source set; and
- a few broader/maximal DESIRED-STATE examples drawn from allowed desired-state sources when these reveal additional requirements.

For each example, record:
- Example ID
- Current-state or desired-state example
- Source ID/title/version
- What requirement pattern it demonstrates

Represent the example as close to its source representation as practical:

- tabular/database source:
  show the example as a row/table with the original field/column names where possible.
  If a complete logical record is distributed across multiple tables, it is acceptable to denormalize the relevant fields into a single illustrative row, but label it as DENORMALIZED and identify the contributing source tables.

- JSON/YAML document:
  show a compact JSON/YAML object preserving source field names and nesting.

- RDF/graph data:
  show triples/quads/edge properties as appropriate.

- free text/document source:
  show only the minimal relevant excerpt/fields necessary to demonstrate the requirement; do not reproduce unnecessary copyrighted text.

- composite/maximal example assembled from several project sources:
  label it COMPOSITE/ILLUSTRATIVE, identify every contributing source, and do not present the assembled record as if it existed verbatim in one source.

Do not fabricate values to make examples look complete.

C. Source-access status

Include a concise statement confirming:

- which linked resources were successfully retrieved;
- which attached files were used;
- whether any fallback human uploads were required;
- whether the review used version-pinned or moving-source URLs;
- any public resources that could not be retrieved.

D. Requirements-collection Feedback Log

Return a completed project-specific copy of the supplied `Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx`, named `[PROJECT]_Requirements_Feedback_Log_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].xlsx`. Follow the template’s `Agent Instructions` and `Controlled Vocabularies`. Record concrete suggestions to improve forms, fields, controlled responses, instructions, or the process, with sheet/field references and rationale where possible. Do not use this log to replace the Review Memo’s project-specific unresolved questions. Do not change the master requirements template or guidance on the basis of feedback. If no issues are identified, report that explicitly in the log or handoff.

Do not proceed to Requirement→SEPIO mapping or generate a SEPIO covering model unless I explicitly ask you to do so.

docs.title: What to provide to the agent
docs.text:
Provide access to:

  • Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx
  • Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx
  • Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md
  • the selected project scope statement
  • the reviewed [PROJECT]_Resource_Inventory.md, when available
  • any private or local project materials identified as necessary

The selected scope statement should clearly identify:

  1. the canonical current-state source set controlling current-state answers; and
  2. the broader evidence set allowed to inform desired-state answers.

If the Resource Inventory provides multiple provisional scope alternatives, the project representative should normally select one before requirements completion.

docs.title: Recommended GitHub-link pattern
docs.text:
During active development, links to main are acceptable:

Requirements forms:
https://github.com/sepio-framework/sepio-linkml/blob/main/docs/requirements-collection/Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx

Instructions and guidance:
https://github.com/sepio-framework/sepio-linkml/blob/main/docs/requirements-collection/Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md

For a reproducible requirements run, prefer links pinned to an exact commit or release.

A direct/raw URL for the XLSX may also be supplied when convenient.

docs.title: Recommended project-specific invocation
docs.text:
Complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms for the following project using REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md.

PROJECT:
[PROJECT NAME]

SELECTED PROJECT SCOPE:
[PASTE THE SELECTED SCOPE STATEMENT]

REQUIREMENTS FORM PROMPT:
[URL TO REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md]

REQUIREMENTS FORMS:
[URL TO Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx]

REQUIREMENTS GUIDANCE:
[URL TO Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md]

FEEDBACK LOG TEMPLATE:
[URL OR ATTACHMENT TO Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx]

RESOURCE INVENTORY:
[URL OR ATTACHMENT FOR PROJECT_Resource_Inventory.md]

Use the selected current-state canonical source set strictly for F1/current-state answers.
Use the broader desired-state source set allowed by the selected scope to build an evidence-supported maximal F2/desired-state requirements set.
If F2 differs from F1, name the desired-state supporting source and support type in Explanation / Considerations.

docs.title: Relationship to resource discovery
docs.text:
For projects where the evidence base or appropriate review scope is not already obvious, run RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md first.

The resulting Resource Inventory should provide: - candidate canonical current-state sources; - broader desired-state evidence sources; - multiple provisional scope statements; - a recommended scope; - representative examples; - access/retrieval guidance; - unresolved questions.

docs.title: What not to provide for this stage
docs.text:
The Requirement→SEPIO mapping registry is intentionally not part of the requirements-elicitation task.

Requirements elicitation should determine what the project currently represents and what it should support independently of current SEPIO coverage. Mapping to SEPIO occurs only after the requirements record has been reviewed and stabilized.

docs.title: Resource Inventory — Guidance for SEPIO Requirements Collection
docs.text:
A Resource Inventory is the evidence package used to support a SEPIO requirements review.

Its purpose is not merely to list project files. It should make clear:

  • which exact source(s) control current-state requirements;
  • which additional sources may inform desired-state requirements;
  • which sources are context only;
  • which versions/releases should be used;
  • what examples best demonstrate the project semantics;
  • what conflicts, missing information, or access issues remain.

For many projects, the easiest way to create a first draft is to use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md.

docs.title: 1. Start with the canonical current-state source
docs.text:
Identify the exact source, dataset, distribution, schema, or release that should control answers to:

Used in Current Data?

Examples:

  • a specific version of indications.xlsx;
  • a current LinkML schema release plus designated canonical records;
  • a particular KG build/export;
  • a database schema plus one named production distribution.

Prefer a version-pinned source when possible.

If several artifacts must be interpreted together—for example a data table plus its canonical data dictionary—identify them as canonical companion artifacts.

Do not automatically include intermediate files, alternate releases, upstream sources, downstream APIs, or papers in the current-state source set.

docs.title: 2. Identify sources that may inform desired state
docs.text:
Desired-state requirements can use a broader project evidence base when the selected scope permits it.

Useful sources may include:

  • explicit requirements or roadmaps;
  • current papers or model documentation;
  • curation/evidence guidance;
  • intermediate curation or analysis artifacts;
  • fields captured in the pipeline but dropped from the canonical export;
  • alternate or earlier project distributions;
  • competency questions;
  • implementation/design documents.

When useful, classify these sources as:

docs.title: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
docs.text:
The project explicitly says it wants or needs the capability.

Examples: - roadmap item; - GitHub issue; - requirements document; - approved competency question.

docs.title: EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
docs.text:
The project already captures or uses the information somewhere, but it is absent from the chosen canonical current-state distribution.

Examples: - semantic-alignment intermediates retained in curation files but dropped from a final compact export; - provenance stored in an internal curation record but not emitted publicly.

docs.title: DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
docs.text:
Authoritative project documentation describes the capability as part of the intended model/product even though it is absent from the selected canonical distribution.

Examples: - a current project paper describing qualifiers not present in the selected release; - a modeling guide describing intended evidence structures.

Do not use a source to justify desired state if it explicitly says the feature is out of scope, rejected, or deprecated unless another authoritative source reverses that decision.

docs.title: 3. Gather representative examples
docs.text:
Real examples are essential because schemas and documentation may not show how fields are actually used.

Try to select a small but diverse set that covers important patterns, for example:

  • a typical claim;
  • a claim with qualifiers/context;
  • a claim with a source/evidence reference;
  • a claim with richer provenance;
  • a record showing normalization or transformation;
  • a case where information exists in an intermediate artifact but is dropped from the canonical export;
  • an alternate distribution exposing a capability absent from the canonical one;
  • an unusual but important edge case.

Assign stable IDs such as E01, E02, E03.

For each example, record:

  • source;
  • claim/record type;
  • what requirement pattern it demonstrates;
  • why it was selected.

docs.title: 4. Useful source categories
docs.text: Depending on the project, useful resources may include:

docs.title: Schemas and formal models
docs.text:
• LinkML
  • JSON Schema
  • SQL schemas
  • SHACL
  • UML/class models
  • data dictionaries
  • export specifications

docs.title: Canonical distributions
docs.text:
• release spreadsheets
  • JSON/YAML datasets
  • KGX/RDF exports
  • database dumps
  • versioned API payload specifications

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• model overview
  • README files
  • architecture/design documents
  • semantic conventions
  • project papers

docs.title: Curation/evidence materials
docs.text:
• curation SOPs
  • evidence classification rules
  • scoring/confidence guidance
  • interpretation guidelines
  • review/approval workflows

docs.title: Pipeline/provenance materials
docs.text:
• ingest/transformation documentation
  • normalization/grounding procedures
  • intermediate curation artifacts
  • source-attribution rules
  • logs or intermediate outputs when they reveal intentionally retained project information

docs.title: Requirements/future intent
docs.text:
• roadmaps
  • GitHub issues
  • requirements documents
  • user stories
  • competency questions
  • approved design proposals

docs.title: 5. Distinguish neighboring resources from project requirements
docs.text:
Pay particular attention to resources that are nearby but not actually part of the scoped project.

Examples:

  • upstream source databases;
  • regulatory documents from which the project extracts information;
  • external ontologies used for normalization;
  • downstream KGs;
  • APIs or user interfaces that add derived information;
  • historical or superseded releases.

These may be useful for context, but they should not automatically control current-state answers.

They may inform desired state only when the selected scope explicitly permits them and the evidence is genuinely project-specific.

docs.title: 6. Record versions and conflicts
docs.text:
For every important resource, record:

  • version;
  • release;
  • tag;
  • commit SHA;
  • DOI/archive version;
  • retrieval date when no immutable version is available.

If two resources disagree:

  1. identify the conflict;
  2. identify which source controls current state;
  3. state whether the other source may still inform desired state;
  4. do not silently merge the two.

Example:

Release v1.3 lacks qualifier fields, but the current project paper explicitly describes contextual hyperrelations. v1.3 controls current state; the paper may support desired state under a maximal scope.

docs.title: 7. Recommended Resource Inventory fields
docs.text:
A useful inventory table includes:

  • Source ID
  • Name
  • Type
  • URL / repository path
  • Version / release / commit
  • Authority level
  • Requirements role
  • Desired-state support type
  • Requirement dimensions supported
  • Important directly observed facts
  • Access status
  • Retrieval / human-assistance guidance
  • Notes / cautions

Suggested requirements-role values:

  • CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL
  • CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION
  • DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT
  • CURRENT_AND_DESIRED
  • CONTEXT_ONLY

Suggested desired-state support values:

  • EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
  • EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
  • DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
  • N/A

docs.title: 8. Access and retrieval guidance
docs.text:
The requirements agent should normally retrieve public resources itself.

A human should need to intervene only when:

  • public retrieval fails;
  • authentication/private access is required;
  • the file exists only locally;
  • multiple plausible versions/files exist and the canonical one is unclear;
  • the human must decide which scope/version is authoritative.

When human help is needed, the inventory should say:

  • exactly what file/resource is needed;
  • why it matters;
  • what question it will resolve;
  • whether the requirements review can proceed provisionally without it.

docs.title: 9. Candidate scope statements
docs.text:
A good Resource Inventory should end with candidate scope statements.

At minimum:

docs.title: Minimal / canonical-distribution-only
docs.text:
Use the canonical distribution as both the current-state and desired-state evidence base.

Best when the goal is to describe one concrete release conservatively.

docs.title: Maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state
docs.text:
Use only the named canonical source(s) for current-state answers, but allow broader project evidence for desired-state requirements.

Best when the goal is to discover the broadest evidence-supported requirements set before human review.

Additional scopes may be useful for projects with multiple legitimate products or distributions.

The project representative should review and select/refine one scope before final requirements completion.

docs.title: 10. Final handoff
docs.text:
Before giving the inventory to the requirements agent, make sure it clearly answers:

  • What controls current-state answers?
  • What may inform desired-state answers?
  • Which scope was selected?
  • Which sources are context only?
  • Which examples should the agent inspect?
  • What versions should it use?
  • What public resources should it retrieve itself?
  • Is any human-provided material genuinely required?
  • What important questions remain unresolved?

If those questions are clear, the inventory is ready to accompany REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md.

docs.title: Resource Inventory Prompt
docs.text:
Use this prompt as the preliminary evidence-discovery and scope-definition step before completing the SEPIO Requirements Forms when the authoritative project evidence base or appropriate requirements-review scope is not already obvious.

The purpose of this task is to:

  1. identify, evaluate, and organize the project resources that can inform requirements elicitation;
  2. distinguish resources that should control current-state requirements from broader resources that may inform desired-state requirements; and
  3. only after the resource inventory has been assembled and source IDs assigned, propose one or more provisional project scope statements for human selection before the requirements forms are completed.

The discovery agent should not complete the requirements forms and should not map requirements to SEPIO.

docs.title: Copyable prompt
docs.text:
<pre><code>You are acting as a resource-discovery, scope-definition, and evidence-preparation agent for the SEPIO requirements-collection workflow.

Your task is to identify, evaluate, and organize the best available resources for understanding the following project/data/model and then recommend one or more reasonable scopes for a subsequent requirements review.

PROJECT
[PROJECT NAME]

INITIAL PROJECT CONTEXT / SCOPE NOTES
[Optional. Insert any initial project description, known canonical distribution, exclusions, questions, or tentative scope notes from the project representative. If nothing is supplied, discover and propose the scope from the available project resources.]

GOAL

Assemble a proposed Resource Inventory / Evidence Package that another AI agent can later use to complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms accurately and reproducibly.

Do not complete the requirements forms yet.
Do not map project concepts to SEPIO yet.
Do not infer project requirements from what SEPIO supports.

A central output of this task is one or more PROVISIONAL SCOPE STATEMENTS that the project representative can review and select before requirements elicitation.

IMPORTANT ORDER-OF-OPERATIONS RULE

Do NOT author the final provisional scope statements before you have:

1. discovered the relevant project resources;
2. assigned each source a stable Source ID such as S01, S02, S03;
3. classified each source's authority and requirements role;
4. identified representative examples;
5. documented important source conflicts, ambiguities, version issues, and scope exclusions; and
6. identified the recommended current-state canonical source set and broader desired-state evidence set.

The scope statements should be written AFTER the Resource Inventory and source classification are established so that they can refer to concrete resources by **Source ID + name/version**.

Think of the workflow this way:

RESOURCE DISCOVERY
    ↓
RESOURCE INVENTORY WITH SOURCE IDs
    ↓
SOURCE ROLE / AUTHORITY CLASSIFICATION
    ↓
RECOMMENDED CURRENT-STATE AND DESIRED-STATE SOURCE SETS
    ↓
PROVISIONAL SCOPE STATEMENTS
    ↓
HUMAN SCOPE SELECTION
    ↓
REQUIREMENTS FORM COMPLETION

The Resource Inventory should make explicit:

- which exact source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or companion artifacts should control CURRENT-STATE requirements answers;
- which broader project resources may be used to identify DESIRED-STATE requirements;
- what resources are context only and must not be used as requirements evidence;
- which materials are publicly accessible and should normally be retrieved directly by the later requirements agent;
- which materials, if any, require a human project representative to download, upload, or clarify.

SCOPE-DESIGN PRINCIPLES

1. Separate current-state scope from desired-state scope.

The subsequent requirements forms contain two distinct concepts:

CURRENT STATE:
What is represented in the selected canonical project source(s) for this review?

DESIRED STATE:
What should the SEPIO-based representation support, based on the broader, evidence-supported project requirements allowed by the selected scope?

Do not assume the same source set must control both.

2. Every provisional scope statement must contain TWO EXPLICIT SUBSECTIONS.

Each proposed scope must be structured with at least:

### Current-state canonical scope

This subsection must state:

- what project/data product is being assessed for current state;
- the exact Source IDs + source names/versions that control current-state / F1 / "Used in Current Data?" answers;
- any explicitly designated canonical companion artifacts;
- what kinds of related resources are excluded from current-state reasoning.

Use language such as:

"Current-state/F1 answers must be based only on S05 — [source name/version] and S06 — [source name/version]. No other resource may change an F1 answer unless the scope is revised."

The later requirements agent must strictly stick to this set for current-state answers.

3. Every provisional scope statement must also contain:

### Desired-state scope

This subsection must state:

- what broader project capabilities are in scope for desired-state/F2 requirements;
- the exact Source IDs + source names/versions that may inform desired state;
- whether each broader source is being used as:
  - EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
  - EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
  - DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
- important exclusions from desired-state reasoning;
- the rule that any F2 answer that differs from F1 must identify its supporting source in `Explanation / Considerations`.

Use language such as:

"Desired-state/F2 answers may additionally draw on S01 — [paper], S08 — [intermediate artifact], and S09 — [alignment/QC artifact] to identify a maximal, evidence-supported requirements set. When F2 differs from F1, the requirements agent must identify the supporting source and support type in `Explanation / Considerations`."

4. The CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET must be precise and reproducible.

This is the exact set of source(s), dataset(s), distribution(s), release(s), or explicitly designated companion artifacts that the later requirements agent must use to populate current-state / "Used in Current Data?" columns.

Examples:
- one versioned `indications.xlsx` distribution;
- one current LinkML schema release plus explicitly designated canonical example data;
- one KG release artifact;
- one database export and its required schema/data dictionary.

Do not broaden current state simply because richer information exists elsewhere in the project.

5. The DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET may be broader.

When relevant and not explicitly out of scope, desired-state evidence may include:
- explicit future requirements or roadmaps;
- current project/model documentation and papers;
- intermediate curation/analysis artifacts;
- data captured elsewhere in the project pipeline but dropped from the canonical export;
- alternate or earlier project distributions;
- other project-maintained representations;
- competency questions;
- curation guidance;
- implementation/design documents.

The purpose is to support an initial MAXIMAL EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED requirements set that a human reviewer can later narrow.

"Maximal" does not mean speculative. Every desired-state capability must be supported by project-specific evidence.

6. Classify desired-state support where useful.

Use these labels when characterizing why a noncanonical resource is informative for desired state:

- EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
  A roadmap, issue, requirements document, competency question, or explicit statement says the project wants/needs the capability.

- EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
  The project already captures or uses the information in an intermediate artifact, alternate distribution, curation workflow, analysis product, or other project-maintained representation, but it is absent from the proposed canonical current-state distribution.

- DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
  A paper, model/design document, curation guide, or other authoritative project document describes the capability as part of the intended project model/data product, even if absent from the proposed canonical current-state source.

7. Do not use a source as desired-state evidence when it explicitly says the capability is out of scope, rejected, deprecated, or intentionally excluded, unless another authoritative project source explicitly reverses that decision.

SOURCE-DISCOVERY RULES

8. Respect supplied project context and discover scope boundaries.

Distinguish the scoped project/data product from:
- upstream source databases;
- internal systems that are outside scope;
- downstream APIs;
- user-interface/display enrichments;
- unrelated derived exports;
- historical/superseded project versions.

For every source, consider whether it describes:
- the canonical project/data model itself;
- a candidate canonical current-state distribution;
- an alternate or historical project representation;
- an intermediate curation/analysis artifact;
- an upstream source;
- a downstream representation;
- an implementation detail;
- future/project intent.

9. Prefer current, authoritative sources, but do not discard older/alternate/intermediate project artifacts that may legitimately inform desired state.

For CURRENT-STATE canonical-source recommendations, prioritize:
a. current authoritative schema/data model;
b. current canonical distribution/release;
c. current authoritative data dictionary;
d. current representative data/examples;
e. explicitly designated canonical companion artifacts.

For DESIRED-STATE evidence, also consider:
f. current model/design documentation and papers;
g. current curation/evidence/provenance guidance;
h. current ingest/transformation/pipeline artifacts;
i. explicit requirements, competency questions, roadmap documents, or issues;
j. intermediate curation/analysis artifacts;
k. alternate or earlier project distributions that expose project capabilities or intent.

When sources conflict:
- identify the conflict;
- state which source should control current state;
- explain whether the conflicting resource remains useful for desired-state evidence;
- do not silently reconcile the difference.

10. Look for sources that can answer questions about:

- the kinds of claims/associations/statements represented;
- how claims are structurally packaged;
- whether claims are represented as reified objects, direct graph edges, slot/value pairs, tabular records, or other forms;
- how subject, relationship/predicate, object, and qualifiers are represented;
- what kinds of evidence items are retained or referenced;
- whether evidence items are represented locally, externally, or both;
- whether evidence direction, strength, grouping, or higher-order synthesis is represented;
- confidence or scoring information;
- provenance about agents, methods, resources, dates, review, extraction, grounding, normalization, encoding, retrieval, or ingest;
- what information is retained from upstream sources versus discarded or transformed;
- what richer information is captured in intermediate project artifacts but lost in the canonical distribution;
- current capabilities versus documented future/intended requirements.

11. Include representative data/examples.

When possible, identify a small but diverse set of examples that covers the major claim and EPC patterns.

Include examples from:
- candidate canonical current-state sources; and
- broader desired-state sources when they reveal additional project requirements.

Prefer examples that collectively test different situations, such as:
- a claim with publication or regulatory support;
- a claim with structured evidence metadata;
- a claim with qualifiers/context;
- a claim with source/provenance but little explicit evidence;
- a case where richer project-internal EPC is dropped from the canonical export;
- a case involving normalization/transformation;
- an alternate distribution exposing a capability absent from the canonical one;
- any unusual but important pattern.

Do not collect large datasets when a small representative sample will establish the relevant structure and semantics.

Assign each representative example a stable ID such as E01, E02, E03.

12. Record precise source locations and source roles BEFORE writing the scope statements.

Assign each source a stable ID such as S01, S02, S03.

For each source, record:
- Source ID
- Source title/name
- Source type
- URL or repository path
- Repository/release/tag/commit/version when available
- Authority level
- Requirements role
- Desired-state support type, when applicable
- Scope relevance
- Requirement dimensions supported
- Important directly observed facts
- Access status
- Whether the later requirements agent should retrieve it directly or human assistance may be required
- Notes/cautions

Use these authority labels where appropriate:
- PRIMARY_AUTHORITATIVE
- SUPPORTING_CURRENT
- REPRESENTATIVE_EXAMPLE
- HISTORICAL_BACKGROUND
- OUT_OF_SCOPE_CONTEXT

Use these REQUIREMENTS ROLE labels:
- CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL
- CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION
- DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT
- CURRENT_AND_DESIRED
- CONTEXT_ONLY

A source should receive CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL or CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION only if you recommend that the later requirements agent be allowed to use it for current-state answers under at least one proposed scope.

13. Capture directly observed facts from key sources.

For each major authoritative source, record concise facts explicitly supported by the source.

Examples:
- "The canonical table contains subject ID, object ID, and a source-text field."
- "The canonical record does not contain evidence-direction or evidence-strength fields."
- "Intermediate curation records retain Name Resolver candidates and LLM QC outcomes, but the final export drops them."
- "The project paper describes hyperrelations absent from the selected release."

Distinguish these directly observed facts from interpretation.

Use labels where helpful:
- DIRECT
- INFERRED
- UNRESOLVED

14. Retrieve publicly accessible materials before asking the human to provide them.

When a potentially important source is publicly accessible:
- first attempt to access/download it yourself;
- follow GitHub, DOI/archive, release, and direct-download links;
- inspect actual files/artifacts when record-level or schema-level details matter.

Human assistance is a fallback, not the default.

15. Identify inaccessible, ambiguous, or human-supplied materials precisely.

Human intervention may be needed when:
- the agent cannot access/download the resource;
- authentication, institutional permission, or a private repository is required;
- the source exists only locally/internally;
- multiple plausible files/versions exist and the canonical one cannot be identified confidently;
- the public copy is stale/incomplete and the representative may have a better copy;
- a human decision is required to choose the canonical source/version or scope.

If human assistance is needed:
- identify the exact file/resource;
- provide the URL/path when known;
- explain why it matters;
- state what question it is needed to answer;
- state whether discovery/requirements elicitation can proceed provisionally without it;
- tell the project representative exactly what to download, upload, or clarify.

16. Distinguish process documentation from stored project content.

A project may document curation, extraction, review, normalization, mapping, evidence assessment, encoding, or transformation.

For each such source, determine whether it shows:
- information actually stored in the proposed canonical current-state source;
- information captured elsewhere by the project but omitted from the canonical export;
- only an implementation process with no evidence that its outputs are retained.

This distinction is especially important for desired-state scope design.

17. Do not begin filling the SEPIO Requirements Forms until the Resource Inventory has been reviewed and one project scope statement has been selected, or the project representative explicitly authorizes the requirements agent to use the recommended scope.

PROVISIONAL SCOPE STATEMENTS

18. Author provisional scope statements ONLY AFTER the Resource Inventory and recommended source sets have been completed.

The scope statements should function as selections over the Resource Inventory.

Do not write vague statements such as:
"Use the current dataset and relevant documentation."

Instead write:
"Use S05 — `matrix_indication_list.xlsx`, v1.3.0 and S06 — `matrix_contraindication_list.xlsx`, v1.3.0 for current state. Desired state may additionally use S01 — MeDIC primary publication and S09 — FDA semantic-alignment/QC intermediates..."

Every named resource should be identifiable from the Resource Inventory by Source ID and name/version.

19. At minimum, provide:

SCOPE A — MINIMAL / CANONICAL-DISTRIBUTION-ONLY

This scope should:
- identify the narrowest defensible CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET;
- restrict current-state answers to those canonical source(s);
- normally restrict desired-state answers to the same canonical source(s), unless a small number of explicitly inseparable canonical companion artifacts are required;
- produce a conservative requirements record describing the canonical distribution itself.

Structure it as:

### Current-state canonical scope
- Scope statement
- Sources: Sxx — [name/version], Syy — [name/version]
- Explicit exclusions

### Desired-state scope
- Scope statement
- Sources: usually the same source set for the minimal option
- Explicit exclusions

### Strengths / tradeoffs

20. Also provide:

SCOPE B — MAXIMAL / CANONICAL CURRENT STATE + BROAD DESIRED STATE

This scope should:
- identify the exact CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCE SET;
- require the later agent to use only that set for current-state/F1 answers;
- identify a broader DESIRED-STATE EVIDENCE SET;
- allow desired-state/F2 answers to draw on project-specific evidence such as:
  - intermediate curation/analysis artifacts;
  - alternate/earlier project distributions;
  - other maintained project outputs;
  - authoritative papers/documentation;
  - curation/modeling guidance;
  - roadmaps/issues/explicit requirements;
- aim for a maximal evidence-supported desired-state requirements set that the human reviewer can later whittle down;
- require the requirements agent to name the desired-state supporting source in `Explanation / Considerations` whenever F2 differs from F1.

Structure it as:

### Current-state canonical scope
- Scope statement
- Exact Source IDs + names/versions
- Canonical companions, if any
- Explicit exclusions
- Rule that no noncanonical source may change F1 unless the scope is revised

### Desired-state scope
- Scope statement
- Exact Source IDs + names/versions
- Desired-state support type for each broader source
- Explicit exclusions
- Rule that F2 differences must cite supporting source + support type in `Explanation / Considerations`

### Strengths / tradeoffs

21. If other reasonable project scopes emerge, provide additional alternatives such as:
- CURRENT RELEASE + CURRENT PIPELINE ARTIFACTS;
- CORE PRODUCT + DESIGNATED COMPANION DATASETS;
- DOMAIN-SPECIFIC SUBSET;
- STRICT HISTORICAL RELEASE;
- CURRENT PRODUCT FAMILY / MULTI-DISTRIBUTION SCOPE.

Every additional scope must use the same explicit two-part structure:

### Current-state canonical scope
### Desired-state scope

22. Recommend one scope.

After presenting alternatives:
- identify the scope you recommend for the initial requirements exercise;
- explain why;
- state the tradeoff between reproducibility/conservatism and broader requirements discovery.

Unless project context argues otherwise, prefer recommending the MAXIMAL scope for the initial requirements pass because it preserves a strict canonical basis for current state while surfacing a broader evidence-supported desired-state requirements set for human review.

DELIVERABLE

Return a Markdown document named:

[PROJECT_NAME]_Resource_Inventory.md

IMPORTANT: Use the following section order. The Resource Inventory and source classification must appear BEFORE the provisional scope statements so that the scope can reference established Source IDs.

A. Project context used

Restate the supplied project context/scope notes and any important assumptions used during discovery.

B. Resource inventory

Provide a table with these columns:

- Source ID
- Name
- Type
- URL / repository path
- Version / release / commit
- Authority level
- Requirements role
- Desired-state support type
- Requirement dimensions supported
- Important directly observed facts
- Access status
- Retrieval / human-assistance guidance
- Notes / cautions

For Desired-state support type, use when applicable:
- EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
- EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
- DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
- N/A

For Access status, use concise values where possible:
- PUBLIC_ACCESSIBLE
- PUBLIC_DOWNLOADABLE
- ACCESS_NOT_VERIFIED
- ACCESS_FAILED
- AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED
- PRIVATE_OR_LOCAL
- CANONICAL_FILE_AMBIGUOUS

For Retrieval / human-assistance guidance, use:
- AGENT_RETRIEVE
- HUMAN_PROVIDE_IF_AGENT_ACCESS_FAILS
- HUMAN_PROVIDE_REQUIRED
- HUMAN_CONFIRM_CANONICAL_VERSION
- HUMAN_CONFIRM_SCOPE
- CONTEXT_ONLY_NO_DOWNLOAD_NEEDED

C. Representative data/examples

List selected examples using stable IDs.

For each:
- Example ID
- Current-state or desired-state example
- Source ID + source name
- Claim/record type
- EPC/model pattern demonstrated
- Why selected
- Whether directly inspected or still needs retrieval

Prefer examples from both:
- canonical current-state sources;
- broader desired-state sources that reveal additional requirements.

D. Upstream/downstream/context resources that should NOT be treated as canonical requirements evidence

List neighboring systems/resources that could cause scope confusion.

Explain whether each is:
- context only;
- allowed only as desired-state evidence under a specific scope;
- fully out of scope.

E. Known source conflicts, ambiguities, or version concerns

Document:
- conflicting sources;
- stale documentation;
- unclear implementation behavior;
- unresolved version questions;
- differences between canonical distribution and richer intermediate/alternate representations;
- uncertainty about which release/file is canonical.

For each conflict:
- state what controls current state;
- state whether another source may still inform desired state.

F. Recommended source sets

Complete this section BEFORE authoring provisional scope statements.

### F1. Recommended current-state canonical source set

Identify the exact sources that should control F1/current-state answers under the scope you expect to recommend.

For each source:
- provide Source ID + source name/version;
- explain why it is canonical;
- identify any canonical companion artifact that must be interpreted together with it;
- state what it is allowed to establish for current state.

### F2. Recommended desired-state evidence set

Identify broader sources that may inform F2/desired-state requirements under a maximal scope.

For each:
- provide Source ID + source name/version;
- state why it is relevant;
- assign one of:
  - EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
  - EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
  - DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
- note limitations or caveats.

### F3. Sources excluded from requirements evidence

List Source IDs that should remain context only or fully out of scope, with a brief reason.

G. Provisional scope statements

Now author the provisional scopes using the Resource Inventory IDs established above.

### Scope A — Minimal / canonical-distribution-only

#### Current-state canonical scope

Provide:
- paste-ready scope text;
- exact Source IDs + names/versions controlling F1;
- canonical companions, if any;
- explicit exclusions.

#### Desired-state scope

Provide:
- paste-ready scope text;
- exact Source IDs + names/versions controlling F2;
- explicit exclusions.

#### Strengths / tradeoffs

### Scope B — Maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state

#### Current-state canonical scope

Provide:
- paste-ready scope text;
- exact Source IDs + names/versions controlling F1;
- canonical companions, if any;
- explicit exclusions;
- explicit statement that noncanonical resources may not change F1 answers.

#### Desired-state scope

Provide:
- paste-ready scope text;
- exact Source IDs + names/versions allowed for F2;
- desired-state support type for each broader source;
- explicit exclusions;
- explicit statement that whenever F2 differs from F1, the requirements agent must identify the supporting source + support type in `Explanation / Considerations`.

#### Strengths / tradeoffs

### Additional reasonable scope alternatives

Include only when justified. Use the same explicit two-part structure:
