- Current-state canonical scope
- Desired-state scope

### Recommended scope

State which scope you recommend and why.

H. Materials the requirements agent should retrieve vs. materials a human may need to provide

Start with this rule:

The requirements-completion agent should first attempt to retrieve all publicly accessible materials itself. The project representative should not need to manually download and upload public resources merely because they are listed in the Resource Inventory.

Then provide:

### H1. Materials the requirements agent should retrieve directly

For each:
- Source ID
- exact resource/file
- URL/path
- why needed
- what should be inspected

### H2. Materials a human may need to provide only if agent retrieval fails

For each:
- Source ID
- exact resource
- why it matters
- what the human should upload if requested

Do not ask the human to provide these preemptively.

### H3. Materials that genuinely require human provision or clarification

List only resources that:
- are private/local;
- require authentication;
- cannot be publicly accessed;
- require a human canonical-version decision;
- require a human scope-selection decision.

If none:
"None identified at this stage."

I. Evidence gaps / unresolved questions

For each unresolved question, indicate whether it:
- can likely be resolved by retrieving a public source;
- requires human-provided material;
- requires a human semantic/project decision;
- requires scope selection;
- can remain unresolved during preliminary requirements elicitation.

J. Recommended handoff for requirements elicitation

End with a compact machine-readable block.

Use this structure:

RECOMMENDED SCOPE:
- Scope B — Maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state

CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCES:
- S01: [name/version]
- S02: [name/version]

CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL COMPANIONS:
- S03: [name/version]

DESIRED-STATE SUPPORT SOURCES:
- S04: EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT — [name/version]
- S05: DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT — [name/version]
- S06: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT — [name/version]

REPRESENTATIVE EXAMPLES:
- E01
- E02
- E03

CONTEXT ONLY / DO NOT USE AS REQUIREMENTS EVIDENCE:
- S08
- S09

AGENT SHOULD RETRIEVE DURING REQUIREMENTS REVIEW:
- S02: [specific file/artifact]
- S04: [specific file/artifact]

HUMAN PROVIDE ONLY IF AGENT RETRIEVAL FAILS:
- S07: [specific file/artifact]

HUMAN-PROVIDED MATERIAL REQUIRED:
- NONE
or
- [specific resource and why]

HUMAN CONFIRMATION REQUIRED:
- Select/approve one provisional scope before final requirements completion
- [other issue]

UNRESOLVED:
- [brief issue]

HANDOFF INSTRUCTION:
Use only CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL SOURCES and explicitly designated CURRENT-STATE CANONICAL COMPANIONS to populate F1/current-state requirements.

Use the DESIRED-STATE SUPPORT SOURCES allowed by the selected scope to populate an evidence-supported maximal F2/desired-state requirements set.

When F2 differs from F1, identify the supporting Source ID + source name and desired-state support type in the form's `Explanation / Considerations` field.

Do not use CONTEXT ONLY sources as requirements evidence.

Attempt to retrieve public resources before asking the project representative to upload them.

Flag unresolved issues for human review rather than guessing.

K. Short resource-discovery summary

Conclude with 5–10 bullets summarizing:
- the canonical model/data product identified;
- the recommended current-state canonical source set;
- the broader desired-state evidence set;
- the recommended scope;
- the main EPC patterns observed;
- important scope exclusions;
- critical source/version conflicts;
- additional public materials the requirements agent should retrieve;
- whether any material currently requires human provision;
- whether the package is ready for scope selection and requirements elicitation.
</code></pre>

docs.title: Human handoff principle
docs.text:
The Resource Inventory should make the division of responsibility explicit:

  1. Public and accessible: the requirements agent retrieves it.
  2. Public but retrieval may fail: the human provides it only if the agent asks.
  3. Private/local/authenticated: the human provides access or uploads it.
  4. Canonical version ambiguous: the human decides which version is authoritative.
  5. Scope alternatives remain: the human selects/approves the scope before final requirements completion.

docs.title: Scope-selection principle
docs.text:
The discovery agent proposes the scope; the project representative owns the scope decision.

The important architectural rule is:

The Resource Inventory defines the evidence catalog; the scope statement selects which catalog entries control current state and which may inform desired state.

For most initial requirements exercises, the recommended default is:

strict canonical current state + maximal evidence-supported desired state

This gives the modeling workflow a conservative, reproducible account of what the selected canonical distribution represents today while exposing a broader set of project-supported capabilities for human review before SEPIO modeling.

docs.title: Relationship to the requirements-form workflow
docs.text:
The completed [PROJECT_NAME]_Resource_Inventory.md is intended to be provided to the requirements-completion agent alongside:

  • Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx
  • Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md
  • the selected project scope statement
  • any materials explicitly identified as genuinely requiring human provision

The selected scope statement should be copied from or derived directly from the Resource Inventory and should preserve its Source IDs.

The later requirements agent should attempt to retrieve all other publicly accessible resources itself.

The Requirement→SEPIO mapping registry is intentionally not used during resource discovery or requirements elicitation.

docs.title: SEPIO Requirements Collection — Project Representative Overview
docs.text: Audience: Project representatives who are asking an AI agent to complete the SEPIO Requirements Forms for their project

docs.title: 1. What this process is for
docs.text:
The SEPIO Requirements Forms describe what a biomedical knowledge project currently represents and what it should support about claims, evidence, interpretation, and provenance.

The goal is not to redesign your project or force it into SEPIO while the forms are being completed.

Instead, the process asks two related questions:

Current state: What does the selected canonical source, dataset, distribution, or model actually represent now?

Desired state: What broader capabilities does project-specific evidence support as requirements for a future SEPIO-based representation?

This distinction is important. Current-state answers should be conservative and reproducible: they are grounded only in the canonical source set explicitly selected for the review. Desired-state answers may use a broader set of project evidence to identify a maximal, evidence-supported requirements set that a human reviewer can later refine or narrow.

After the forms are reviewed and confirmed, a separate SEPIO requirements-to-model workflow can use them to:

  • identify relevant SEPIO classes and attributes;
  • generate a candidate project-specific SEPIO covering model;
  • identify partial SEPIO coverage;
  • identify model gaps or extension needs;
  • generate implementation guidance; and
  • identify questions requiring project or SEPIO modeler review.

The completed forms are therefore a description of your project's requirements, not a list of SEPIO features you have chosen.

docs.title: 2. What is in this starter package
docs.text:
This folder contains:

  • QUICK_START.md — a short orientation and five-step entry point.
  • Requirements_Collection_Overview.md — this comprehensive overview of the requirements-collection workflow.
  • Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx — the authoritative requirements workbook the agent should complete.
  • Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx — the separate post-completion feedback workbook for issues and suggested improvements to the forms and process.
  • Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md — detailed semantic and field-by-field instructions intended primarily for the AI agent.
  • REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md — the ready-to-copy prompt for tasking an agent to complete the requirements workbook.
  • RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md — an optional agent prompt for discovering, classifying, and organizing project resources and proposing candidate scope statements.
  • RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md — practical guidance for assembling and reviewing a Resource Inventory.
  • RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md — guidance for gathering and reviewing project schemas, documentation, examples, and other evidence.
  • examples/example_scope_statement.md — example project scope statements.
  • examples/example_completed_requirements_review.md — an example Requirements Review Memo.
  • CONTENTS.md — a list of files included in the package.

These files are designed to stay together in one directory in the repository.

docs.title: 3. The five-step workflow
docs.text:
At a high level:

  1. Define the scope. Decide what canonical source(s) control current-state answers and what broader evidence may inform desired-state requirements.
  2. Create a Resource Inventory. Identify the best sources, examples, versions, conflicts, access needs, and candidate scope statements.
  3. Give the agent the scope, inventory, forms, guidance, feedback template, and needed resources; have it complete the Requirements Forms, Review Memo, and Feedback Log.
  4. Inspect the completed workbook and Requirements Review Memo; separately triage the Feedback Log. Resolve uncertainties and correct anything that does not accurately reflect the project.
  5. Move to SEPIO mapping. Once confirmed, use the requirements record as input to the separate requirements-to-model workflow.

The remainder of this document explains each part in more detail.

docs.title: 4. Step 1 — Define the project scope
docs.text:
Before asking the requirements agent to populate the forms, define a project scope statement.

Biomedical projects often have several related representations:

  • an internal curation model;
  • a canonical public distribution;
  • intermediate curation or analysis artifacts;
  • one or more source databases;
  • an ingest/transformation pipeline;
  • alternate or historical releases;
  • an API representation;
  • a knowledge-graph export;
  • a user-interface representation.

Without an explicit scope, an agent can easily mix these together and produce answers that are neither reproducible nor clearly interpretable.

A useful scope statement identifies two evidence sets.

docs.title: 4.1 Current-state canonical source set
docs.text:
This is the exact source, dataset, distribution, release, schema, or explicitly designated companion artifact that controls the workbook's current-state / “Used in Current Data?” answers.

The requirements agent should strictly use only this source set when populating current-state columns.

Examples include:

  • one versioned indications.xlsx distribution;
  • one current LinkML schema release plus designated canonical example records;
  • one KG release/export;
  • one production database schema plus its canonical data dictionary.

The fact that richer information exists elsewhere in the project does not make it part of current state unless the scope explicitly includes that resource in the canonical source set.

docs.title: 4.2 Desired-state evidence set
docs.text:
This is the broader set of project-specific resources the agent is allowed to use when deciding what the future SEPIO-based representation should support.

Depending on the selected scope, this can include:

  • explicit future requirements or roadmap items;
  • current papers and project documentation;
  • model/design documentation;
  • intermediate curation or analysis artifacts;
  • information captured elsewhere in the project pipeline but dropped from the canonical export;
  • alternate or earlier project distributions;
  • competency questions;
  • curation guidance;
  • implementation/design documents.

The desired-state evidence set supports a maximal but evidence-supported first-pass requirements record. “Maximal” does not mean speculative: every desired-state Y/M answer should still have project-specific support.

docs.title: 4.3 Minimal versus maximal scope
docs.text: The Resource Inventory workflow is designed to propose at least two reasonable scope choices.

docs.title: Minimal / canonical-distribution-only
docs.text:
A minimal scope limits the review to one canonical source set.

Example:

Current-state canonical source: MeDIC matrix_indication_list.xlsx, version 1.3.0. Current-state and desired-state requirements should both be limited to information represented in this canonical distribution.

This produces a conservative description of one concrete release.

docs.title: Maximal / canonical current state + broad desired state
docs.text:
A maximal scope preserves a strict current-state source while allowing broader project evidence to inform desired state.

Example:

Current-state canonical source: MeDIC matrix_indication_list.xlsx, version 1.3.0. Current-state answers must be based only on this distribution. Desired-state evidence: additional MeDIC-maintained intermediate curation artifacts, alternate distributions, the MeDIC paper and project documentation, and explicit project requirements may be used to identify a broader, evidence-supported desired-state requirements set. Where desired state differs from current state, the supporting source must be named in Explanation / Considerations.

This is often the preferred starting point because it gives a reproducible account of current representation while surfacing a broader set of requirements for human review.

docs.title: 4.4 Other reasonable scopes
docs.text:
Some projects may justify additional alternatives, for example:

  • current release + current pipeline artifacts;
  • core product + designated companion datasets;
  • domain-specific subset;
  • strict historical release;
  • current product family / multi-distribution scope.

If substantially different products have different evidence/provenance behavior, separate requirements reviews may be clearer.

docs.title: 4.5 How to obtain a scope statement
docs.text:
If the scope is already obvious, write it directly.

If not, use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md. The resource-discovery agent should produce:

  • a minimal scope;
  • a maximal scope;
  • additional reasonable alternatives when appropriate; and
  • a recommended scope with tradeoffs.

The project representative should review or refine the proposed scope and place the selected statement into the SELECTED PROJECT SCOPE section of REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md.

docs.title: 5. Step 2 — Create a Resource Inventory
docs.text:
A Resource Inventory is a structured evidence package for the requirements review.

It is more than a list of files. It should tell the later requirements agent:

  • which resources are canonical for current state;
  • which resources may inform desired state;
  • which examples should be inspected;
  • which sources are historical, upstream, downstream, or context only;
  • which versions/releases should be used;
  • what source conflicts or uncertainties exist;
  • which public resources the agent should retrieve itself;
  • which materials may require human provision or clarification.

Use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md for detailed guidance.

docs.title: 5.1 Two ways to create the inventory
docs.text:
Option A — Assemble it yourself. If you already know the key schema, canonical distribution, documentation, examples, curation guidance, and provenance materials, create a simple inventory or manifest with precise pointers to them.

Option B — Ask an AI agent to take a first pass. Use RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md when project evidence is distributed across repositories, documentation sites, papers, DOI archives, generated artifacts, or multiple versions.

The agent-generated Resource Inventory should be reviewed before requirements completion.

docs.title: 5.2 Resource roles
docs.text:
The inventory should distinguish source roles such as:

  • CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL
  • CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION
  • DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT
  • CURRENT_AND_DESIRED
  • CONTEXT_ONLY

Only sources designated as current-state canonical or canonical companions should control current-state answers under the selected scope.

docs.title: 5.3 Desired-state support types
docs.text: When a broader source supports desired state, it is useful to distinguish why:

docs.title: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT
docs.text: A roadmap, issue, requirements document, competency question, or explicit project statement says the capability is wanted or needed.

docs.title: EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT
docs.text: The project already captures or uses the information in an intermediate artifact, alternate distribution, curation workflow, analysis product, or other project-maintained representation, but the selected canonical distribution does not expose it.

docs.title: DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT
docs.text:
A paper, model/design document, curation guide, or other authoritative project document describes the capability as part of the intended project model or data product, even though it is absent from the selected canonical source.

A source that explicitly says a capability is out of scope, rejected, deprecated, or intentionally excluded should not normally be used to justify desired state unless another authoritative project source explicitly reverses that decision.

docs.title: 5.4 Useful resources
docs.text:
Typical resources include:

Resource type Why it helps Canonical dataset/distribution Establishes what is actually represented in current state. Authoritative schema or data model Shows entities, relationships, fields, structure, and constraints. Data dictionary / field documentation Explains field meaning, allowed values, cardinality, and intended use. Model/design documentation Explains why structures exist and what the project intends to represent. Representative example records Shows how the model is actually used in practice. Intermediate curation/analysis artifacts May reveal existing project capabilities omitted from the canonical export. Source/ingest documentation Shows which upstream information is retained, transformed, or discarded. Curation guidelines / SOPs Helps interpret claims, evidence evaluation, confidence, review, and provenance. Pipeline / normalization documentation Helps identify semantic-alignment and process provenance. Project papers / overview documents Provides project goals, intended semantics, and model intent. Requirements / competency questions / roadmap Captures desired capabilities not yet fully implemented.

You do not need every resource type. The goal is to assemble enough evidence to answer each form question responsibly.

docs.title: 5.5 Representative examples
docs.text:
The inventory should identify a small, diverse set of examples rather than hundreds of repetitive records.

Useful examples may include:

  • a typical claim;
  • a claim with qualifiers/context;
  • a claim with source or evidence support;
  • a claim with richer provenance;
  • a normalization or transformation example;
  • a case where intermediate information is dropped from the canonical export;
  • an alternate distribution that exposes a capability absent from the canonical one.

Assign stable IDs such as E01, E02, and E03.

docs.title: 5.6 Public resources and human uploads
docs.text:
Public resources are retrieval tasks for the AI agent, not preemptive upload tasks for the project representative.

The requirements agent should first try to retrieve public materials itself.

Human assistance is appropriate when:

  • public retrieval fails;
  • authentication/private access is required;
  • a source exists only locally;
  • multiple plausible versions/files exist and the canonical one cannot be identified confidently;
  • a human scope or canonical-version decision is required.

If human help is needed, the agent should say exactly what resource is needed, why it matters, and whether the review can proceed provisionally without it.

docs.title: 6. Step 3 — Give the agent what it needs and populate the forms
docs.text:
Give the requirements agent:

  1. REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md
  2. the selected project scope statement
  3. Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx
  4. Requirements_Instructions_and_Guidance_for_AI.md
  5. the reviewed [PROJECT]_Resource_Inventory.md
  6. any private/local materials identified as necessary

For the forms and guidance, you may either upload the files or provide links/pointers to the exact versions you want used.

For project evidence, you may:

  • upload local files;
  • provide public repository/documentation/DOI links;
  • provide a manifest or Resource Inventory with precise pointers;
  • point to specific files/directories rather than entire repositories.

For large datasets, representative records plus structural documentation may be enough unless the agent needs the full dataset to answer a specific requirement.

docs.title: 6.1 Current-state rule
docs.text:
For every current-state/F1 answer, the agent should ask:

Is this capability represented in the selected current-state canonical source set?

It should not mark something current merely because it appears in:

  • an intermediate artifact;
  • a historical or alternate distribution;
  • a paper;
  • a roadmap;
  • an upstream source;
  • a downstream API/UI;
  • process documentation;

unless the selected scope explicitly includes that resource in the current-state canonical source set.

docs.title: 6.2 Desired-state rule
docs.text:
For every desired-state/F2 answer, the agent should ask:

Is this capability supported as a project requirement by one or more resources allowed in the selected desired-state evidence set?

The initial desired-state pass should generally be maximal but evidence-supported.

When desired state differs from current state, the agent should identify the supporting source in Explanation / Considerations.

A useful pattern is:

Current state: [brief observation from canonical source]. Desired-state support: [SUPPORT TYPE] — [Source ID/title/version]: [brief evidence and rationale].

docs.title: 6.3 How the agent should reason
docs.text:
The agent should triangulate across:

Selected project scope
        +
Current-state canonical source set
        +
Broader desired-state evidence set
        +
Representative records/examples
        +
Curation / pipeline / provenance documentation
        +
Known requirements / use cases

For each substantive answer, it should be able to answer:

What project evidence supports this answer, and is that source allowed to support current state, desired state, or both?

If that cannot be answered, the response should be marked uncertain rather than guessed.

docs.title: Current representation vs desired requirement
docs.text: A capability may be absent from the canonical current-state distribution but still be a valid desired-state requirement.

docs.title: Upstream source capability vs project capability
docs.text: If an upstream source contains rich EPC information that the project neither stores nor explicitly requires, it should not automatically become a project requirement.

docs.title: Canonical distribution vs intermediate project capability
docs.text: An intermediate project artifact may contain information omitted from the canonical export. Under a maximal scope, this can support desired state as EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT without changing the current-state answer.

docs.title: Canonical model vs downstream API/UI enrichment
docs.text: Downstream computation or display enrichment should not be treated as current canonical representation unless explicitly included in scope.

docs.title: Claim semantics vs evidence/provenance
docs.text: A project may support many biomedical claim types while using one relatively simple evidence/provenance envelope. Assess these dimensions separately.

docs.title: Evidence item vs evidence interpretation
docs.text: A publication, source passage, dataset, or experimental result is not the same thing as an interpreted argument about whether evidence supports or disputes a proposition.

docs.title: Scientific evidence strength vs extraction/alignment confidence
docs.text: A score indicating confidence in entity normalization or extraction should not be treated as scientific evidence strength unless project semantics explicitly say so.

docs.title: Process documentation vs stored provenance
docs.text: Documentation that an LLM, normalization service, curator, or pipeline step was used does not prove that provenance about that process is stored in the canonical data.

docs.title: Missing information vs negative requirement
docs.text: Silence is not automatically “N.” Use M / Maybe / Needs discussion or another review flag when evidence is insufficient.

docs.title: 6.5 Requirements-first rule
docs.text:
The Requirement→SEPIO mapping registry should not be used to decide what the project's requirements are.

The agent should determine project requirements independently of current SEPIO coverage.

docs.title: 7. Step 4 — Inspect the deliverables
docs.text:
The agent should return three distinct deliverables: the completed requirements workbook, the Requirements Review Memo, and a project-specific copy of Feedback_Log_Template.xlsx. The Feedback Log captures suggestions about the collection process and is reviewed separately from the substantive project requirements. Feedback does not automatically change the authoritative forms or instructions.

The requirements agent should return two primary artifacts.

docs.title: A. Completed Requirements Workbook
docs.text:
The agent should populate the provided Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx template while preserving its existing structure and formatting.

The output filename should include project name, version, date, and 24-hour time, for example:

MeDIC_Requirements_v0.2_20261013_1643.xlsx

The HHMM form avoids filename problems caused by colons on some operating systems.

docs.title: B. Requirements Review Memo
docs.text:
The memo filename should follow the same version/date/time convention, for example:

MeDIC_Requirements_Review_Memo_v0.2_20261013_1643.md

The memo should include:

  • the selected project scope;
  • the exact current-state canonical source set;
  • the broader desired-state evidence set;
  • exact versions/releases/commits/DOI archive versions/retrieval dates where relevant;
  • high-confidence conclusions;
  • answers requiring human review;
  • source conflicts or missing information;
  • inaccessible resources;
  • important assumptions;
  • difficult form/guidance questions;
  • observations that may improve the workflow;
  • representative data examples.

docs.title: 7.1 Representative examples in the memo
docs.text:
The memo should include a small, diverse set of concrete examples:

  • a few current-state examples directly from the selected canonical source; and
  • a few broader desired-state/maximal examples when noncanonical project evidence reveals additional requirements.

Represent examples as close to their source representation as practical:

  • tabular/database source: show rows/tables using source column names where possible;
  • JSON/YAML: show compact objects preserving source field names and nesting;
  • RDF/graph: show triples/quads/edge properties;
  • free text: show only the minimal excerpt needed;
  • multi-source example: label it COMPOSITE/ILLUSTRATIVE;
  • record assembled across tables: label it DENORMALIZED and identify contributing tables.

Do not fabricate values to create a complete-looking example.

docs.title: 7.2 Human review checklist
docs.text:
Focus review on:

Review question What to check Scope Did the agent use the selected project/data product and correct canonical source set? Current state Is every F1/current-state Y/M answer supported by the allowed canonical source set? Desired state Is every broader F2/desired-state Y/M answer supported by an allowed project source? Source traceability When F2 differs from F1, does Explanation / Considerations identify the supporting desired-state source and rationale? Claims Are the major kinds of assertions represented by the project captured? Evidence Are important evidence item categories and relationships represented? Interpretation Did the agent distinguish evidence from interpreted evidence, direction/strength, grouping, and higher-level synthesis? Provenance Are source, authorship, method, process, semantic alignment, encoding, retrieval, and other provenance requirements captured at the right level? Upstream EPC Did the agent avoid treating richer upstream content as current project representation? Intermediate artifacts If used for desired state, were they kept separate from current-state claims? Downstream enrichment Did the agent avoid treating API/UI enrichment as canonical current-state representation? Uncertainty Did it flag unsupported or ambiguous answers rather than guessing? Consistency Do responses across worksheets and the memo tell a coherent story? Examples Are current-state and desired-state examples accurate, sourced, and useful?

Correct anything that does not accurately reflect the project.

Once you are comfortable with the workbook, treat it as the confirmed project requirements input.

docs.title: 8. Step 5 — What happens after the forms are confirmed
docs.text:
The confirmed workbook becomes the project requirements input for the later SEPIO requirements-to-model workflow.

That later workflow uses:

Confirmed Requirements Forms
        +
Requirement→SEPIO Mapping Registry
        +
SEPIO source schema
        ↓
Requirements-to-Model Output Package

That package can include:

  1. Candidate SEPIO Covering Model
  2. Requirements Summary
  3. Requirements-to-Model Traceability
  4. Requirements Follow-Up & Modeling Decisions
  5. Gap & Extension Analysis
  6. Implementation Guidance
  7. Requirements Collection & Form Feedback (downstream mapping artifact, not the Starter Kit agent Feedback Log)
  8. Generation Manifest

During the current AI-first pilot phase, an AI agent can generate these artifacts with transparent provenance. A future production workflow can move exact schema extraction, dependency closure, validation, traceability, and manifest generation into deterministic code.

The project representative does not need to perform these mappings manually.

docs.title: 9. Evidence hierarchy and conflict handling
docs.text: A single global evidence hierarchy is no longer sufficient because current state and desired state intentionally use different source sets.

docs.title: For current-state answers
docs.text:
The selected scope controls.

Within the allowed current-state source set, prefer:

  1. explicitly designated canonical release/distribution;
  2. canonical schema/data model;
  3. canonical companion data dictionary/specification;
  4. representative records from the same release;
  5. other explicitly designated canonical companion artifacts.

A noncanonical paper, intermediate artifact, or alternate distribution should not override current state.

docs.title: For desired-state answers
docs.text:
Use the broader evidence set allowed by the selected scope.

Prefer the strongest project-specific evidence, such as:

  1. explicit future requirements / approved roadmap / competency questions;
  2. current authoritative project/model documentation;
  3. existing project-maintained intermediate or alternate artifacts that demonstrate a capability;
  4. current curation/modeling guidance;
  5. current implementation/design documentation;
  6. older or historical project sources when they remain relevant and are not contradicted by authoritative current sources.

When sources disagree:

  • identify the conflict;
  • state which source controls current state;
  • state whether the conflicting resource may still inform desired state;
  • do not silently reconcile them.

docs.title: 10. What project representatives are not expected to do
docs.text:
Project representatives do not need to:

  • learn the complete SEPIO model before filling out the forms;
  • manually map project fields to SEPIO classes and slots;
  • decide whether a SEPIO gap exists;
  • design SEPIO extensions;
  • understand dependency closure; or
  • create the Candidate Covering Model themselves.

Their responsibility is to help establish:

  1. a defensible scope;
  2. an accurate evidence base; and
  3. accurate project requirements.

docs.title: 11. Minimum evidence standard
docs.text:
Before considering a requirements workbook ready for confirmation, the workflow should ideally have:

  • a selected project scope statement;
  • a clearly named current-state canonical source set;
  • at least one authoritative structural source;
  • representative examples from the canonical source;
  • enough information to distinguish current project content from upstream/downstream information;
  • one or more sources supporting desired-state requirements when F2 goes beyond F1;
  • source/version information sufficient to reproduce the review;
  • explicit review flags for questions the available evidence cannot answer.

Projects lacking one or more of these can still participate, but the resulting workbook should contain more uncertainty/review flags.

docs.title: 12. Key principle
docs.text:
The requirements process is requirements-first, not SEPIO-first.

The project representative and agent should first answer:

What does the selected canonical source currently represent, and what broader capabilities does project evidence support as desired requirements?

Only after those requirements are reviewed should the SEPIO mapping workflow ask:

How well does SEPIO represent those needs?

docs.title: Evidence, Provenance, Confidence (EPC) Requirements Collection
docs.text:
Detailed Instructions & Guidance for AI Agents Completing the SEPIO Requirements Forms

This document provides the detailed semantic and field-level guidance an AI agent should use when completing Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx on behalf of a project. It is intended to be used together with REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md, the selected project scope statement, the reviewed project Resource Inventory, and the project-specific source materials identified there.

For human-facing orientation to the overall process, see QUICK_START.md and Requirements_Collection_Overview.md. For guidance on assembling and classifying the evidence base before requirements completion, see RESOURCE_INVENTORY_GUIDANCE.md and RESOURCE_INVENTORY_PROMPT.md.

docs.title: I. Why Start with Requirements Collection
docs.text:
Before defining a shared SEPIO Covering Model or a set of reusable profiles, the consortium should first establish what each participating project actually needs to represent. A structured requirements-collection exercise provides the evidence base for deciding which SEPIO concepts and patterns are needed, which requirements recur across projects, and where project-specific differences must be preserved.

The requirements process should be artifact-centered and use-case-centered rather than asking project representatives to reason directly in SEPIO terms. Project representatives are usually best positioned to describe the claims they represent, the information they treat as evidence, how that evidence is assessed, and what provenance must be retained. The SEPIO/modeling group can then perform the second-stage semantic analysis: determining whether those requirements map to concepts such as DataItem, StudyResult, Statement, EvidenceLine, Contribution, or other SEPIO structures.

This separation also supports later implementation with LinkML and LinkML-Map. If the requirements effort captures the semantics of source fields, important distinctions in the source model, and what must survive transformation, those results can directly inform the design of SEPIO-based profiles and declarative mappings between project models.

docs.title: Recommended Overall Process
docs.text:
A practical path is to organize the consolidation effort into four phases:

  • Phase 1 — Project requirements collection. Each project establishes a reviewed Resource Inventory, selects a project scope, and describes the claim, evidence, provenance, and confidence information that is currently represented or desired. Agent-assisted execution: The Resource Inventory first identifies and classifies relevant project sources, including the exact source set that controls current-state/F1 answers and the broader evidence set allowed to inform desired-state/F2 answers. The project representative selects or refines one proposed scope. A requirements agent then uses REQUIREMENTS_FORM_PROMPT.md, the selected scope, the reviewed Resource Inventory, this guidance, and the required project materials to prepare a first-pass population of the forms. A project representative reviews, corrects, and confirms the requirements.

  • Phase 2 — Cross-project semantic analysis. The modeling group compares requirements across projects and asks which SEPIO concepts are involved, which needs recur, and which differences are semantic rather than merely structural. Agent-assisted execution: After project requirements are confirmed, an agent can apply the Requirement → SEPIO Mapping Registry to identify direct mappings, partial coverage, implementation guidance, open questions, and recurrent requirements across projects.

  • Phase 3 — Model architecture. Based on that analysis, determine what belongs in the Covering Model, how many Covering Models are useful, which reusable profiles are warranted, and which requirements may require extension of SEPIO. Mapping from elements in the requirements forms to specific features of the SEPIO model can help to automate some of this process. Agent-assisted execution: During the current pilot phase, an AI agent may generate candidate covering-model content and associated review artifacts from the confirmed forms and mapping registry. These outputs remain candidates for modeler review.

  • Phase 4 — Mapping and validation. Use real source examples from each project to demonstrate that required semantics can be represented in the chosen profile and mapped using LinkML-Map without unacceptable information loss. Agent-assisted execution: Agents can help compare representative project records with the proposed SEPIO-based representation, identify information loss or ambiguity, and document issues for project and SEPIO modelers.

Real example records should be required throughout this process. Abstract descriptions alone often hide important distinctions—for example, whether something called “evidence” is actually source information, an interpretation of that information, a provenance activity, or a higher-order argument. Representative examples allow the modeling group to classify these objects correctly before assigning SEPIO classes or defining profile constraints.

docs.title: Role of AI Agents in Requirements Collection
docs.text:
The detailed guidance, documentation, and forms described below are designed with the expectation that AI agents will assist in preparing a first-pass set of project requirements. A project representative may task an AI agent with reviewing the project's available materials and preparing an initial population of the forms.

To do this effectively, the agent needs a reviewed Resource Inventory and a selected project scope statement. The Resource Inventory is the evidence catalog: it assigns stable Source IDs, records versions and roles, identifies representative examples, and distinguishes canonical current-state sources from broader desired-state support. Relevant resources may include data-model and schema documentation, canonical datasets or distributions, representative records, project documentation, provenance conventions, curation guidelines, software or pipeline artifacts, papers, requirements, issues, competency questions, and other project-specific materials.

The selected scope determines how those resources may be used. F1/current-state answers must be based only on the sources explicitly designated as CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL or CURRENT_STATE_CANONICAL_COMPANION in the selected scope. Richer information found elsewhere in the project must not be used to broaden F1. F2/desired-state answers may draw on the broader DESIRED_STATE_SUPPORT sources allowed by the selected scope, but only where those sources provide affirmative project-specific evidence. The agent should clearly identify uncertainties or gaps and leave final validation and refinement to project representatives.

AI agents completing the requirements forms should not attempt to assign SEPIO classes or slots on the project's behalf unless explicitly asked to perform the later mapping step. Respondent-facing answers should remain grounded in the project's own concepts, data structures, and requirements. Stable Requirement IDs provide the later machine-facing bridge from these project-centered descriptions to the Requirement → SEPIO Mapping Registry.

docs.title: Core Behavioral Rules for AI Agents
docs.text:
The following behavioral instructions apply when an AI agent prepares a first-pass population of the requirements forms (and may also be useful to human respondents).

  • Ground responses in project evidence, not plausibility. Populate fields from project schemas, documentation, example records, publications, repositories, curation guides, meeting notes, or other supplied materials. Do not infer that a project has a requirement simply because that requirement would be sensible for a project of that type.

  • Treat the Resource Inventory as the evidence catalog and the selected scope as the authority for source use. Refer to sources by their Resource Inventory Source IDs where useful. Do not silently expand the allowed source set during form completion. If a source appears important but is not permitted by the selected scope, flag it for human review rather than using it.

  • Classify broader desired-state support when F2 goes beyond F1. Where useful, use the Resource Inventory support labels: EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT, EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT, or DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT. If no project-specific evidence supports a broader desired-state capability, do not mark it Y simply because it seems useful.

  • When F2 differs from F1, make the evidence for that difference explicit. In the form's Explanation / Considerations field, identify the supporting Source ID + source name/version and, when applicable, the desired-state support type. A useful pattern is: Current state: [canonical observation]. Desired-state support: [SUPPORT TYPE] — [Source ID — source name/version]: [brief rationale].

  • Apply the selected scope literally when distinguishing current and desired state. For F1/current-state questions, use only the exact canonical source set named in the selected scope. A capability found only in an intermediate artifact, alternate release, paper, roadmap, upstream source, downstream representation, or process description must not be marked current unless that resource is explicitly included in the current-state canonical source set. For F2/desired-state questions, use the broader source set allowed by the selected scope and capture a maximal but evidence-supported requirement set rather than a speculative one.

  • Do not convert project terminology into SEPIO classes prematurely. Describe the project's native information and requirements first. For example, report that a project stores publication excerpts and assesses whether they support a mechanism; do not decide on the project's behalf that these “must be DataItem and EvidenceLine objects.” Mapping to SEPIO is a later modeling task. Unless explicitly asked to perform the later modeling step, do not edit content in the SEPIO Mapping Summary columns or use those summaries to decide what the project's requirements should be. Do not edit predefined Requirement IDs. For any new project-specific row added under an “Other” option, assign a stable custom ID using the form-specific prefix shown in the guidance (for example EI.CUSTOM.001) so that the new requirement can later be added to the mapping registry.

  • Preserve semantic distinctions even when the source data do not. In particular, keep separate: the information used as evidence; how that information was semantically aligned or grounded; how it was interpreted as evidence; confidence in extraction/alignment; scientific evidence strength; overall confidence in a claim; and downstream retrieval/encoding provenance. If a source field conflates several of these, say so rather than silently assigning it to one category.

  • Use real examples whenever available. For current-state examples, prefer actual records from the selected canonical source set. For desired-state capabilities that are absent from current canonical data, prefer real examples from allowed desired-state support sources. Preserve the source's native representation as closely as practical (for example, a table row, JSON/YAML object, or RDF triple). If an example is assembled across records/tables, label it DENORMALIZED; if it combines information from multiple sources, label it COMPOSITE/ILLUSTRATIVE. Do not fabricate values to make an example look complete.

  • Do not manufacture specificity. Never invent identifiers, evidence types, workflows, agent names, confidence scales, interpretation rules, or provenance requirements to make a form look complete. Enter Unknown, Not documented, Needs discussion, or Not applicable where appropriate.

  • Treat lack of evidence carefully. For F1, if the relevant canonical artifact has been directly inspected and a capability is demonstrably absent, N may be appropriate. If the canonical source was not fully inspected or the documentation is incomplete, use M / Needs discussion rather than assuming N. For F2, absence from current data does not imply the capability is undesired; use the allowed desired-state evidence set to determine whether there is affirmative support.

  • Identify meaningful variation within the project. Do not assume that one workflow applies everywhere. Look for differences among claim types, data sources, human versus automated curation, or production versus experimental pipelines. Conversely, do not create separate claim types merely because their predicates differ if their evidence/provenance requirements are essentially identical.

  • Use the minimum number of Claim Types needed to expose EPC differences. When many claim types share the same Evidence, Provenance, and Confidence requirements, group them appropriately. Split them when their evidence sources, interpretation approaches, provenance needs, or confidence models materially differ.

  • For Evidence Item Types, describe what the information is—not how it was obtained. An experimental result remains an experimental result whether it was entered manually or extracted by an LLM. Human/AI extraction belongs primarily in provenance unless the manner of extraction changes the semantic nature of the information artifact.

  • For Evidence Interpretation, determine the actual unit of judgment. Do not assume one Evidence Line per snippet, paper, or study. Determine whether the project assesses each item independently, groups multiple items into one argument, or performs nested/higher-order assessments. If this is unclear, flag it as an open question.

  • For Semantic Alignment Provenance, distinguish mapping from evidentiary reasoning. Extraction, entity/relation recognition, grounding, normalization, and mapping source semantics into a structured representation are alignment activities. Deciding whether that aligned information supports or disputes a target claim is Evidence Interpretation.

  • For Provenance, distinguish the five layers explicitly. Ask separately: how did the evidence information come to exist; how was its meaning aligned to structured semantics; how was it interpreted/reasoned over to generate knowledge; how was the resulting artifact encoded; and how was that encoded artifact later retrieved or transformed between systems.

  • Record disagreements and ambiguity rather than resolving them silently. If documentation or project representatives appear to use a term inconsistently, or two sources imply different requirements, note the discrepancy and identify it as something requiring human review.

  • Prioritize requirements, not implementation details. Capture what information the project needs to represent and why. Do not overfocus on the exact YAML shape, property name, database column, or current technical implementation unless it reveals an important semantic requirement.

  • Make proposed additions obvious. If the agent thinks a requirement may be useful but cannot find evidence that the project actually needs it, put it in a clearly labeled Suggested follow-up / Possible requirement note rather than filling it in as a project requirement.

  • Preserve traceability to source material. For every substantive requirement, retain the relevant Resource Inventory Source ID(s) and, where useful, representative Example ID(s). F1 conclusions should trace to the selected current-state canonical source set. Broader F2 conclusions should trace to allowed desired-state support sources. When F2 differs from F1, this traceability should appear in the form's Explanation / Considerations field, not merely in private drafting notes.

  • End with unresolved questions for the project representative. After populating the forms, generate a short list of the highest-value uncertainties that need human confirmation—for example, “Is evidence strength actually authored or intended to be derived?” or “Are multiple publication excerpts normally treated as independent arguments or grouped by study?”

  • Treat the completed form as a draft until a project representative validates it. AI assistance should reduce the burden of requirements collection, but the agent should not present inferred requirements as authoritative project decisions.

As a general rule, a partially completed form with clearly marked unknowns is preferable to a fully populated form containing inferred or invented project requirements.

Finally, requirements-completion agents should produce two outputs:

  1. The populated requirements workbook, preserving the supplied workbook structure and formatting. Use a filename of the form [PROJECT]_Requirements_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].xlsx (24-hour HHMM, with no colon).

  2. A Requirements Review Memo, named [PROJECT]_Requirements_Review_Memo_v[VERSION]_[YYYYMMDD]_[HHMM].md, containing:

  3. the selected project scope;
  4. the exact current-state canonical source set used for F1;
  5. the broader desired-state evidence set used for F2;
  6. relevant source versions/releases/commits;
  7. high-confidence conclusions;
  8. fields or answers requiring human review;
  9. conflicting or missing information;
  10. inaccessible resources, if any;
  11. important assumptions;
  12. the highest-value unresolved questions; and
  13. a small set of representative examples from both canonical current-state sources and, where they reveal additional requirements, broader desired-state sources.

The memo should make it possible for the project representative to see why current-state and desired-state answers differ without auditing every workbook cell.

docs.title: II. Key Concepts and Terminology
docs.text: Below we define and share preferred names for several foundational concepts where a shared understanding will be useful in this modeling requirements collection effort. Project representatives should understand the meaning of and distinctions between these concepts, and use the recommended terminology in describing their data and requirements.

docs.title: “Statements” (as “Claims” vs “Concept Definitions”)
docs.text:
Description: An information artifact that expresses a proposition, hypothesis, or judgment about the world. A Statement may be an assertion which states a purported fact about our objective reality, or a more subjective judgement or definition that is offered from a particular point of view, but not grounded in an objective, provable reality.

In our work we are concerned with two high level kinds of Statements: Claims and Concept Definitions. It is important to define and distinguish these two types of Statements because it represents a fundamental divide across the statements reported by projects in our consortium, which may ultimately use different models, and require different requirements collection forms.

  • “Claims”: put forth propositions about how entities in the domain of discourse relate or behave, and that can in principle be evaluated for truth or validity.

  • Examples: “Variant X causes loss of function in Protein X”, “CFTR dysfunction contributes to the pathophysiology of cystic fibrosis.”

  • Claims are the types of things that have evidence and confidence, and are reported in Knowledgebases such as the Monarch KG, Translator, and DisMech.

  • Note that a particular claim is defined/identified by both its “proposition” (the inherent meaning of what it is putting forth as true), and the occasion on which it is made (when and by whom it was put forth). If two curators put forth the same proposition that “Variant X causes loss of function in Protein X”, these are separate Claims instances because they were made by different people on different occasions.

  • “Concept Definitions”: characterize terms or concepts that refer to entities in the domain of discourse - e.g. assign names, definitions, identifiers, or synonyms to concepts, place them into a hierarchical classification, or provide mappings between terms representing them.

  • Examples: “The string xxx is the preferred name for the concept of yyy”, “The term xxx is defined as yyy”, “The name xxx is a synonym of the term yyy “, “The concept xxx is a subtype of the concept yyy.”

  • Such ‘definitions’ represent expert but ultimately subjective opinions about the best way to define or name a concept - they are given from a particular point of view but not grounded in an objective, provable reality.

  • Concept Definitions are most often reported in ontologies and other terminological artifacts such as Mondo. They typically have provenance and rationale describing why a particular naming, classification, or mapping decision was made. They are not usually supported or assessed using the same evidence-and-confidence framework applied to empirical Claims, because they represent terminological or modeling judgments rather than assertions about objective states of the world. For this reason. collect their modeling requirements separately in our effort.

  • In our work, we will use “Concept” to refer to the abstract notion of some thing that exists in reality, “Name” to refer to labels used to refer to concepts in speech or writing, and “Term” to refer to a formal characterization of a concept in a terminological artifact - which often provides things like identifiers, preferred and alternate names, synonyms, and mappings to other terms.)

docs.title: “Evidence”
docs.text:
Description: Evidence is information—such as data, observations, study results, text, images, or other knowledge—that is used by an agent in reasoning about the truth or validity of a claim; information plays the role of evidence only when it is interpreted as bearing on a particular claim.

We call an individual piece of information that is used as evidence an “Evidence Item”.

Example 1: Results from several in vitro and in vivo functional assays that are interpreted to support the conclusion that Variant X markedly reduces Protein X activity.

Example 2: One or more passages from biomedical publications describing CFTR dysfunction, in Cystic Fibrosis (CF) together with the source publications or other structured information from which those passages were obtained - from which an AI Agent derives a structured claim purporting that CFTR dysfunction is causal for CF.

Note that the notion of “evidence” is relevant for Claims, but not Concept Definitions - which are more subjective characterizations of concepts or terms rather than statements about the entities in reality that these terms reference.

docs.title: “Evidence Interpretation”
docs.text:
Description: Evidence Interpretation is the act of evaluating one or more information artifacts and determining whether, in what direction, and with what strength they bear on the truth of a target claim.

Example 1: A domain expert reviews the functional-assay results to assess if and how strongly they support that Variant X can cause loss of function in Protein X.

Example 2: An AI-assisted DisMech curation workflow extracts and grounds concepts and relationships from publication text, then and assesses if and how strongly the extracted statements support the claim that CFTR dysfunction contributes to cystic-fibrosis pathophysiology.

docs.title: “Evidence Line”
docs.text:
Description: An Evidence Line is a single argument for or against the validity of a target claim, based on interpretation of a set of one or more evidence Items. Evidence Lines are the output of an Evidence Interpretation process - and typically report in what direction, and with what strength the assessed evidence bears on the truth of a target claim.

Example 1: An argument based on functional assay results that determines they provide very strong (strength) evidence disputing (direction) the claim that Variant X causes loss of function in Protein X.

Example 2: An argument based on structured statements extracted from text that determines them to strongly (strength) support (direction) the claim that CFTR dysfunction contributes to cystic-fibrosis pathophysiology.

docs.title: “Confidence”
docs.text:
Description: The degree of certainty that an agent has in the accuracy of reported information. For a Claim, this may be confidence that the proposition put forth in a claim is true. For a semantic alignment output, this may be confidence that the agent mapped text strings to correct terms or codes. Confidence may be reported using a qualitative term (e.g.”high”, “medium”, “low”) or quantitative value (e.g. a probability between 0 and 1, or some custom score on bespoke scale)

Example 1: A human curator reports “high” confidence that Variant X reduces the function of Protein X.

Example 2: An AI-Agent reports a numerical score of 0.6 that indicates its confidence that it correctly identified and mapped a concept in text to a correct ontology term.

Note that, like “evidence”, the notion of “confidence” is relevant for Claims, but not Concept Definitions - which are more subjective characterizations of concepts or terms, rather than statements about the entities in reality that these terms reference.

docs.title: “Agent”
docs.text:
Description: An autonomous actor that participates in an activity or process, often in pursuit of an intended outcome. In this document, an Agent may be a person, organization, software program, or AI system. Where relevant, the specific type of Agent will be stated explicitly (for example, human, organization, software agent, or AI agent).

Example 1: A clinical scientist or expert panel interpreting functional-assay results for a variant to determine whether they support its pathogenicity..

Example 2: An AI curation agent extracting and interpreting mechanistic evidence from literature, and a human curator who reviews and validates the result.

docs.title: “Provenance”
docs.text:
Definition: Information about the origins and history of data or knowledge artifacts, including the processes, inputs, agents, and transformations involved in their creation, interpretation, curation, retrieval, or modification.

Note that, unlike “evidence” and “confidence”, the notion of “provenance” is relevant to both Claims and Concept Definitions - however the levels and kinds of provenance differ between them. In this document we focus on characterization of Claim Provenance.

Below, we make an explicit distinction between five ‘levels’ of provenance relevant to Claims encoded in biomedical knowledgebases. It is important to understand these levels, as they provide a framework for understanding and collecting EPC requirements in the forms that follow.

docs.title: Five Levels of Claim Provenance
docs.text:
1. Evidence Item Provenance: Describes how information items that may later be used as evidence for claims - such as experimental measurements or observations, derived statistical results, images, datasets, or prior claims - were originally generated, measured, extracted, curated, or otherwise produced - before they were used in evidence-based reasoning.

  2. Semantic Alignment Provenance: Describes how a human or AI agent understands a claim representation encountered in a source text or record and maps the concepts, relationships, and contextual information expressed in the source to the normalized concepts and relationships used in a structured target representation. For human agents, this is usually an implicit and undocumented cognitive task, but for AI agents, each step in this process (extraction, grounding, normalization) may be recorded to allow provenance tracing and accuracy checking.

  3. Knowledge Provenance: Describes the curation, interpretation, and reasoning processes involved in generating knowledge from evidence. This includes how information is selected, organized, evaluated, and interpreted as supporting or disputing a possible fact (Evidence Interpretation Provenance), and how multiple evidentiary arguments are subsequently combined and weighed to reach a final conclusion or assertion (Assertion Provenance).

  4. Encoding Provenance: Describes how a claim, evidence item, or other information artifact is expressed or serialized in a concrete representation so that it can be stored, discovered, exchanged, or consumed - for example, as an English sentence in a publication, a Biolink-compliant edge in a Neo4j knowledge graph, an object in a JSON document, or a row in a table.

  5. Retrieval Provenance: Describes downstream operations by which an existing encoded representation of knowledge or evidence is retrieved, transferred, transformed, normalized, aggregated, or otherwise passed between systems. It concerns the handling of an already encoded record, rather than the original generation of the knowledge or its initial serialization.

In short:

  • Evidence Item Provenance → how the raw informational inputs came to exist (independent of and prior to their future use as evidence)
  • Semantic Alignment Provenance → how one source’s representation of those inputs was understood and mapped into the concepts/relationships used by the target curator or system.
  • Knowledge Provenance → how those aligned inputs were interpreted as evidence (Evidence Interpretation Provenance) and ultimately reasoned over to make a claim (Assertion Provenance)
  • Encoding Provenance → how that claim was concretely serialized in a particular format or language
  • Retrieval Provenance → how that serialization was subsequently moved/transformed between data systems

docs.title: Illustrative Examples
docs.text:
Variant functional-impact interpretation

  1. Evidence Item Provenance: The Functional Genomics Laboratory at Redwood Biomedical Institute generated protein-activity measurements on March 12, 2026 using its FGX-17 cell-based assay protocol, and analyzed the results with BioQuant Analysis Suite v4.3.

  2. Semantic Alignment Provenance: n/a - in this case as the agent is a human and semantic alignment is an implicit cognitive process that needs no documentation.

  3. Knowledge Provenance: Dr. Elena Marquez and the Redwood Variant Interpretation Panel reviewed the in vitro and mouse-model results on March 20, 2026 using Functional Evidence Guideline v2.1, judged them to provide very strong support for the proposition that Variant X causes loss of function in Protein X, and approved that conclusion by panel consensus.

  4. Encoding Provenance: On March 21, 2026, the approved conclusion was encoded by the Redwood Variant Curation System as a structured variant-functional-impact assertion in JSON, linking the normalized variant identifier, protein identifier, evidence lines, and the panel's strength assessment.

  5. Retrieval Provenance: On March 25, 2026, the variant-evidence-ingest pipeline retrieved that JSON record, normalized the gene and variant identifiers to HGNC and VRS identifiers, transformed the record into the Translational Genomics KG schema, and loaded it as a graph assertion.

AI-assisted DisMech curation

  1. Evidence Item Provenance: Nguyen and colleagues generated measurements of CFTR chloride transport in cultured airway epithelial cells and reported the finding that CFTR dysfunction contributes to cystic-fibrosis pathophysiology, as described in several key passages and figures in a 2024 publication.

  2. Semantic Alignment Provenance: On May 10, 2026, the DisMech Curation Agent, running the mechanism-extraction-v3 workflow extracted and grounded the CFTR finding from a passage in this publication into a structured representation using the terms HGNC:1884 for CFTR and MONDO:0009061 for cystic fibrosis.

  3. Knowledge Provenance: On May 10, 2026, the DisMech Curation Agent, running model version MedCurator-3.2 interpreted the confidence in the semantic alignment, along with additional information about the location of the passage in the text, to determine the passage provides strong support for the claim that CFTR dysfunction contributes to cystic-fibrosis pathophysiology; curator Maya Patel reviewed and approved that interpretation on May 11.

  4. Encoding Provenance: After approval, the DisMech curation system serialized the mechanistic claim, supporting evidence items, evidence-line direction and strength, source references, and curation metadata into the corresponding DisMech YAML disorder record.

  5. Retrieval Provenance: On May 12, 2026, the dismech-to-monarch pipeline retrieved the YAML record, mapped its identifiers and relationships into the Monarch/Biolink representation, generated the corresponding knowledge-graph edge and provenance metadata, and loaded them into the Monarch KG.

docs.title: III. Populating Requirements Collection Forms
docs.text:
The bundled Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx workbook contains the following worksheets for collecting Evidence, Provenance, and Confidence (EPC) requirements for your project:

  1. Project Overview Form: reports on the scope and goals for your project

  2. Claim Type Form: enumerates the key kinds of claims your project reports (as context for understanding/enumerating the kinds of evidence and provenance that need to be represented)

  3. Claim Representation Structure Form: reports how claims are packaged or embedded in current project data, and what representation structures the project wants to preserve or support in future implementations

  4. Reified Claim Semantics Form: for projects requiring a reified Claim / Statement object, reports what semantic information that object must represent, including textual and structured proposition semantics, proposition placement, and qualifiers.

  5. Evidence Item Type Form: reports the kinds of information or artifacts the project currently represents, or wants to represent, as evidence for its claims

  6. Evidence Interpretation Form: reports what information about evidence interpretation and organization need to be captured in your project.

  7. Provenance Types Form: reports what types of provenance information you want to be able to capture about how information used as evidence is originally produced, how this evidence is organized and interpreted, and how claims are generated and encoded, and retrieved across systems.

Guidance and instructions for populating each form are provided below; complete the corresponding worksheet in Requirements_Collection_Forms.xlsx. Note that a separate set of requirements forms will be provided for Concept Definitions and related terminological statements that make up much of the content of ontologies and other terminological systems.

docs.title: General Requests for Populating Forms
docs.text:
• Use Key Concepts and Terminology: Respondents do not need to understand the SEPIO model. But please describe your project and data using terms from the “Key Concepts and Terminology” section above where possible. This will provide requirements with maximal clarity, consistency, and utility for data modelers.

  • Response conventions used across the forms:

  • Y = Yes, N = No, and M = Maybe / Needs discussion.
  • For F1/current-state questions, use only the current-state canonical sources and explicitly designated canonical companions named in the selected scope. If an allowed canonical artifact was directly inspected and the feature is demonstrably absent, N may be appropriate. If the evidence is incomplete or ambiguous, use M and explain why.
  • For F2/desired-state questions, use only sources included in the selected desired-state evidence set. Answer Y when there is affirmative project-specific support for the capability, including support documented as EXPLICIT_FUTURE_REQUIREMENT, EXISTING_PROJECT_CAPABILITY_NOT_IN_CANONICAL_EXPORT, or DOCUMENTED_MODEL_INTENT. Do not mark a feature desired merely because it seems useful.
  • “Desired in SEPIO-based Data” means desired support in the project’s future SEPIO-based representation; in this phase, these answers are used to determine what must be available in a project-level SEPIO Covering Model, not to define profile-level cardinality or requiredness constraints.
  • When F2 differs from F1, identify the supporting desired-state Source ID + source name/version and support type in Explanation / Considerations.
  • Agents should complete only respondent-facing fields. Do not edit content in the SEPIO Mapping Summary columns, and do not use those summaries to decide what the project's requirements should be.
  • Where a field provides a predefined set of permissible values, use the labels exactly as written rather than paraphrasing them. Multiple permitted values should be separated with semicolons. Free-text explanation and example fields provide context for mapping and validation, but should not by themselves be treated as deterministic mapping triggers unless a mapping rule explicitly says so.
  • Required vs. optional fields: Each respondent-facing question/field is marked as required (r) or optional (o). A few fields are marked (r*) - which indicates a conditional requirement that is described in the Dictionary for that form. Please complete optional fields whenever you reasonably can, as these details often provide important context for modeling and implementation. If an optional field cannot be completed or is not relevant, it is still helpful to say so briefly (for example, “n/a” “not available,” “not applicable,” or “not currently known”) and explain why when useful.
  • “Used in Current Data?” vs. “Desired in SEPIO-based Data?”: These columns intentionally use different evidence rules. F1 is a conservative description of the selected canonical source set. F2 is a maximal but evidence-supported statement of what the project should support under the selected desired-state scope. A current capability will often also be desired, unless evidence indicates that it is legacy, incidental, deprecated, or intentionally excluded. A capability absent from F1 may still be Y in F2 when allowed project evidence supports it. If desired-state intent remains uncertain, use M (Maybe / Needs discussion) and explain the uncertainty. All AI-generated F2 responses remain provisional until human review.

docs.title: 1. Project Overview Form (PO)
docs.text:
Purpose: Use this form to provide enough high-level context for the modeling group to understand your project, the kinds of knowledge it manages, and why evidence/provenance representation matters for your use cases. Keep responses concise; detailed requirements are collected in the later forms.

How to complete it: Describe the project according to the selected scope. Current-state descriptions should be grounded in the designated canonical source set; planned or desired capabilities should be drawn only from the allowed desired-state evidence set. AI agents should not infer requirements from what similar projects do. If something is uncertain, use “Unknown” or “Needs discussion.”

docs.title: Dictionary
docs.text:
• Project Name (r) is the name of the project or resource.

  • Representative(s) (r) identifies the people contributing requirements on its behalf.

  • Description (o) briefly summarizes the kinds and sources of knowledge the project contains, major workflows, and primary users/use cases.

  • Evidence/Provenance Needs (o): briefly explains why the project needs evidence and provenance represented and the main use cases those representations need to support. Provides high level context/use cases for the more specific requirements captured in the remaining forms.

docs.title: 2. Claim Type Form (CT)
docs.text:
Purpose: Use this form to identify the main kinds of claims for which your project needs evidence, provenance, or confidence represented. The goal is not necessarily to enumerate every predicate in your data, but to distinguish claim types where the underlying semantics or EPC requirements differ.

How to complete it: Define Claim Types using the categories of entities involved, the relationship asserted between them, and important qualifiers. See guidance below about the granularity at which to distinguish claim types when reporting them in the form. Use real project examples wherever possible. Claim Types with essentially the same evidence/provenance requirements may be grouped; separate them when their EPC requirements materially differ. Do not try to map these claims to SEPIO classes yet.

Guidance for AI agents: Do not create separate Claim Types simply because predicates differ if the project treats their evidence/provenance identically. Conversely, do not collapse claims that have materially different evidence or provenance requirements.

Additional Resources: See the Guidance below for How to Define/Distinguish Claim Types, as well as a Dictionary that defines and provides examples of values in each column/field in the form, as well as Populated Example of the form.

docs.title: How to Define / Distinguish Claim Types
docs.text:
A Claim Type is defined based on the category of things the claims connect (subject category, object category), and the type of relationship they assert to hold between them (relationship). Formally, Claim Type = Scat + Rel + Ocat. Examples:

  • Drug - treats - Disease

  • Disease - characterized by - Phenotype

  • Chemical - affects - Gene/GeneProduct

You can be as granular as you see fit in distinguishing types of claims defined in this way - depending on the number/diversity of claim types in your dataset, and the specific evidence and provenance requirements for each.

In selecting the subject and object categories to define a Claim Type, you can use very specific categories (e.g. “Drug”, “Pathological Process”), or broad categories / sets of categories (e.g. “Thing”, “Chemical Entity”, “Process”, “Gene Protein or Transcript”) as appropriate. But try NOT to lump claim types together if they have different evidence/provenance modeling requirements.

If your project deals in only a handful of claim types, it may be reasonable to list each separately even if they have the same types of E/P requirements.

If your project reports very many and diverse claim types, feel free to collapse them to a reasonable number by specifying many subject/object categories or relationship types in one Claim Type description - as long as the evidence and provenance modeling requirements for those claims are roughly the same.

For example, if your project uses NLP to extract several kinds of triples from text, and the EPC for all types of triples is the same, you can define your Claim Type as “Thing - related to - Thing”, or enumerate categories and say “Gene/Chemical - causes / interacts_with / affects - Gene/Chemical”.

The goal here is to distinguish as few Claim types as necessary to convey the diversity of knowledge in your datasets, while reporting areas where different types of claims may require different modeling.

docs.title: Dictionary
docs.text:
The data dictionary below describes the types of information to provide about each claim type (r= required, o = optional).

NOTE that the form includes two example entries for illustrative purposes. The second one shows a case where multiple subject and object types and predicates are grouped together into a single Claim Type entry for brevity/convenience - because claims of this type generally have the same kind and level of EPC metadata and modeling requirements. You can leave these examples in the form or delete and overwrite them.

  • Identifier (r): A numerical identifier of the form “C###” that serves as the project-level stable key for the Claim Type and can be used to reference that Claim Type from elsewhere in the requirements package. Claim Type identifiers are reference identifiers only; they are not Requirement IDs and do not directly trigger mappings to SEPIO model elements.

  • Examples: “C001”. “C002”, …

  • Descriptor (r): A short name by which we can reference the type of claim

  • Examples: “Causal Relationships”. “Disease Treatment” “Disease-Phenotype Association”, “Disease Pathophysiology”, “All Term-Level Relationships”.

  • Subject Categor(ies) (r): The types of entities that are subjects of this type of claim (semi-colon separated list if more than one)

  • Examples: “Entity”, “Gene; Protein; Transcript”, "Chemical Entity”, “Biological Process; Molecular Function”, “Drug; Small Molecule; Molecular Mixture”, “Disease; Phenotype”

  • Object Categor(ies) (r): The types of entities that are objects of this type of claim (semi-colon separated list if more than one)

  • Examples: “Entity”, “Gene; Protein; Transcript”, "Chemical Entity”, “Biological Process; Molecular Function”, “Drug; Small Molecule; Molecular Mixture”, “Disease; Phenotype”

  • Relationship Type(s) (r): The types of relationships asserted to hold between entities in the subject and object categories (semi-colon separated list if more than one)

  • Examples: “associated with”, “causes”, “treats”, “has phenotype”, “affects”, “acts upstream of”

  • Qualifying Information (o): types of additional information that refine, extend, or add context to the claim expressed by the subject–relationship–object structure.

  • Examples: “anatomical context”, “frequency; severity”, “disease context”, “relevant population”

  • Example Claim(s) from Your Data (r): One or more concrete examples of an instance of this type of claim, to illustrate the nature of the subjects and objects and relationships reported and how they are encoded/framed.

  • Examples:

    • “Cystic fibrosis has phenotype chronic respiratory infection“,

    • “The EGFR V600E variant predicts sensitivity to afatinib in patients with Lung Carcinoma”;
